solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so split the time interval there. Using $x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ from (i):
$$x(0) = 0, \qquad x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1 - 2\cos 0 = -1, \qquad x(\pi) = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 1 + 1 = 2$$
Distance for $0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $|-1 - 0| = 1$ m.

Distance for $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t \le \pi$: $|2 - (-1)| = 3$ m.

$\therefore$ Total distance $= 1 + 3 = 4$ m.
criteria: Splits at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (change of direction) and finds the displacements, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
An isosceles trapezium $ABCD$ is drawn with its vertices on a semicircle centre $O$ and diameter 20 cm. Perpendiculars $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn to meet the diameter $AD$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{568_q16_1}
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from rendered images | AUDIT audit-v1: ok

parts.label: i
parts.latex: If $EO=OF=\dfrac{x}{2}$, show that $BE=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400-x^2}$.

dif.r: one Pythagoras step with radius

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
Show that the area of the trapezium $ABCD$ is given by
$$A=\dfrac{1}{4}(x+20)\sqrt{400-x^2}.$$

dif.r: identify BC=x, trapezium area formula

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Hence find the length of $BC$ so that the area of the trapezium $ABCD$ is maximum.

dif.r: product rule with surd, solve, justify maximum

figures.cap: isosceles trapezium ABCD inscribed in semicircle centre O, diameter AD = 20 cm, perpendiculars BE and CF, EO = OF = x/2

solutions.latex:
$O$ is the centre and the diameter is $20$ cm, so $OB = 10$ cm (radius).

In right-angled triangle $BEO$ (right angle at $E$), $EO = \dfrac{x}{2}$. By Pythagoras:
$$\begin{aligned} BE^2 &= OB^2 - EO^2 \\ &= 100 - \dfrac{x^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{400 - x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BE = \dfrac{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2}$$
criteria: Uses $OB=10$ (radius) and Pythagoras in triangle $BEO$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$BCFE$ is a rectangle, so $BC = EF = EO + OF = x$. The parallel sides are $AD = 20$ and $BC = x$, and the height is $BE$.

Area of a trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(AD + BC)\times BE \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(20 + x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}(x + 20)\sqrt{400 - x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $BC=x$ and finds the height $BE$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Substitute into the trapezium area formula
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on $(x+20)\sqrt{400-x^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+20 & v&=\sqrt{400-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{400-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\sqrt{400 - x^2} + (x + 20)\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{400 - x^2 - x^2 - 20x}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-2(x^2 + 10x - 200)}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= -\dfrac{(x + 20)(x - 10)}{2\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$: since $0 < x < 20$, $x + 20 \neq 0$, so $x = 10$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} x &< 10 &&\text{(just below)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &> 0\\ x &> 10 &&\text{(just above)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &< 0\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ changes from $+$ to $-$, so $x = 10$ gives a maximum.

$\therefore$ Since $BC = x$, the area is maximised when $BC = 10$ cm. (The maximum area is $75\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$.)
criteria: Finds and simplifies $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A brand of rechargeable batteries provides power for 25 hours when first purchased fully charged.

After its first recharge it only provides power for a further 20 hours.

After its second recharge it only supplies power for 16 hours.

Each subsequent recharge after the second recharge results in the battery having 90% of its previous power available.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the available power after the third recharge?

dif.r: one multiplication, 90% of 16

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the total expected battery life in hours?

dif.r: limiting sum of tail plus first three terms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If the battery is discarded when its power level falls below one hour after recharging, how many recharge cycles would it undergo before being disposed of?

dif.r: log inequality on GP term with recharge-count offset

solutions.latex:
After the 3rd recharge it will be $90\%$ of $16$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} &= 16 \times 0.90 \\ &= 14.4 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

$$S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = \dfrac{14.4}{1 - 0.9} = 144 \text{ hours}$$
The battery will last
$$\begin{aligned} &= 25 + 20 + 16 + 144 \\ &= 205 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$T_n < 1$, $n = ?$
$$\begin{aligned} 14.4 \times 0.9^{n-1} &< 1 \\ 0.9^{n-1} &< \dfrac{1}{14.4} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} (n-1)\log 0.9 &< \log\left(\dfrac{1}{14.4}\right) \\ n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{1}{14.4}\right)}{\log 0.9} \\ n &> 25.3152 + 1 \\ n &> 26.3152 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} n &= 27 + 2 \text{ previous charges} \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The power is less than $1$ hour after the $29^{\text{th}}$ charge.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinates, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $\tan x=2$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: equate curves, divide by cos x

req: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities
A.note: equate curves then tan=sin/cos; no skill for the identity itself

B.note: Only step is sin x = 2cos x -> tan x = 2 (tan = sin/cos, Y11-098); no skill names this identity; Reciprocal trigonometric ratios is the only skill listing Y11-098

Reciprocal trigonometric ratios.reason: Only tan x = sin x / cos x is used; no sec, cosec or cot.

Graphical solution of equations and ineq.reason: Intersections are found algebraically (sin x = 2cos x gives tan x = 2), not read from the graph.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence show in simplest exact form that the region enclosed by the two curves has area $2\sqrt{5}$ square units.

dif.r: non-exact limits alpha, pi+alpha; triangle for sin, cos alpha

figures.cap: graphs of y = sin x and y = 2cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π with enclosed region shaded

solutions.latex:
At points of intersection, $\sin x=2\cos x$.

$\therefore\ \tan x=2$, $0\le x\le 2\pi$

meta.top_criterion_original: Explains why the $x$ coordinates of intersection points satisfy $\tan x=2$

solutions.latex:
Area is given by
$$A=\int_\alpha^{\pi+\alpha}(\sin x-2\cos x)\,dx$$
where $0<\alpha<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan\alpha=2$.

[Right triangle with opposite 2, adjacent 1, hypotenuse $\sqrt{5}$.]
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left[-\cos x-2\sin x\right]_\alpha^{\pi+\alpha}\\ &=-\{\cos(\pi+\alpha)-\cos\alpha\}-2[\sin(\pi+\alpha)-\sin\alpha]\\ &=2\cos\alpha+4\sin\alpha\\ &=2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}$$
Area enclosed by the two curves is $2\sqrt{5}$ sq. units.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. obtains the anti-derivative and evaluates in terms of $\alpha$, $\beta$
Some progress, e.g. writes the definite integral and anti-derivative is partially correct

questions.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.
questions.review_note: scan transcription (parse_path=scan)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $v=1-2e^{-t}$ and $x=t+2e^{-t}$.

dif.r: integrate twice with initial conditions, sign of v

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form when and where the particle is at rest.

dif.r: v=0 exponential with logs, then exact x

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\ln 8$ seconds of its motion.

dif.r: distance over turning point with exact log values

solutions.latex:
$a=2e^{-t}$

$v=-2e^{-t}+c$

When $t=0$, $v=-1$, so $-1=-2+c$.

$\therefore\ c=1$

$\therefore\ v=1-2e^{-t}$

$x=t+2e^{-t}+d$

When $t=0$, $x=2$, so $2=2+d$.

$\therefore\ d=0$

$\therefore\ x=t+2e^{-t}$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds $v$ in terms of $t$

meta.top_criterion_original: Uses integration to find required expressions for both $v$ and $x$ in terms of $t$

solutions.latex:
When $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ e^t&=2\\ \therefore\ t&=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=t+2e^{-t}\\ &=\ln 2+2\times\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=1+\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
At rest $(1+\ln 2)$ m to the right of $O$ at time $\ln 2$ seconds.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds time when particle at rest

meta.top_criterion_original: Finds time and position when particle at rest

solutions.latex:
When $t=\ln 8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\ln 8+2e^{\ln\frac{1}{8}}\\ &=3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Hence in the first $\ln 8$ seconds:

the particle travels left $2-(1+\ln 2)$ metres,

then is instantaneously at rest before moving off to the right (since $a>0$),

travelling a further $\left(3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-(1+\ln 2)$ metres.

Required distance is $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\ln 2\right)$ metres.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds simplified expression for $x$ when $t=\ln 8$

meta.top_criterion_original: Adds distances travelled left and right in the first $\ln 8$ seconds

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ .

dif.r: single quotient rule, given answer

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Use the result in part (a) to show that $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx=\ln 2-1$ .

dif.r: recognise integrand as f'/f of (a), log of logs

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)&=\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot x-(\ln x)\cdot 1}{x^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Applies an appropriate rule for differentiation

solutions.latex:
If $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, then
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}&=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\times\dfrac{x}{\ln x}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx&=\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)\right]_e^{e^2}\\ &=\left[\ln(\ln x)-\ln x\right]_e^{e^2}\\ &=\ln 2-\ln 1-(2-1)\\ &=\ln 2-1\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. obtains anti-derivative and partially evaluates

meta.top_criterion_original: Recognises integration pattern to obtain anti-derivative as a log function then evaluates
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: integrand in the evaluation line read $\dfrac{1-x}{x\ln x}$.

parts.latex: The graph of the function $y=2^x$ is shown below. \exfigure{1346_q5_1} What is the area bounded by the curve $y=2^x$ and the $y$-axis from $y=1$ to $y=4$?

dif.r: area against y-axis via rectangle complement, base-2 exponential

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: graph of y=2^x through (0,1) and (2,4)

solutions.latex:
The region is between the curve and the $y$-axis, from $y = 1$ ($x = 0$) to $y = 4$ ($x = 2$).

It is the rectangle $0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le 4$ minus the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\times 4 - \int_0^2 2^x\,dx \\ &= 8 - \left[\dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2}\right]_0^2 \\ &= 8 - \dfrac{4 - 1}{\ln 2} \\ &= 8 - \dfrac{3}{\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the distance between the maximum and minimum:
$$\text{Amplitude} = \dfrac{5 - (-1)}{2} = 3$$
The period of $\cos 6x$ is
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
For the phase, factor the $6$ out of the angle:
$$6x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 6\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$$
so the phase is $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

A bricklayer is building a wall in the shape of a triangle where each row contains 3 bricks less than the row immediately below.

The bottom row of the wall contains 150 bricks.

If it takes the bricklayer 10 seconds to install each brick, how many rows of the wall will be completed after 6 hours?

dif.r: MCQ: unit conversion then quadratic in n from S_n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
In 6 hours the bricklayer lays
$$\dfrac{6\times 60\times 60}{10} = 2160 \text{ bricks}$$
The rows form an arithmetic series with $a = 150$ and $d = -3$:
$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times 150 + (n-1)(-3)\big) = \dfrac{n}{2}(303 - 3n)$$
$$\begin{aligned} S_{17} &= \dfrac{17}{2}(303 - 51) = 2142 \le 2160 \\ S_{18} &= 9(303 - 54) = 2241 > 2160 \end{aligned}$$
So 17 rows are completed.

parts.latex: For what values of $b$ is the function $y=x^4+bx^3-3x^2$ concave up and decreasing at the point where $x=1$?

dif.r: two derivative inequalities in parameter b

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 + 3bx^2 - 6x \\ y'' &= 12x^2 + 6bx - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Decreasing at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 + 3b - 6 &< 0 \\ b &< \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Concave up at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12 + 6b - 6 &> 0 \\ b &> -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1 < b < \dfrac{2}{3}, \text{ that is } b \in \left(-1, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$$

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

figures.cap: option A: option A: x-t graph starting at x=2, local min near t=1, local max near t=2, then decreasing
option B: option B: x-t graph starting at x=-2, local max near t=1, local min near t=2, then increasing
option C: option C: concave-down parabola starting at x=-2 crossing t-axis at t=1 and t=2
option D: option D: decreasing straight line crossing t-axis between 1 and 2

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

parts.latex: The following table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$. \extable{Tp70_1} Given that $E(X)=2.08$, find the values of $p$ and $q$.

dif.r: sum to 1 and E(X) give simultaneous equations

solutions.latex:
Sum of probabilities equals 1:
$$\begin{aligned}0.05+p+p+q+0.01&=1\\ 2p+q&=0.94\quad(1)\end{aligned}$$
$E(X)=2.08$:
$$\begin{aligned}(0\times 0.05)+(1\times p)+(2\times p)+(3\times q)+(4\times 0.01)&=2.08\\ 3p+3q&=2.04\\ p+q&=0.68\quad(2)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Ashford ($A$), Brookdale ($B$) and Carlton ($C$) are three country towns.

dif.r: components to AB, several angle chases, sine rule twice, sum

figures.cap: triangle ABC with north arrows at A, B, C; AD = 85 km east, DB = 33 km north; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$AB=\sqrt{85^2+33^2}=91.181\ldots$$
$$\text{Angle }DAB=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{33}{85}\right)=21^\circ 13'$$
$$\text{Angle }CAB=90^\circ-26^\circ-21^\circ 13'=42^\circ 47'$$
$$\text{Angle }ACB=(360^\circ-321^\circ)+26^\circ=65^\circ\quad\text{(angles at a point and alternate angles)}$$
$$\text{Angle }ABC=180^\circ-65^\circ-42^\circ 47'=72^\circ 13'\quad\text{(angle sum of triangle }ABC\text{)}$$
By the sine rule:
$$AC=\dfrac{\sin 72^\circ 13'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=95.800$$
$$BC=\dfrac{\sin 42^\circ 47'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=68.335$$
Alternatively, $BC$ may be determined using the cosine rule:
$$BC=\sqrt{91.181^2+95.800^2-2\times 91.181\times 95.800\times\cos 42^\circ 47'}=68.335$$
Perimeter of triangle $ABC$:
$$91.181+95.800+68.335=255.316$$
The total distance travelled is 255 km, correct to the nearest kilometre.

Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x-2}}$.

Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=\sqrt{x-2}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{4x}{2\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Solve $f'(x)=0$ to find any stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{x-2}-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}&=0\\ 4(x-2)-2x&=0\\ 4x-8-2x&=0\\ 2x&=8\end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=4$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{4\times 4}{\sqrt{4-2}}=8\sqrt{2}$$
A stationary point exists at $(4,8\sqrt{2})$.

Using a table of gradients to determine the nature of the stationary point:

\extable{Ts71_1}

Hence the stationary point is a local minimum.

parts.latex:
The rate of fuel consumption of a particular vehicle may be modelled by the formula

$$R=5+4e^{-0.5t},$$

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

In the first hour of travel, the vehicle consumed 25 litres of fuel.

Determine the amount of fuel consumed after 4 hours of travel, correct to the nearest litre.

dif.r: integrate rate, C from F(1)=25 not t=0

solutions.latex:
The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$
At time $t=1$, the vehicle has consumed 25 litres of fuel since the start of the journey.

Finding the constant of integration, $c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25 &= 5(1)-8e^{-0.5(1)}+c \\ 20 &= -8e^{-0.5}+c \\ c &= 20+8e^{-0.5} \end{aligned}$$
At time $t=4$, the amount of fuel the vehicle consumed is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F &= 5(4)-8e^{-0.5(4)}+20+8e^{-0.5} \\ &= 43.7695\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ After 4 hours of travel, the vehicle has consumed 44 litres of fuel.
criteria: Finds the value of the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Correctly integrates expression representing rate of fuel consumption, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graph below shows the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4$.

Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$, determine how much the Trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve. \exfigure{1346_q30_1}

dif.r: two-strip trapezoidal plus exact cubic integral, subtract

figures.cap: curve y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4 with trapezium chords; heights 4 at x=0, 5.125 at x=1.5, 13 at x=3

solutions.latex:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$
$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$
$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.
criteria: Finds the area using integration and the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$

Maximise the volume by maximising the area of the cross-section, since the depth is constant.

Let $A$ be the area of the cross-section of the tent.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5x\times h \\ &= 5xy+\dfrac{5xh}{2} \end{aligned}$$
From parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5x(10-4x)+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-20x^2+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Determine the stationary point and its nature:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x &= 0 \\ \left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x &= 25 \\ x &= 25\div\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right) \\ &= 2.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)=-24.387\ldots<0$$

parts.latex:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^3-2x$ and $y=x^2$. \exfigure{1346_q33_1} The graphs intersect at $A$, $B$ and the origin, $O$.

By finding the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{37}{12}$.

dif.r: cubic and parabola, three intersections, two regions with swap

figures.cap: graphs of y=x^3-2x and y=x^2 intersecting at A, O, B with the two enclosed regions shaded

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up a sum of two integrals, including correct bounds for each integral, and attempts to find the area between the two curves, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos(90^\circ-\theta)}(1+\tan^2\theta)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}[1+\tan^2(90^\circ-\theta)] \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}(1+\cot^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
It is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx$.

dif.r: unscaffolded spotting of f'/f from given derivative

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx \\ &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$$
and
$$\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$$

$$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$
Hence,
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c \\ &= \ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes substantial progress toward correct solution, such as recognising that the integral is in the form $\displaystyle \int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and hence will result in a log function by using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A function $f(x)$ is given such that: $$\int_{-k}^{k} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx.$$ Which of the following could be a possible function for $f(x)$?

dif.r: even-function property, identify the even option

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Splitting the integral at $0$:
$$\int_{-k}^{k} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-k}^{0} f(x)\,dx + \int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx$$
So the condition says $\displaystyle\int_{-k}^{0} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{k} f(x)\,dx$: the area on the left of the $y$-axis equals the area on the right. This is true when $f$ is even (its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis).

$\sin 2x$, $\tan 2x$ and $\operatorname{cosec} 2x$ are odd functions; $\cos 2x$ is even, since $\cos(-2x)=\cos 2x$.

$\therefore$ $f(x)=\cos 2x$.

parts.latex: A die is rolled twice. Let events $X$ and $Y$ be: $$X=\{\text{The first roll is a }'1'\}$$ $$Y=\{\text{Sum of two rolls is }'7'\}$$ Which of the following statements is true?

dif.r: test independence via product over 36 outcomes

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

options.label: C
options.latex: Event $X$ is a subset of event $Y$.

options.label: D
options.latex: The probabilities of events $X$ and $Y$ are different.

solutions.latex:
There are $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$P(X)=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac16$$
A sum of $7$ comes from $(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)$, so
$$P(Y)=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac16$$
Both events happen only for $(1,6)$, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\cap Y)&=\dfrac{1}{36}\\ &=\dfrac16\times\dfrac16\\ &=P(X)\times P(Y) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

($X$ and $Y$ can both happen, so they are not mutually exclusive; $X$ is not a subset of $Y$; $P(X)=P(Y)$.)

parts.latex: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$. In which domain is the function decreasing and concave down?

dif.r: two derivative sign conditions on cubic

solutions.latex:
Decreasing: $f'(x)<0$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2-6x\\ &=3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)<0$ for $0<x<2$.

Concave down: $f''(x)<0$
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
$f''(x)<0$ for $x<1$.

Both hold for $0<x<1$.

$\therefore$ The function is decreasing and concave down on $(0,1)$.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=\ln(x-1)$, what is the domain of the composite function $f(g(x))$?

dif.r: nested condition ln(x-1)>=0 plus log domain

solutions.latex:
$$f(g(x))=\sqrt{\ln(x-1)}$$
Conditions:

$\ln(x-1)$ is defined: $x-1>0$, so $x>1$.

The square root needs a non-negative input: $\ln(x-1)\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln(x-1)&\ge 0\\ x-1&\ge 1 \quad(\text{since } \ln 1=0 \text{ and } \ln \text{ is increasing})\\ x&\ge 2 \end{aligned}$$
$x\ge2$ also satisfies $x>1$.

$\therefore$ Domain: $[2,\infty)$

parts.latex: A probability density function is given below: $$f(x)=\begin{cases} x-1, & 1\le x\le a \\ 0, & else\ where \end{cases}$$ Which one of the following, is the correct way to find the value of $'a'$?

dif.r: triangle area equals 1 gives quadratic in a

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^a (x-1)\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_1^a &= 1 \\ \left(\dfrac{a^2}{2}-a\right)-\left(\dfrac12-1\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{a^2}{2}-a-\dfrac12 &= 0 \\ a^2-2a-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The roots are
$$a=1\pm\sqrt2$$
The domain is $1\le x\le a$, so $a>1$. The smaller root $1-\sqrt2$ is negative, so $a$ is the larger root, $a=1+\sqrt2$.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function is given by: $f'(x)=e^x\sin x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate and simplify $g(x)=e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x$.

dif.r: two product rules, simplify to 2e^x sin x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, find $f(x)$ if it is known that $f(\pi)=\dfrac{e^{\pi}}{2}$.

dif.r: hence primitive with factor 1/2, constant from f(pi)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on each term. For $e^x\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
For $e^x\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= \sin x\cdot e^x+e^x\cos x-[\cos x\cdot e^x+e^x(-\sin x)] \\ &= e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x-e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x \\ &= 2e^x\sin x \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Some students made mistake with the negative sign.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \int f'(x)\,dx &= \int e^x\sin x\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\int2e^x\sin x\,dx \end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=\dfrac12[e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x]+C$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(\pi) &= \dfrac12(e^\pi\sin\pi-e^\pi\cos\pi)+C \\ \dfrac{e^\pi}{2} &= \dfrac12(0+e^\pi)+C \\ C &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac12(e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x)$$

questions.stem: Given the series $1\dfrac{1}{3}+2\dfrac{1}{9}+4\dfrac{1}{27}+8\dfrac{1}{81}\ \ldots$ . Find the expression of the:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: general term.

dif.r: split mixed numbers into two GPs; general term

parts.label: b
parts.latex: sum.

dif.r: sum of two GPs once split

solutions.latex:
Each term is a whole number plus a fraction:
$$1+\dfrac13,\quad 2+\dfrac19,\quad 4+\dfrac1{27},\quad 8+\dfrac1{81},\ \ldots$$
The whole numbers $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ form a GP with $a_1=1$, $r_1=2$.

The fractions $\dfrac13,\dfrac19,\dfrac1{27},\dfrac1{81},\ldots$ form a second GP with $a_2=\dfrac13$, $r_2=\dfrac13$.

So the general term is the sum of the general terms of the two GPs:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a_1r_1^{n-1}+a_2r_2^{n-1} \\ &= 1(2)^{n-1}+\dfrac13\left(\dfrac13\right)^{n-1} \\ &= 2^{n-1}+\dfrac{1}{3^n} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises two separate geometric progressions, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}+\dfrac{a_2(1-r^n)}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1(2^n-1)}{2-1}+\dfrac{\frac13\left(1-\frac{1}{3^n}\right)}{1-\frac13} \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_n=2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \text{ or } \dfrac{2^{n+1}-3^{-n}-1}{2}$$

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Let the equation of a curve be $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{e^x+1}$. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $x=1$ in general form.

dif.r: quotient rule, normal, messy general form with (e+1)^3

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(e^x+1)-e^xx}{(e^x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)+1}{(e^x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(1)=\dfrac{1}{(e+1)^2}$$
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-(e+1)^2$$
$$f(1)=\dfrac{1}{e+1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(x-1) \\ (e+1)y-1 &= -(e+1)^3x+(e+1)^3 \\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-(1+(e+1)^3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $y=mx+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(1)+c \\ c &= \dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-(e+1)^2x+\dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2$$
$$\therefore\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-1-(e+1)^3=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $f(x)=\ln(\tan^2 x)$ and simplify your answers in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

dif.r: log laws on tan^2, combine with Pythagorean identity

A.note: Log laws first is the model method but chain rule alone works

B.note: Solution splits ln(sin^2 x / cos^2 x) with log laws; direct chain rule on ln(tan^2 x) is an alternative.

Logarithm laws in differentiation.reason: Expanding with log laws first is one method; the chain rule directly on ln(tan^2 x) also works.

Chain rule.reason: Differentiating ln sin^2 x (or ln tan^2 x) needs the chain rule with a non-linear inner function.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln(\tan^2x) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}\right) \\ &= \ln\sin^2x-\ln\cos^2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{2\cos x}{\sin x}+\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{2\cos^2x+2\sin^2x}{\sin x\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{2(\cos^2x+\sin^2x)}{\sin x\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin x\cos x} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A right circular cone has height, $H$, and a base of radius $R$. A square prism is inscribed in the cone so that the base of the prism is on the cone's base. The prism has height, $h$, and a square base of side length $x$. \exfigure{1365_q30_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By using similar triangles, show that $x=2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)$.

dif.r: similar triangles set-up

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the height of the prism, in terms of $H$, that will maximise the volume of the prism.

dif.r: parametric volume maximisation in h, justify max

figures.cap: cone with inscribed square prism, and cross-section showing H and R

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, the triangle above the prism (height $H-h$, base $\dfrac{x}{2}$) is similar to the whole right-angled triangle (height $H$, base $R$): common angle at the apex, both right-angled (equiangular).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{H-h}{H} &= \dfrac{\frac{x}{2}}{R} \\ x &= 2R\left(\dfrac{H-h}{H}\right) \\ &= 2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Be careful that the correct ratio is used.
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct ratio. Do NOT need any geometric reasoning
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the question named the radius $r$ but part (a) and this working use $R$; the question now says $R$.
meta.explained: Similar-triangle reasoning explained in words (owner request, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= x^2h \\ &= \left(2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\right)^2h \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)^2 \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{H}+\dfrac{h^2}{H^2}\right) \\ &= 4R^2h-\dfrac{8R^2h^2}{H}+\dfrac{4R^2h^3}{H^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dh}=4R^2-\dfrac{16R^2h}{H}+\dfrac{12R^2h^2}{H^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{4h}{H}+\dfrac{3h^2}{H^2}\right) &= 0 \\ 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{3h}{H}\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=H \text{ or } h=\dfrac{H}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2h}{H^2}$$
At $h=H$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=\dfrac{8R^2}{H}>0$$
$\therefore$ concave up.

At $h=\dfrac{H}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2} &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2(\frac{H}{3})}{H^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{8R^2}{H} \\ &= -\dfrac{8R^2}{H}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave down.

$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{H}{3}$ is a maximum.
criteria: Finds $V$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: It is easier to differentiate when expanded.

parts.latex:
A ten-sided die has faces numbered 1 to 10.

The die is constructed so that the probability of obtaining the number 1 is greater than the probability of obtaining any of the other numbers. The numbers 2 to 10 are equally likely to occur.

When the die is rolled 153 times, a 1 is obtained 72 times.

By using the relative frequency of rolling a 1, which of the following is the best estimate for the probability of rolling a 10?

dif.r: share remaining relative frequency equally across nine faces

solutions.latex:
Using relative frequency:
$$P(1)\approx\dfrac{72}{153}=\dfrac{8}{17}$$
The remaining probability is shared equally by the 9 numbers 2 to 10:
$$\begin{aligned} P(10) &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left(1-\dfrac{8}{17}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\times\dfrac{9}{17} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{17} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $f'(1)=2$, so over the short interval from $x=1$ to $x=1.1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(1.1) &\approx f(1)+0.1\times f'(1) \\ &= 6+0.1\times 2 \\ &= 6.2 \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: chain rule e^x f'(e^x)=0; only positive stationary x count

A.note: Count stationary points of f(e^x) via chain rule.

B.note: Stationary points of f(e^x) via chain rule, using e^x>0 and the given graph of f.

figures.cap: quartic-like graph of y=f(x) with three stationary points

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}f\left(e^x\right)=e^x f'\left(e^x\right)$$
Since $e^x>0$, this is zero only when $f'\left(e^x\right)=0$, that is, when $e^x$ equals the $x$-coordinate of a stationary point of $f$.

$e^x$ takes only positive values.

Of the three stationary points of $f$, two have positive $x$-coordinates (near $x=1$ and $x=2$) and one has a negative $x$-coordinate.

So $y=f\left(e^x\right)$ has 2 stationary points.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=5x^3-\dfrac{2}{x^2}-9$ at the point $(1,-6)$.

dif.r: negative index derivative then point-gradient tangent

solutions.latex:
Writing with negative indices and differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 5x^3-\dfrac{2}{x^2}-9 \\ y &= 5x^3-2x^{-2}-9 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 15x^2+4x^{-3} \\ y' &= 15x^2+\dfrac{4}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 15(1)+\dfrac{4}{(1)} \\ y' &= 19 \end{aligned}$$
Using the point–gradient form:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1) \\ y+6 &= 19(x-1) \\ y+6 &= 19x-19 \\ y &= 19x-25 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{e^x}$.

solutions.latex:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{e^x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{2xe^x-x^2e^x}{e^{2x}}\\ &= \dfrac{xe^x(2-x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^x>0$:
$$x=0 \text{ or } x=2$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= 0\\ f(2) &= \dfrac{4}{e^2}=0.541\ldots\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts602_1}
$$\therefore\ \text{Minimum at } (0,0) \text{ and maximum at } \left(2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The gradients of $y=e\ln x$ and $y=ax^2+c$ at point of intersection are both equal to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(e\ln x) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{e}{x} &= 1 \\ x &= e \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ y=e$, so $y=ax^2+c$ has gradient of 1 at point $(e,e)$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ax^2+c\right]=2ax$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax &= 1 \quad\text{at } x=e \\ 2a\cdot e &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
and $y=ax^2+c=e$ at $x=e$:
$$\begin{aligned} e &= \dfrac{1}{2e}\cdot e^2+c \\ e &= \dfrac{e}{2}+c \\ c &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2e},\ c=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x)=x\sin x.$$

dif.r: product rule show-that, simplify to x sin x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx$.

dif.r: use primitive from (a), evaluate cos(2025 pi)

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The regions bounded by the $x$-axis and the graph of $y=x\sin x$ for $x\ge 0$ are shown.

\exfigure{1630_q25_1}

Let $A_n=\displaystyle\int_{(n-1)\pi}^{n\pi}x\sin x\,dx$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

It can be shown that $\left|A_n\right|=(2n-1)\pi$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find the exact total area of the regions bounded by the curve $y=x\sin x$, and the $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=2025\pi$.

dif.r: area vs signed integral, sum absolute areas as AP

figures.cap: graph of y=x sin x for 0<=x<=4pi with regions shaded

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $x\cos x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x) &= \cos x-\left[x\times(-\sin x)+\cos x\right] \\ &= \cos x+x\sin x-\cos x \\ &= x\sin x \quad\text{as required} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\sin x-x\cos x$ is a primitive of $x\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx &= \Big[\sin x-x\cos x\Big]_0^{2025\pi} \\ &= (\sin 2025\pi-2025\pi\cos 2025\pi)-(0) \\ &= 0-2025\pi\times(-1) \\ &= 2025\pi \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses part (a) to rewrite the definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total area is $|A_1|+|A_2|+\cdots+|A_{2025}|$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Exact area of regions} &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+(2\times 2025-1)\pi \\ &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+4049\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is an arithmetic series with $a=\pi$, $d=2\pi$, $n=2025$ and $l=4049\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}(a+l) \\ S_n &= \dfrac{2025}{2}(\pi+4049\pi) \\ &= 2025\times 2025\times\pi \\ &= (2025)^2\pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sums an arithmetic sequence, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A piece of wire is 100 cm long. Some of the wire is to be used to make a circle of radius $r$ cm. The remainder of the wire is used to make an equilateral triangle of side length $x$ cm.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the combined area of the circle and equilateral triangle is given by

$$A(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right).$$

dif.r: wire split: r from 2pi r+3x=100, two area formulas

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By considering the quadratic function in part (a), show that the maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all the wire is used for the circle.

dif.r: concave-up quadratic so maximum at endpoint; compare endpoints

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of A(x) on its domain (endpoint labelled 33 1/2 in source)

solutions.latex:
The circumference of the circle and the perimeter of the triangle add to 100 cm:
$$2\pi r+3x=100$$
$$r=\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}$$
Area of circle $\pi r^2$; area of the equilateral triangle $\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} A(x) &= \text{Area of circle}+\text{area of equilateral triangle} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \pi\left(\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}\right)^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}\,x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $r$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$A(x)$ is a quadratic with positive coefficient of $x^2$, so $A$ has a minimum stationary point.

The maximum will therefore occur at an endpoint of the domain.

When $x=0$ (all wire used for the circle):
$$r=\dfrac{50}{\pi}$$
$$\text{Area}=\pi r^2=\dfrac{50^2}{\pi}\approx 796$$
When $r=0$ (all wire used for the triangle):
$$x=33\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times 33.333^2\approx 481$$
\exfigure{1630_q26_s1}

$\therefore$ The maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all wire is used for the circle.
criteria: Finds the value of $A$ at an endpoint, or equivalent merit
Identifies that the quadratic will have a minimum turning point, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The shaded region is bounded by the graph $y=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x$, the coordinate axes and $x=2$.

\exfigure{1630_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the shaded region.

dif.r: direct trapezoidal formula, two strips

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the exact area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{3}{4\ln 2}$.

dif.r: a^x primitive with base 1/2, exact evaluation

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Using your answers from part (a) and part (b), deduce $e<2\sqrt{2}$.

dif.r: concavity gives overestimate, then log manipulation to inequality

figures.cap: shaded region under y=(1/2)^x from x=0 to x=2

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule use $n=2$ strips:
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$$
so $x_0=0$, $x_1=1$, $x_2=2$, with
$$f(0)=1, \quad f(1)=\dfrac{1}{2}, \quad f(2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)\right]\Big\} \\ &= \dfrac{2-0}{2\times 2}\left\{1+\dfrac{1}{4}+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{4}+1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^0}{\ln\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-\frac{3}{4}}{-\ln 2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides the correct antiderivative of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The function is concave up, so the exact value is less than the trapezoidal approximation:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} &< \dfrac{9}{8} \\ 24 &< 36\ln 2 \\ 2 &< 3\ln 2 \\ 2 &< \ln 8 \\ e^2 &< 8 \\ e &< \sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ e<2\sqrt{2}$$
criteria: Provides correct initial inequality, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A farmer wants to use a straight fence to divide a circular paddock of radius 10 metres into two segments. The smaller segment is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the paddock and is shaded in the diagram. The fence subtends an angle of $\theta$ radians at the centre of the circle as shown.

\exfigure{1630_q28_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\theta=\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

dif.r: set up segment area equal to quarter circle, rearrange

parts.label: b

dif.r: must see intersection with y=theta on graph, then arc length

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: circle radius 10 m with shaded minor segment, angle theta at centre; NOT TO SCALE
grid graph of y=sin(theta)+pi/2 for 0<=theta<=7.3
solution sketch: intersection of y=theta and y=sin(theta)+pi/2

solutions.latex:
Area of shaded segment $=$ area of sector $-$ area of triangle, and the segment is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the paddock:
$$\text{area of sector}-\text{area of triangle}=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\text{area of circle}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\sin\theta &= \dfrac{10^2\pi}{4} \\ 50\theta-50\sin\theta &= 25\pi \\ 50(\theta-\sin\theta) &= 25\pi \\ \theta-\sin\theta &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ \theta &= \sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides a correct expression relating the areas in the diagram, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1630_q28_s1}

From part (a), $\theta=\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\theta$ is the $\theta$-coordinate of the point of intersection of $y=\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

From the graph:
$$\theta\approx 2.3 \text{ radians}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Arc length} &= r\theta \\ &= 10\times 2.3\\ &= 23 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $\theta$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The point $T$ is the peak of a mountain and the point $O$ is directly below the mountain's peak. The point $Y$ is due east of $O$ and the angle of elevation of $T$ from $Y$ is $60^\circ$. The point $F$ is 4 km south-west of $Y$. The points $O$, $Y$ and $F$ are on level ground. The angle of elevation of $T$ from $F$ is $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1630_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Let the height of the mountain be $h$.

Show that $OY=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $h$, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the bearing of point $O$ from point $F$, correct to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

figures.cap: 3D diagram: mountain TO height h, Y east of O with elevation 60 deg, F 4 km from Y with elevation 45 deg; NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: 30-60-90 triangle
solution sketch: triangle FOY with theta at F

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle TYO$, right-angled at $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{OY} \\ \therefore\ OY &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The exact value $\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ comes from the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle:

\exfigure{1630_q29_s1}

In $\triangle TFO$, $\angle TFO=45^\circ$, $\angle TOF=90^\circ$

$\therefore\ \angle OTF=45^\circ$

$\therefore\ \triangle TFO$ is isosceles and $OF=h$

In $\triangle FOY$, $\angle OYF=45^\circ$ ($F$ is south-west of $Y$ and $O$ is due west of $Y$). By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= \left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+4^2-2\times 4\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 45^\circ \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+16-\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{2h^2}{3}+\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}}-16=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\pm\sqrt{\frac{64}{6}+4\times\frac{2}{3}\times 16}}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 3.03 \quad\text{since } h>0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds a quadratic expression in $h$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to use the cosine rule to find a value for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1630_q29_s2}

In $\triangle FOY$, let $\theta=\angle OFY$. By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}} &= \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{h} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}} \\ \theta &= 24.09\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 24^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$Y$ is on a bearing of $045^\circ$ from $F$, and $O$ is $\theta$ further anticlockwise:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 45^\circ-24^\circ \\ &\approx 021^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to find the bearing, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The parabola with equation $y=(x-1)(x-5)$ is translated both horizontally to the right and vertically up by $k$ units, where $k$ is positive.

The translated parabola passes through the point $(6,11)$.

Find the value of $k$.

dif.r: apply two translations correctly, substitute point, solve quadratic in k

solutions.latex:
Translating right by $k$ and up by $k$: replace $x$ with $x-k$ and $y$ with $y-k$. Then substitute the point $(6,11)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-k &= (x-k-1)(x-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (6-k-1)(6-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (5-k)(1-k) \\ 11-k &= 5-6k+k^2 \\ k^2-5k-6 &= 0 \\ (k-6)(k+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$k$ is positive, so
$$k=6$$
criteria: Obtains a quadratic in $k$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $x-k$ and $y-k$ into equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The equation $\cos px=\dfrac{1}{2}$ has 2 solutions where $0\le x\le 2\pi$ and $p>0$.

Find all possible values of $p$.

dif.r: parameter range via dilation of solutions; endpoint inclusion reasoning

figures.cap: solution sketch: y=cos x with cos x=1/2
solution sketch: y=cos px, lowest p
solution sketch: y=cos px, highest p

solutions.latex:
Solve $\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $x\ge 0$ first:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$
\exfigure{1630_q31_s1}

$y=\cos px$ is a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{p}$, so its solutions are these values multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{p}$.

Lowest value of $p$ to get 2 solutions (second solution at $x=2\pi$):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s2}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{5\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Highest value of $p$ (at this value a third solution appears at $x=2\pi$, so it is excluded):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s3}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{7\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5}{6}\le p<\dfrac{7}{6}$$

dif.r: read intercepts and end behaviour

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

figures.cap: cubic with x-intercepts -4, 1 and 3

solutions.latex:
The $x$-intercepts are $-4$, $1$ and $3$, so $f(x)=k(x+4)(x-1)(x-3)$.

As $x \to \infty$, $y \to \infty$ (the graph rises to the right), so the leading coefficient is positive: $k>0$.
$$f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x+4)$$

parts.latex:
A study of Year 8 students shows that there is a positive correlation between the number of hours spent studying each week and the students’ test scores. The Pearson’s correlation coefficient is $0.62$.

From this information it can be concluded that
parts.note: Bivariate data (interpreting Pearson's correlation coefficient) is not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus. · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

options.label: A
options.latex: $62\%$ of students who study more hours achieve higher test scores.

options.label: B
options.latex: the number of hours students study causes an increase in test scores.

options.label: C
options.latex: $62\%$ of students with higher test scores choose to study more hours each week.

options.label: D
options.latex: students who study for more hours each week tend to achieve higher test scores.

solutions.latex:
A positive correlation means that as the number of hours spent studying increases, test scores tend to increase.

Correlation does not show causation (B is incorrect), and $r=0.62$ is not a percentage of students (A and C are incorrect).

So students who study for more hours each week tend to achieve higher test scores.

An object is thrown vertically upwards from the top of a tall building. The height, $h$ metres, of the object above the ground after $t$ seconds is given by

$$h=45+12t-2t^2.$$

The object reaches its maximum height 3 seconds after it is thrown. The diagram shows the graph of $h(t)$ for $t\ge 0$.

$\therefore$ the object rises $63-45=18$ m above the top of the building.

parts.latex:
A section of the graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\ge 0$ is shown, where $f(x)$ is an odd function.

\exfigure{1632_q8_1}

Four integrals based on this graph are given.

$$\begin{array}{r@{\;}l@{\qquad\qquad}r@{\;}l} P= & \displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx & R= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{1} f(x)\,dx \\[3ex] Q= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx & S= & \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{0} f(x)\,dx \end{array}$$

Which of the following options identifies the integrals in ascending numerical order?

dif.r: MCQ: odd symmetry, compare areas from grid, order four integrals

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: graph of odd function y=f(x) for x>=0 on a grid, crossing x-axis at 1

solutions.latex:
Let $A_1$ be the area between the curve and the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le 1$ (above the axis) and $A_2$ the area for $1\le x\le a$ (below the axis). From the grid, $A_1>2A_2$.

$f$ is odd, so the integral over $[-a,a]$ is $0$ and the integral over $[-a,0]$ is the negative of the integral over $[0,a]$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=A_1-A_2>0\\ Q&=0\\ R&=Q-\int_1^a f(x)\,dx=A_2\\ S&=-P \end{aligned}$$
Since $A_1-A_2>A_2>0$, the order is $S<Q<R<P$.

It is given that $h(x)=\sin^2 x-\sin x$ is a composite function of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ where $f(x)=x^2-x$ and $g(x)=\sin x$ for all real values of $x$.

For what values of $k$ does the equation $\sin^2 x-\sin x=k$ have real solutions?

dif.r: range of quadratic over restricted u=sin x interval

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

solutions.latex:
Let $u=\sin x$, so $-1\le u\le 1$ and $k=u^2-u$.

The parabola $k=u^2-u$ has its vertex at $u=\dfrac{1}{2}$, which lies in $[-1,1]$:
$$k=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}$$
At the end points, $u=-1$ gives $k=2$ and $u=1$ gives $k=0$.
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{4}\le k\le 2$$

dif.r: one derivative, substitute x=-1

solutions.latex:
Differentiating,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+3$$
At $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3(-1)^2+3\\ &=6 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the gradient of the tangent is $6$.

meta.check: Derivative by power rule; numeric central difference at x=-1 gives 6.

questions.stem:
The number of cars parked in a carpark is recorded each day for thirteen days. The dataset is listed in ascending order:

$$12,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 19,\ 20,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 28,\ 30 \text{ and } m.$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the interquartile range of this dataset?
parts.note: Interquartile range of a data set: Standard data analysis, not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-11-08

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the greatest value of $m$ such that this dataset has no outlier?
parts.note: Outliers via Q3 + 1.5 IQR: Standard data analysis, not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
There are $13$ values, so the median is the 7th value, $22$.

The lower half is $12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 20$, so
$$Q_1=\dfrac{15+17}{2}=16$$
The upper half is $24, 25, 27, 28, 30, m$ (since $m\ge 30$), so
$$Q_3=\dfrac{27+28}{2}=27.5$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=27.5-16\\ &=11.5 \end{aligned}$$

meta.check: Quartiles by the median-of-halves method (NESA convention); IQR does not depend on m since m is the 13th value.
meta.concern: Uses the HSC median-of-halves quartile method (median excluded); some calculators give the same 16 and 27.5 here.

solutions.latex:
An outlier is greater than $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$ (or less than $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$).
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=27.5+1.5\times 11.5\\ &=27.5+17.25\\ &=44.75 \end{aligned}$$
The lower bound is $16-17.25=-1.25$, so $12$ is not an outlier.

$m$ is a number of cars, so it is a whole number with $m\le 44.75$.

$\therefore$ the greatest value of $m$ is $44$.

meta.check: Fence computed twice; checked that m=44 gives no outlier and m=45 does (quartiles unchanged).
meta.concern: Answer 44 assumes m must be a whole number (count of cars); a marker may also accept 44.75 if m is not taken as an integer.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How many seats are in the first row?

dif.r: two AP terms give simultaneous equations for a

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many seats will this theatre have if there are 9 rows?

dif.r: direct S_9 with a and d known from (a)

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: theatre stage with six curved rows of seats

solutions.latex:
The number of seats in row $n$ is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=a+2d=30\\ T_6&=a+5d=42 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting, $3d=12$, so $d=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=30-2(4)\\ &=22 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ there are $22$ seats in the first row.

meta.check: Solved simultaneous equations; listed sequence 22, 26, 30, 34, 38, 42 matches T3 and T6.

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=22$, $d=4$ and $n=9$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_9&=\dfrac{9}{2}\big(2(22)+8(4)\big)\\ &=\dfrac{9}{2}\times 76\\ &=342 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the theatre has $342$ seats.
criteria: Substitutes correctly into a sum formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the range and period of the function $h(x)=3\cos(2x)+1$.

dif.r: range by scaling/shifting cos, period 2pi/2

solutions.latex:
Range: since $-1\le\cos(2x)\le 1$,
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \cos(2x)\le 1\\ -3&\le 3\cos(2x)\le 3 &&(\text{multiply by } 3)\\ -2&\le 3\cos(2x)+1\le 4 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$
So the range is $-2\le h(x)\le 4$.

Period: for $\cos(nx)$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, with $n=2$:
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$
criteria: Finds the correct range or the correct period, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Sampled h numerically: min -2, max 4, h(x+pi)=h(x).

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=4^{x^2+3}$.

dif.r: chain rule with a^f(x) derivative including ln 4

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{f(x)}\right)=f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\ln a$ (chain rule), with $f(x)=x^2+3$ and $f'(x)=2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x\cdot 4^{x^2+3}\ln 4\\ &=2x\ln 4\cdot 4^{x^2+3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates $4^{u}$ as $4^{u}\ln 4$ or finds $f'(x)=2x$ in a chain rule, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Checked symbolically with sympy and numerically at x=0.5.

why: Checker got a different answer — Final line '2x\ln 4.4^{x^2+3}' uses a period as multiplication, so it renders as 2x ln(4.4)^{x^2+3}; should be 2x\ln 4\cdot 4^{x^2+3} (the preceding line 2x·4^{x^2+3} ln 4 is correct).

questions.stem:
Researchers were interested in whether the critics’ scores for movies could be used to predict the general public’s scores for movies.

A random sample of movies was selected, and the average score from the critics and the average score from the public were recorded.

A scatterplot of the dataset and the least-squares regression line are shown.

\exfigure{1632_q16_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What was the lowest score given by the public for a movie, correct to 1 decimal place?
parts.note: Bivariate data (reading a scatterplot) is not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus. · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The gradient of the least-squares regression line for the dataset is $0.54$.

Interpret the gradient in the context of the dataset.
parts.note: Bivariate data (interpreting the gradient of a least-squares regression line) is not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus. · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
A new data point is included in the dataset. The critics’ score is $7.2$ and the public’s score is $6$.

Identify ONE effect this would have on the least-squares regression line.
parts.note: Bivariate data (effect of a new point on a least-squares regression line) is not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus. · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

figures.cap: scatterplot of public's score against critics' score with least-squares regression line

solutions.latex:
The lowest point on the scatterplot is at a critics' score of $7.4$, with a public's score of $6.1$.

$\therefore$ the lowest score given by the public was $6.1$.

meta.check: Measured the dot's centre in pixels against the 6.0 and 6.5 grid lines: 6.09.
meta.concern: Read from graph; tolerance of about 6.1 likely.

solutions.latex:
The gradient is the change in the public's score for each increase of $1$ in the critics' score.

For each $1$ point increase in the critics' score, the public's score increases by $0.54$ points on average (predicted).
criteria: States that the public's score increases as the critics' score increases, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Standard interpretation; line through (7.0, 6.55) and (10.0, 8.15) has gradient about 0.53, consistent with 0.54.

solutions.latex:
At a critics' score of $7.2$ the regression line gives a public's score of about $6.65$, so the new point $(7.2,\ 6)$ lies well below the line at the left end of the data.

Including it pulls the left end of the line down, so the gradient of the least-squares regression line increases (the line becomes steeper) and the $y$-intercept decreases.

meta.check: Re-fitted a least-squares line to the 23 points read from the scatterplot with and without (7.2, 6): gradient 0.53 to 0.57, intercept 2.82 to 2.42.
meta.concern: Open-ended 'identify ONE effect': increased gradient, decreased y-intercept (or weaker fit) should all be acceptable; solution names gradient increase as the main effect.

questions.stem:
A large rechargeable battery has a maximum storage capacity of 40 kWh when new.

After 1 year, the maximum storage capacity is 32 kWh.

The process of decay can be modelled by the function

$$y=ka^t$$

where $y$ is the maximum storage capacity of the battery, in kWh, $t$ years after it starts being used.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What are the values of $k$ and $a$?

dif.r: substitute t=0 then t=1

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Interpret the value of $a$ in this context.

dif.r: interpret factor 0.8 as 20% annual decrease in context

solutions.latex:
Each year the maximum storage capacity is multiplied by $a=0.8$.

So each year the maximum storage capacity is $80\%$ of what it was the year before: it decreases by $20\%$ per year.

meta.concern: Either '80% retained each year' or '20% lost each year' should be accepted.

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=7-3x$ and $y=-x^2+x+12$. The graphs intersect at two points.

\exfigure{1632_q18_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the two points of intersection are $x=-1$ and $x=5$.

dif.r: equate, solve factorising quadratic

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the area enclosed by the line $y=7-3x$ and the parabola $y=-x^2+x+12$.

dif.r: standard area between curves, bounds given

figures.cap: parabola with x-intercepts -3 and 4 and a decreasing line

solutions.latex:
At the points of intersection the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 7-3x&=-x^2+x+12\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-1 \text{ or } x=5$$
criteria: Equates the two functions to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Substituted x=-1 (y=10 both) and x=5 (y=-8 both).

solutions.latex:
Between $x=-1$ and $x=5$ the parabola is above the line (at $x=0$: $12>7$), so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{5}\big((-x^2+x+12)-(7-3x)\big)\,dx\\ &=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{125}{3}+50+25\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\ &=\dfrac{100}{3}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\ &=36\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=36 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes a correct integral for the area, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Antiderivative evaluated by hand; cross-checked with the parabola-chord formula (b-a)^3/6 = 6^3/6 = 36.

dif.r: derivative sketch: max of f' at inflection, asymptote to zero

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

req: Graphs of f, f′ and f″
Graphs of f, f′ and f″

Asymptotes and limiting behaviour.evidence: As x→∞, f(x)→5 (horizontal asymptote), so f'(x)→0
Asymptotes and limiting behaviour.reason: Non-hyperbola horizontal asymptote/limit needed for f' behaviour as x→∞.

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: concave up for x<5 and concave down for x>5, so f' increases
Concavity and points of inflection.reason: Criterion needs maximum of f' at the point of inflection; requires concavity/POI meaning.

Stationary points and their nature.reason: Criterion 1 mark: shows f'(2)=0 at the local minimum.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with minimum at x=2, inflection at x=5, asymptote y=5
blank axes with x marks 2 and 5
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)$ is the gradient of $y=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le x<2 &&f \text{ decreasing}\\ f'(2)&=0 &&\text{local minimum}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x>2 &&f \text{ increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$f$ is concave up for $x<5$ and concave down for $x>5$, so $f'$ increases up to $x=5$ and then decreases: $f'(x)$ is greatest at the point of inflection $x=5$.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to5$ (horizontal asymptote), so $f'(x)\to0$ from above: the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote of $y=f'(x)$.

\exfigure{1632_q19_s1}
criteria: Sketch with $f'(2)=0$, the correct sign of $f'(x)$ either side of $x=2$ and a maximum at $x=5$, or equivalent merit
Shows $f'(2)=0$ with the correct sign of $f'(x)$ on either side of $x=2$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Read monotonicity and concavity from the given graph; checked the drawn curve against them (negative to x=2, max at 5, tends to 0+).
meta.concern: Heights of f'(0) and the maximum are not determined by the graph; drawn qualitatively. Exact rubric weighting for the asymptote is a guess.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
One student at the school is selected at random.

What is the probability that this student walks to school and is not wearing the correct school uniform?

dif.r: multiply along two tree branches

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Two students at the school are selected at random.

What is the probability that at least one of these students walks to school and is not wearing the correct school uniform?

dif.r: at least one via complement of neither: 1-(0.97)^2

figures.cap: probability tree: walk/not walk then correct/not correct uniform

solutions.latex:
Walks and not wearing the correct uniform (multiply along the branches):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{3}{10}\times\dfrac{1}{10}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{100}\end{aligned}$$

From (a), each student independently walks and is not wearing the correct uniform with probability $\dfrac{3}{100}$, so the probability that a student does not is $\dfrac{97}{100}$.

At least one is the complement of neither:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one})&=1-\left(\dfrac{97}{100}\right)^2\\ &=1-\dfrac{9409}{10\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{591}{10\,000}\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: Assumes independence of the two selections (large school).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the first derivative of $g(x)=\dfrac{x}{\ln x}$ is $g'(x)=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}$.

dif.r: direct quotient rule with ln x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the global maximum of $g(x)$ on the interval $[2,5]$?

dif.r: stationary point is a minimum; maximum must be at endpoint

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=\dfrac{1\cdot\ln x-x\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Numerical derivative at x=3 matches formula.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points: $g'(x)=0$ when $\ln x-1=0$, so $x=e$, which lies in $[2,5]$.

The denominator $(\ln x)^2>0$, so the sign of $g'(x)$ is decided by $\ln x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 2\le x<e &&\text{decreasing}\\ g'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } e<x\le5 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=e$ is a local minimum, and the global maximum is at an endpoint:
$$\begin{aligned} g(2)&=\dfrac{2}{\ln2}\approx2.885\\ g(5)&=\dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.107\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the global maximum is } \dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.11 \text{ (at } x=5)$$
criteria: Shows $x=e$ is a minimum and evaluates $g$ at an endpoint, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point at $x=e$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Evaluated g on a fine grid over [2,5]: max at x=5, 3.1067.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}$.

dif.r: one-line algebraic split of numerator

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Describe the transformations required to obtain the graph $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$ from the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$.

dif.r: hence: two translations, left/right direction from x+1

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+2}{x+1}&=\dfrac{(x+1)+1}{x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}$$

From (a), $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$.

Replacing $x$ by $x+1$ in $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$: a translation $1$ unit to the left.

Adding $1$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$: a translation $1$ unit up.

$\therefore$ Translate the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ $1$ unit to the left and $1$ unit up.
criteria: Describes one of the two translations correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Asymptotes move from x=0, y=0 to x=-1, y=1, consistent with both translations.

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a block of land $ABCD$. It also shows the bearing of each of the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, from point $O$.

\exfigure{1632_q23_1}

The distance from $O$ to $C$ is 25 km, $OA=OB$ and $\angle AOB=45^\circ$.

The area of the shaded triangle $AOB$ is $80\text{ km}^2$.

What is the distance from $B$ to $C$, to the nearest kilometre?

dif.r: area gives side, bearings give angle, then cosine rule

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: block of land ABCD with bearings of A, B, C, D from O
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1632_q23_s1}

Let $OA=OB=x$ km. The area of triangle $AOB$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin45^\circ&=80\\ x^2&=\dfrac{160}{\sin45^\circ}\\ &=160\sqrt2\\ x&\approx15.04\end{aligned}$$
From the bearings of $B$ and $C$:
$$\angle BOC=253^\circ-101^\circ=152^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $BOC$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2&=x^2+25^2-2\times x\times25\cos152^\circ\\ &\approx226.27+625-2\times15.04\times25\cos152^\circ\\ &\approx1515.4\\ BC&\approx38.9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC\approx39 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Applies the cosine rule with $\angle BOC=152^\circ$ and $OB\approx15.04$ km, or equivalent merit
Finds $OB\approx15.04$ km, and finds $\angle BOC=152^\circ$, or equivalent merit
Uses the area formula to form an equation for $OB$, or finds $\angle BOC=152^\circ$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Python: x=sqrt(160*sqrt2)=15.042, BC^2=1515.36, BC=38.93; angle BOC also checked as 360-(253-101) reflex = 208 so the non-reflex is 152.

why: Random spot-check: passed every automatic check
look: Read the question and solution against the source page

questions.stem:
Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: 75% decayed means 25% remains; solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $t$ when the rate of change of $A$ is $-9.48$ g/year, correct to the nearest year.

dif.r: differentiate exponential, set rate, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $A=1000e^{kt}$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-9.48$ with $k=-0.1315$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(-0.1315)e^{-0.1315t}&=-9.48\\ e^{-0.1315t}&=\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\\ -0.1315t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\right)\\ t&\approx20.0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx20 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$ and equates it to $-9.48$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Solved with rounded and unrounded k: t = 19.9987 and 19.9961, both 20.

parts.latex:
The weights of watermelons produced by a certain farm are normally distributed with a mean of 4.82 kg. Long-term quality control data show that when a watermelon from this farm is randomly selected, the probability that it weighs less than 3.75 kg is $0.116$.

A watermelon is labelled as being the ideal size if it weighs between 4.82 kg and 5.89 kg.

What is the probability that a watermelon selected at random is the ideal size?

dif.r: spot symmetric distances about mean, subtract from 0.5

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The normal distribution is symmetric about the mean $4.82$, and $3.75$ and $5.89$ are the same distance from it:
$$4.82-3.75=1.07=5.89-4.82$$
So, by symmetry, $P(X>5.89)=P(X<3.75)=0.116$.

Half of the distribution lies above the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(4.82<X<5.89)&=0.5-P(X>5.89)\\ &=0.5-0.116\\ &=0.384\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses symmetry to obtain $P(X>5.89)=0.116$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Symmetry argument; cross-checked with z-score: P(Z<-z)=0.116 gives z=1.195, P(0<Z<1.195)=0.384.

questions.stem:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: At what value(s) of $t$ does the particle change direction in this interval?

dif.r: v changes sign where graph crosses axis

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

req: Particles at rest and changing direction
Particles at rest and changing direction
B.note: 1 mark: t=0.5 can be read from the given v-t graph or found by solving e^{cos(pi t)}=1, cos(pi t)=0.

Trigonometric equations.evidence: cos(pi t) = 0, pi t = pi/2 (0<=pi t<=1.25pi)
Trigonometric equations.reason: Solving cos of linear argument on restricted domain.

Exponential equations.reason: Unknown in an index solved by equal bases / logs.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0.5$.

dif.r: chain rule on e^{cos(pi t)}, substitute

parts.label: c

dif.r: trapezoidal rule but distance needs |v| over sign change

B.note: Distance needs |v| across the sign change at t=0.5.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph v(t) for 0<=t<=1.25

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=0\\ e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=1\\ \cos(\pi t)&=0\\ \pi t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&(0\le\pi t\le1.25\pi)\\ t&=0.5\end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $t$-axis there ($v<0$ before, $v>0$ after).
$$\therefore\ t=0.5$$

meta.check: Graph crosses at 0.5; cos(pi t)=0 has no other solution in [0,1.25pi].

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{f(t)}=f'(t)e^{f(t)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\ &=-\big(-\pi\sin(\pi t)\big)e^{\cos(\pi t)}\\ &=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)e^{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\\ &=\pi\times1\times e^0\\ &=\pi \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Distance is the area between the graph and the $t$-axis, so use $|v|$ ($v\le0$ for $0\le t\le0.5$ and $v\ge0$ for $0.5\le t\le1$):
$$\text{distance}=\int_0^1|v|\,dt$$
Four subintervals of $[0,1]$: $h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=0.25$, with $t=0,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.75,\ 1$ as in the table.

Trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(t_0)+2\big(f(t_1)+f(t_2)+f(t_3)\big)+f(t_4)\big]$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1|v|\,dt&\approx\dfrac{0.25}{2}\big[1.72+2(1.03+0+0.51)+0.63\big]\\ &=0.125\times5.43\\ &=0.67875\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}\approx0.68 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with $h=0.25$ to the table values (e.g. finds the displacement), or equivalent merit

meta.check: Hand sum 5.43 x 0.125; exact integral of |v| is 0.710, so the estimate is reasonable.
meta.concern: Distance (not displacement) needs |v|; since v=0 at the node t=0.5, applying the rule to |v| equals splitting at t=0.5. Rounding of final answer (0.68 vs 0.679) not specified.
