parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, show that $P(X\ge 1.5)=\dfrac{67}{256}$

dif.r: one definite integral of known pdf

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the mode of the probability distribution function is $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$.

dif.r: differentiate cubic pdf, choose stationary point

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^2 x^2(2-x)\,dx&=1\\ k\left[\dfrac{2x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2&=1\\ \dfrac{4k}{3}&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Lets the integral equal $1$ and takes $k$ out as a common factor (with $dx$), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: If the integration was conducted correctly and k was solved to equal $\dfrac{3}{4}$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 1.5)&=\dfrac{3}{4}\int_{1.5}^2 x^2(2-x)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[\dfrac{2x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{1.5}^2\\ &=\dfrac{67}{256}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the integral from $1.5$ to $2$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Solving correctly for $\dfrac{67}{256}$ or showing that 1 – p[X<5] was giving the same value was given a mark
meta.marker_note: Showing that $1-P(X<1.5)$ gives the same value was also accepted. No mark was given for the integration itself, as it was already done in part (a).

solutions.latex:
The mode is where the probability density function is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}P(x)&=\dfrac{3}{4}x^2(2-x)\\ P'(x)&=3x-\dfrac{9}{4}x^2\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x\left(1-\dfrac{3}{4}x\right)&=0\\ x&=0\text{ or } x=\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}P''(x)&=3-\dfrac{9}{2}x\\ P''\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)&=-3<0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ is a maximum, and the mode is $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$.
criteria: Shows $P'(x)=0$ and states $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Showing $P''(x)=3-\dfrac{9}{2}x$ and solving for $-3$ or showing that the Nature of the points around the value determined a maximum point to give the mode was also acceptable
meta.marker_note: Showing the nature of the stationary point with the first derivative test (a maximum gives the mode) was also accepted.

questions.stem:
The velocity of a particle moving in a straight line at the end of $t$ seconds is given by

$$v(t)=3t^2-15t+18,\quad\text{where } 0\le t\le 4$$

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise find the total distance travelled by the particle between $t=1$ to $t=3$.

dif.r: split integral at given rest time, absolute value

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3t^2-15t+18&=0\\ t^2-5t+6&=0\\ (t-2)(t-3)&=0\\ t&=2\text{ or } t=3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Lets $v(t)=0$ and attempts to find the values of $t$, or attempts to substitute the given values of $t$ to show $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working sets $v(t)=0$ and divides by $3$ (source wrote $v(t)=3t^2-15t+18=t^2-5t+6$).

solutions.latex:
From part (a), the particle changes direction at $t=2$, so split the distance there:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\int_1^2\left(3t^2-15t+18\right)dt+\left|\int_2^3\left(3t^2-15t+18\right)dt\right|\\ &=\dfrac{5}{2}+\left|-\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\ &=3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds two definite integrals using the correct bounds, but makes minor arithmetic errors, or equivalent merit

dif.r: explicit conditional, ratio of table values from (a)

figures.cap: standard normal curve shaded to the left of z

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned}z_1&=\dfrac{62-72}{8}=-1.25\\ z_2&=\dfrac{92-72}{8}=2.5\end{aligned}$$
From the table and symmetry, $P(z<-1.25)=1-P(z<1.25)=0.1057$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(62<X<92)&=P(-1.25<z<2.5)\\ &=0.9938-0.1057\\ &=0.8881\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the two corresponding $z$-scores, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the probability in $z$ is $P(-1.25<z<2.5)$ (source wrote $P(-1.25<X<92)$).

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<62\mid X<92)&=\dfrac{P(X<62\cap X<92)}{P(X<92)}\\ &=\dfrac{P(z<-1.25\cap z<2.5)}{P(z<2.5)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.1057}{0.9938}\\ &=0.10635\ldots\\ &=0.1064\ (4\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct conditional probability formula for the question, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The normal to the curve $y=(x+2)^2$ at the point $A(-3,1)$ meets the curve again at $B$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1366_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal

dif.r: chain derivative, perpendicular gradient, normal equation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the coordinate of $B$ is given by $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$

dif.r: solve normal with parabola, quadratic, reject known root

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the angle between the line AB and the tangent at $B$.

dif.r: angles of inclination of two lines, then subtract

skills: Angle of inclination of a line

figures.cap: parabola y=(x+2)^2 with the normal at A(-3,1) meeting the curve again at B
solution sketch: diagram with tangent at B drawn, angle theta at B, angle alpha (tangent inclination) and beta (normal inclination) marked

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$y'=2(x+2)$$
At $A(-3,1)$:
$$y'(-3)=-2$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent:
$$m_{\text{normal}}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Using the point–gradient form:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)\\ y&=\dfrac{1}{2}x+\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct linear equation of the normal
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the gradient at $A$ is $y'(-3)=-2$ (source printed $y'(2)=-2$).

solutions.latex:
Solving the normal and the curve simultaneously:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}x+\dfrac{5}{2}&=(x+2)^2\\ \dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}&=x^2+4x+4\\ 2x^2+7x+3&=0\\ (2x+1)(x+3)&=0\\ x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ or } x=-3\end{aligned}$$
$x=-3$ is the point $A$, so at $B$, $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$y\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=2\dfrac{1}{4}$$
$$\therefore B\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Uses simultaneous equations to solve for the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection, but makes minor errors, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Finds the second point of intersection (both x- and y- value) using simultaneous equation
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $B\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$ (source printed $B\left(-3,2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$ on the last line).

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1366_q27_s1}

The gradient of the tangent at $B$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=2(x+2)\\ y'\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=3\end{aligned}$$
The tangent at $B$ makes an angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\alpha&=3\\ \alpha&=\tan^{-1}(3)\\ &=71.565\ldots^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Line $AB$ (the normal, gradient $\dfrac{1}{2}$) makes an angle $\beta$ with the $x$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\beta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \beta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=26.565\ldots^\circ\end{aligned}$$
By the exterior angle of a triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\alpha-\beta\\ &=71.565\ldots^\circ-26.565\ldots^\circ\\ &=45^\circ\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent at $B$ and converts it to an angle of inclination, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The graph shows the water level under a bridge over a 12-hour period.

\exfigure{1366_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the equation of the curve that models the water level as a function of time after 12:00 am is given by:

$$w(t)=1.1\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+7.4$$

dif.r: amplitude, midline, period from graph

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate how long in the 12-hour period shown that the rate of change of water level is increasing at more than 0.55 metres per hour? Correct your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: differentiate model, solve trig inequality on derivative, time length

figures.cap: water level (metres) against time from 12 am to 12 pm: cosine curve through (0, 8.5), minimum (6, 6.3), (12, 8.5)

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the maximum level is $8.5$ and the minimum is $6.3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Midline}&=\dfrac{8.5+6.3}{2}=7.4\\ \text{Amplitude}&=8.5-7.4=1.1\end{aligned}$$
The period is $12$ hours:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{a}&=12\\ a&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Explains two of the three features (amplitude, period and midline), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Explain all three features with reference to the amplitude, period and midline

solutions.latex:
$$w(t)=1.1\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+7.4$$
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$w'(t)=-\dfrac{11\pi}{60}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$$
The level rises faster than $0.55$ m/h when $w'(t)>0.55$. Solving $w'(t)=0.55$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{11\pi}{60}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=0.55\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=-\dfrac{3}{\pi}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with $0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\le 2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=\pi+\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\text{ or } 2\pi-\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\\ t&=8.424418\ldots\text{ or } 9.5755811\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$w'(t)>0.55$ between these times:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Time}&=9.5755811\ldots-8.424418\ldots\\ &=1.151162\ldots\text{ hours}\\ &\approx 1\text{ hour } 9\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the derivative of $w(t)$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $w(t)=1.1\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+7.4$ and $w'(t)=-\dfrac{11\pi}{60}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$ (source printed $+7.5$ and dropped the minus sign, in the working and the criterion).

\exfigure{1366_q30_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the graph of $f(t)=(t-1)^2e^{-t},\ 0\le t<\infty$.

Showing clearly the exact coordinates of all stationary points.

dif.r: near twin of 2025 Q16: stationary points of poly times e^{-t}

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The function $f(t)$ is transformed to $g(t)=2f(t)+5$.

It is given that the shaded area shown above, bounded by the curve $f(t)=(t-1)^2e^{-t},\ 0\le t\le a$ and the $x$-axis is $1-\dfrac{2}{e}\text{ unit}^2$. \textit{(Do not prove this).}

Therefore evaluate the following integral

$$\int_0^a g(t)\,dt$$

dif.r: linearity of integral with given area, read a=1

figures.cap: part of the graph of f(t)=(t-1)^2 e^{-t} from t=0 decreasing to touch the t-axis at a, then rising; region from 0 to a under the curve hatched
solution sketch: completed graph of f(t) with stationary points at t=1 (on the axis) and t=3, labelled (1, 4e^-3) in the sample

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=(t-1)^2 & v&=e^{-t}\\ u'&=2(t-1) & v'&=-e^{-t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(t)&=2e^{-t}(t-1)-e^{-t}(t-1)^2\\ &=e^{-t}(t-1)(3-t)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(t)=0$; since $e^{-t}>0$:
$$t=1\text{ or } t=3$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=0\\ f(3)&=4e^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $f(t)\to 0$ (the exponential dominates), so the $t$-axis is an asymptote.

\exfigure{1366_q30_s1}
criteria: Correctly shows the turning point or $f(t)\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the turning points of $f(t)$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the derivative of $f(t)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Splitting the integral and using the given area:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a\left(2f(t)+5\right)dt&=2\int_0^a f(t)\,dt+\int_0^a 5\,dt\\ &=2\left(1-\dfrac{2}{e}\right)+5a\\ &=7-\dfrac{4}{e}\quad(a=1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(t)\,dt=1-\dfrac{4}{e}$ or correctly integrates $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\,dt$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A wire total length 60 cm is to be cut into two pieces.

The first piece is bent to form an equilateral triangle of side length $x$ cm.

The second piece is bent to form a circular sector of radius $x$ cm with an angle of $\theta$ radians at the centre.

\exfigure{1366_q31_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$x\theta=60-5x$$

dif.r: perimeter of triangle and sector set-up

B.note: constraint for later optimisation

Setting up optimisation problems.reason: Only a perimeter constraint (covered by Arc length); no expression to be optimised is built.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The total area of the two shapes is $\boldsymbol{A}\text{ cm}^2$.

Hence, or otherwise, show that

$$A=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)x^2+30x$$

dif.r: two area formulas, substitute theta from (a)

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the maximum total area of both shapes to two decimal places.

dif.r: maximise concave-down quadratic, evaluate

figures.cap: equilateral triangle with sides x and a circular sector of radius x with angle theta

solutions.latex:
The wire forms the three sides of the triangle ($3x$) and the two radii and arc of the sector ($2x+x\theta$):
$$\begin{aligned}3x+2x+x\theta&=60\\ x\theta&=60-5x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct expression for the perimeter of the triangle or the perimeter of the sector, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ for the equilateral triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of triangle}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{x^2\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ for the sector, with $\theta=\dfrac{60-5x}{x}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of sector}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\dfrac{60-5x}{x}\\ &=30x-\dfrac{5x^2}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Adding:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{x^2\sqrt{3}}{4}+30x-\dfrac{5x^2}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)+30x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)x^2+30x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct simplified expressions for both the area of the triangle and the area of the sector, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct simplified expression for the area of the triangle or the area of the sector, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{x^2}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)+30x\\ A'&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)x+30\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point where $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)x+30&=0\\ x&=-\dfrac{60}{\sqrt{3}-10}\end{aligned}$$
This is the maximum turning point because $A$ is a concave-down parabola (its $x^2$ coefficient $\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}-10\right)<0$).
$$\therefore A\left(-\dfrac{60}{\sqrt{3}-10}\right)\approx 108.85\text{ cm}^2$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the maximum follows because $A$ (not $A'$) is a concave-down parabola.

parts.latex: Find all the values of $k$, such that the equation $x^2+(4k+3)\,x+\left(4k^2-\dfrac{9}{4}\right)=0$ has two real solutions for $x$, where one of the solutions is positive and the other is negative.

dif.r: opposite-sign roots needs product of roots < 0

req: Discriminant and the nature of roots
A.note: opposite-sign roots; model solution uses product of roots (outside Advanced), discriminant route also works

B.note: solution uses product of roots (Ext 1); Advanced route is f(0) < 0 for a concave-up parabola

Discriminant and the nature of roots.reason: Solution uses product of roots <0, which guarantees real roots; Δ never used.

solutions.latex:
Roots of opposite sign require the product of roots to be negative (this also guarantees two real roots):
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta=4k^2-\dfrac{9}{4}&<0\\k^2&<\dfrac{9}{16}\\-\dfrac{3}{4}<k&<\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2}\dfrac{2-x}{1-\sqrt{x-1}}$

dif.r: limit by rationalising; outside functions topic

solutions.latex:
Rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2-x}{1-\sqrt{x-1}}\times\dfrac{1+\sqrt{x-1}}{1+\sqrt{x-1}}&=\dfrac{(2-x)\left(1+\sqrt{x-1}\right)}{1-(x-1)}\\ &=1+\sqrt{x-1}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 2}\left(1+\sqrt{x-1}\right)&=1+1\\ &=2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Using the table below, what is the maximum possible value for $E(X)$?

\extable{1367_q10_t1}

dif.r: MCQ: maximise E(X) subject to table constraints

B.note: max E(X) over valid k: probabilities >= 0 constrain k

Global maxima and minima.reason: Max of -3k^2-7k+2 on 0<=k<=sqrt5-2 can be found from the parabola vertex without calculus; solution uses no derivative.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$ for every $k$:
$$k^2+3k+k+\left(-k^2-4k+1\right)=1$$
Each probability must be non-negative:
$$\begin{aligned}3k&\ge 0 &&\text{so } k\ge 0\\ -k^2-4k+1&\ge 0 &&\text{so } -2-\sqrt{5}\le k\le\sqrt{5}-2\end{aligned}$$
Hence $0\le k\le\sqrt{5}-2$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-k^2+0+k+2\left(-k^2-4k+1\right)\\ &=-3k^2-7k+2\end{aligned}$$
$E(X)$ decreases for $k\ge 0$, so the maximum is at $k=0$:
$$E(X)=2$$

parts.latex:
Solve for $x$:

$$2\ln(x)-\ln(x+3)=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

dif.r: log laws to quadratic, reject negative root

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln\left(x^2\right)-\ln(x+3)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ \ln\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x+3}\right)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ \dfrac{x^2}{x+3}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2x^2&=x+3\\ 2x^2-x-3&=0\\ (2x-3)(x+1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ or } x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$\ln x$ needs $x>0$, so
$$x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$
criteria: Obtains all possible solutions, or equivalent merit
Equates the arguments of the logarithms, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence or otherwise, find the value of $a$, where $a>0$ such that

$$\int_{-\frac{3}{4}}^{a}\Big(2\,|2x+1|-1\Big)\,dx=0$$

dif.r: signed triangle areas of abs graph cancel; find upper bound

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y = 2|2x+1| - 1 with the regions between the graph and the x-axis from x = -0.5 to 0 hatched; x = a marked

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1367_q13_s1}

From part (a)(iii), $y=2|2x+1|-1$ has its vertex at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},-1\right)$ and crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

For $-\dfrac{3}{4}\le x\le -\dfrac{1}{2}$ the region is a triangle below the axis, of area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\times 1=\dfrac{1}{8}$$
From $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $x=0$ the line rises from $-1$ to $1$, so its integral there is $0$.

So the integral from $-\dfrac{3}{4}$ to $a$ is zero when the area above the axis from $0$ to $a$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$. For $x\ge 0$, $2x+1>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a\left(2|2x+1|-1\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ \int_0^a(4x+1)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ \Big[2x^2+x\Big]_0^a&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ 2a^2+a&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ 16a^2+8a-1&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $a>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-8\pm\sqrt{8^2+4\times 16}}{2\times 16}\\ &=\dfrac{-8\pm 8\sqrt{2}}{32}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the triangle below the axis for $-\dfrac{3}{4}\le x\le -\dfrac{1}{4}$ has area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
so the triangle above the axis from $x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$ to $x=a$ (height $2(2a+1)-1$) must also have area $\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(a+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\times\big(2(2a+1)-1\big)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \left(a+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)(4a+1)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 4a^2+2a+\dfrac{1}{4}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 16a^2+8a-1&=0\end{aligned}$$
and, as above, $a=-\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$.
criteria: Obtains the correct integral, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the parts below the axis are written as areas (the source set their integrals equal to positive values, e.g. $\displaystyle\int_{-0.75}^{-0.5}=\dfrac{1}{8}$, and jumped to $\displaystyle\int_0^a$ without the zero integral from $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $0$), and the discriminant is $8^2+4\times 16$ (source printed $8^2-4\times 16$).

parts.latex:
Initially there are 250 litres of water in a tank. Water starts to flow into the tank.

The rate of increase of the volume of water in litres is given by

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=250-7.5t$$

where $t$ is the time in hours.

Find the volume of water in the tank (correct to the nearest litre) when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.

dif.r: twin of 2024 Q15: integrate rate, find C, dV/dt=0

solutions.latex:
Integrating the rate:
$$V(t)=250t-3.75t^2+C$$
Initially $V(0)=250$, so $C=250$:
$$V(t)=250t-3.75t^2+250$$
$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned}250-7.5t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{100}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}V\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)&=250\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)-3.75\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)^2+250\\ &=4416.66\ldots\\ &\approx 4417\text{ litres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $t$, or equivalent merit
Obtains the $V(t)$ equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
For the function:

$$f(x)=xe^x$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary point(s) and determine the nature, the coordinates of the point(s) of inflection, and sketch the curve of $f(x)$, showing all key features.

dif.r: full xe^x analysis: stationary point, inflection, asymptote, sketch

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, find the value(s) of $k$, where $k$ is a real number for which the equation $xe^x=k$ has $2$ solutions.

dif.r: interpret horizontal line meeting curve between min and asymptote

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x) = xe^x with local minimum (-1, -1/e) and point of inflection (-2, -2/e^2)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=e^x+xe^x\\ &=e^x(x+1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$; since $e^x>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=-1\\ f(-1)&=-\dfrac{1}{e}\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $f'(x)$ is decided by $x+1$:

\extable{Ts1383_1}

$\therefore$ $\left(-1,-\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ is a local minimum.

Differentiating again (product rule on $xe^x$):
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=e^x+e^x+xe^x\\ &=e^x(x+2)\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection where $f''(x)=0$; since $e^x>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=-2\\ f(-2)&=-\dfrac{2}{e^2}\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $f''(x)$ is decided by $x+2$:

\extable{Ts1383_2}

$\therefore$ $\left(-2,-\dfrac{2}{e^2}\right)$ is a point of inflection (concavity changes from down to up).

As $x\to-\infty$, $f(x)\to 0^-$ (asymptote $y=0$).

\exfigure{1367_q15_s1}
criteria: Correct shape and scale of the graph of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit
Proves there is a point of inflection, or equivalent merit
Shows the stationary point is a local minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds the coordinates of the stationary point, or equivalent merit

The line $y=k$ meets $y=xe^x$ twice when it lies between the minimum value $-\dfrac{1}{e}$ and the asymptote $y=0$:
$$-\dfrac{1}{e}<k<0$$

questions.stem:
A random variable $X$ has this probability distribution:

\extable{1367_q16_t1}

dif.r: explicit conditional from discrete table

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the variance of $X$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

dif.r: compute E(X) and E(X^2), then variance

solutions.latex:
Using $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2\mid X<4)&=\dfrac{P(X\ge 2\cap X<4)}{P(X<4)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.1+0.25}{0.2+0.1+0.25}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{11}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies all possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-\left[E(X)\right]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}E\left(X^2\right)&=0.2+2^2\times 0.1+3^2\times 0.25+4^2\times 0.3+5^2\times 0.15\\ &=11.4\\ E(X)&=0.2+2\times 0.1+3\times 0.25+4\times 0.3+5\times 0.15\\ &=3.1\\ \mathrm{Var}(X)&=11.4-3.1^2\\ &=1.79\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Joe plays soccer, a sport where a team can win, lose or draw.

Joe is prone to injury, and misses $20\%$ of his team's games.

When Joe plays, his team has a $77\%$ chance of winning and a $10\%$ chance of losing.

When Joe does not play, his team has a $53\%$ chance of winning and a $25\%$ chance of losing.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the probability that Joe's team loses any given game.

dif.r: total probability over two branches

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that Joe's team does not lose in a particular match, what is the probability that Joe played in that match?

dif.r: reverse conditional with not-lose = win or draw

figures.cap: solution sketch: tree diagram: J 0.8 (W 0.77, D 0.13, L 0.1), J-bar 0.2 (W 0.53, D 0.22, L 0.25)

criteria: Identifies all possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When Joe plays, the team does not lose with probability $0.77+0.13=0.9$ (win or draw).

Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(J\mid\bar{L}\right)&=\dfrac{P\left(J\cap\bar{L}\right)}{P\left(\bar{L}\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.8\times(0.77+0.13)}{1-0.13}\\ &=\dfrac{24}{29}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies all possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)}\left(1+\tan^2\theta\right)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\left(1+\tan^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\right)=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta$$

dif.r: complementary-angle and Pythagorean identities, long four-term simplification

solutions.latex:
Using $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta$, $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$ and $\sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\operatorname{cosec}\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\\ &=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress towards the answer, or equivalent merit
Applies trigonometric identities, or equivalent merit
Applies trigonometric ratios of complementary angles, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: line 2, second term is $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$ (source printed $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$).

questions.stem:
The number of concert tickets sold, $N$, is given by

$$N=1000\times 1.6^{kt}$$

Where $t$ is the number of weeks after being available for sale, and $k$ is a constant. Initially, 1000 tickets were sold, and after 2 weeks, the total number of tickets sold was doubled.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: exponential base 1.6 used in reverse with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what rate was the number of tickets sold increasing after 4 weeks? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: differentiate a^{kt} with ln a, substitute exact k

solutions.latex:
Initially $N=1000$, and after $2$ weeks $N=2000$, so when $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}1000\times 1.6^{2k}&=2000\\ 1.6^{2k}&=2\\ 2k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.6}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times k\times 1.6^{kt}\times\ln 1.6\\ &=1000k\ln(1.6)\times 1.6^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times\ln 1.6\times 1.6^{\frac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times 4}\\ &=1386.29\ldots\\ &\approx 1386\text{ tickets/week}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A fisherman's boat is trying to reach the open sea, however, it is heavily affected by the ocean tides. To reach the open sea, the boat must cross a sandbar which requires the water to be at least 4 metres deep. On a particular day, high tide occurred at midnight, and the depth, $D$, of water over the sandbar on the ensuing day is given by $D=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $D=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3$, for $0\le t\le 25$, showing all key features.

dif.r: sketch cosine with awkward period 12.5

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the times when the fisherman would not be able to cross the sandbar in his boat.

dif.r: solve cos=1/2, intervals below 4 m over two periods

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of D = 2cos(4πt/25) + 3 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 25, maxima 5 at t = 0, 25/2, 25, minima 1 at t = 25/4, 75/4; parts below D = 4 in red

criteria: Two of the amplitude, shape and period correct, or equivalent merit
One of the amplitude, shape and period correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The boat can cross only when $D\ge 4$. Solving $D=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3&=4\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and for $0\le t\le 25$, $0\le\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\le 4\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}\\ 4t&=\dfrac{25}{3},\ \dfrac{125}{3},\ \dfrac{175}{3},\ \dfrac{275}{3}\\ t&=\dfrac{25}{12},\ \dfrac{125}{12},\ \dfrac{175}{12},\ \dfrac{275}{12}\end{aligned}$$
From the graph in part (a), $D<4$ between the first and second, and between the third and fourth, of these times:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{25}{12}&<t<\dfrac{125}{12} &&\text{0205 to 1025 hrs}\\ \dfrac{175}{12}&<t<\dfrac{275}{12} &&\text{1435 to 2255 hrs}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the boat cannot cross between 0205 and 1025 hrs, and between 1435 and 2255 hrs (exclusive of these times).
criteria: Correct values of $t$, or equivalent merit
The correct value of $\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\,dx=1$.

dif.r: multiply by e^x to get f'/f, simplify log to 1

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^x$ gives $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ form:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{e^x}\,dx&=\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\,dx\\ &=\Big[\ln\left|1+e^x\right|\Big]_{-1}^{1}\\ &=\ln|1+e|-\ln\left|1+e^{-1}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{1+e}{1+\frac{1}{e}}\cdot\dfrac{e}{e}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{e(1+e)}{1+e}\right|\\ &=\ln e\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, rewrite the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}&=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}-\dfrac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=1+\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\end{aligned}$$
and integrate to obtain the primitive
$$x+\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|$$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution of limits, or equivalent merit
Obtains an integrable form of the integrand by manipulating the original integrand, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the alternative primitive is $x+\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|$, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(1+e^{-x}\right)=\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}$ (source printed $x-\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|$, which gives $3$).

questions.stem: It is known that $T_1=1+\cos A$, $T_2=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $T_3=1-\cos A$ form the first three consecutive terms of a geometric sequence, with $T_1>T_2>T_3$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $A$, given $\angle A$ is an angle within a triangle.

dif.r: GP condition gives cos^2 A, choose sign from ordering

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

req: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences
A.note: b^2=ac gives cos^2 A = 3/4; solved on 0<A<pi

req: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

Trigonometric equations.reason: not_when: quadratic in a trig ratio belongs to Quadratic trigonometric equations; also its prerequisite.

Quadratic trigonometric equations.reason: Equation reduces to a quadratic in cos A.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Using the value of $A$ found in part (a), show that the series

$$\Big(1+\cos A\Big)+\dfrac{1}{2}+\Big(1-\cos A\Big)+\cdots$$

has a limiting sum.

dif.r: compute r=2-sqrt3 and check |r|<1

solutions.latex:
$T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ are geometric, so $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos A}&=\dfrac{1-\cos A}{\frac{1}{2}}\\ 1-\cos^2 A&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \cos^2 A&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \cos A&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is an angle in a triangle, so $0<A<\pi$:
$$A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ or } A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
Since $T_1>T_2>T_3$, the ratio $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}<1$.

If $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\approx 0.2679<1$$
If $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}\approx 3.73>1$$
$$\therefore A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ only}$$
criteria: Finds $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (other potential solutions include $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $\cos A=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$), or equivalent merit
Recognises a geometric series and writes $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$ in terms of the cosine terms, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: fully correct solution, with due consideration of the possible quadrant for $\angle A$ and also $T_1>T_2>T_3$

solutions.latex:
With $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=1+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ T_2&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\ &\approx 0.2679<1\end{aligned}$$
Since $|r|<1$, a limiting sum exists.
criteria: Uses the value of $A$ to find the common ratio, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: fully showing the reason why the series has a limiting sum

parts.latex: If $y^2=(2m-y)\,(2n-y)$, show that $\dfrac{1}{m},\dfrac{1}{y},\dfrac{1}{n}$ (in this order) forms the terms of an arithmetic sequence.

dif.r: abstract show-that: rearrange and test common difference

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Expanding and making $y$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned}y^2&=(2m-y)(2n-y)\\ y^2&=4mn-2my-2ny+y^2\\ 2my+2ny&=4mn\\ y&=\dfrac{2mn}{m+n}\\ \dfrac{1}{y}&=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\end{aligned}$$
Checking $T_2-T_1$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_2-T_1&=\dfrac{1}{y}-\dfrac{1}{m}\\ &=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}-\dfrac{1}{m}\cdot\dfrac{2n}{2n}\\ &=\dfrac{m+n-2n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{m-n}{2mn}\end{aligned}$$
Checking $T_3-T_2$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{y}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{n}\cdot\dfrac{2m}{2m}-\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{2m-m-n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{m-n}{2mn}\\ &=T_2-T_1\end{aligned}$$
As $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$, the three terms form an arithmetic sequence.
criteria: Finds $T_3-T_2$ and $T_2-T_1$ in terms of $y$, $m$ and $n$, or equivalent merit
Expands the $y^2$ equation, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Note that students who automatically assumed $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$ can only receive 2 out of 3 marks maximum, as they assumed the terms were equal prior to showing the terms form an arithmetic sequence
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the denominator of $T_2-T_1$ is $2mn$ (source printed $\dfrac{m+n-2n}{2n}=\dfrac{m-n}{2n}$).

questions.stem:
A tall pole $OT$ is held in place vertically by ropes anchored by two pegs in the ground 10 metres apart at $A$ and $B$ as shown. $A$ is due west of $O$, and $B$ is at a bearing of $240^\circ\text{T}$ from $O$. The rope connecting the top of the pole $T$ to the peg at $A$ is $3\sqrt{3}$ metres long and makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground.

\exfigure{1367_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}$ metres.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence or otherwise, find the length of the rope, $\ell$, connecting $T$ and $B$.

Give your answer to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

figures.cap: 3D diagram: vertical pole OT, pegs A (due west of O) and B on the ground, AB = 10 m, TA = 3√3 m at 60° to the ground, TB = ℓ, bearing 240° from O

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $AOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{3\sqrt{3}}\\ AO&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is due west of $O$ (bearing $270^\circ$) and $B$ is on a bearing of $240^\circ$ from $O$:
$$\angle AOB=270^\circ-240^\circ=30^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}10^2&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2+(OB)^2-2\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(OB)\cos 30^\circ\\ 100&=\dfrac{27}{4}+(OB)^2-3\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(OB)\\ (OB)^2-\dfrac{9}{2}(OB)-\dfrac{373}{4}&=0\\ 4(OB)^2-18(OB)-373&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}OB&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{18^2-4\times 4\times(-373)}}{2\times 4}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{6292}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm 22\sqrt{13}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pm 11\sqrt{13}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $OB>0$:
$$OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\text{ metres}$$

parts.latex:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y=\ln(kx)$, where $k>0$.

Find the value of $m$, in terms of $k$.

dif.r: two tangency conditions give x=e/k then m

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point of contact:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(kx)\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{k}{kx}=\dfrac{1}{x}\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
At the point of contact the line and the curve meet:
$$mx=\ln(kx)$$
Substituting $m=\dfrac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(kx)&=\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ \ln(kx)&=1\\ kx&=e\\ x&=\dfrac{e}{k}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore m=\dfrac{1}{\frac{e}{k}}=\dfrac{k}{e}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ in terms of $k$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Two curves $y=2e^{-x}$ and $y=e^x-1$ intersect at point $P$.

\exfigure{1367_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the coordinates of $P$ are $(\ln 2,1)$.

dif.r: quadratic in e^x, reject negative root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, calculate the shaded area in simplest exact form.

dif.r: standard area between exponentials, ln2 bounds

figures.cap: curves y = 2e^{-x} and y = e^x - 1 intersecting at P; region between the curves and the y-axis, left of P, shaded

solutions.latex:
At $P$ the curves meet; multiplying by $e^x$ gives a quadratic in $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x-1&=2e^{-x}\\ e^{2x}-e^x-2&=0\\ \left(e^x-2\right)\left(e^x+1\right)&=0\\ e^x&=-1\text{ or } e^x=2\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x&=2\\ x&=\ln 2\\ y&=e^{\ln 2}-1\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore P(\ln 2,1)$$
criteria: Factorises the exponential equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le\ln 2$, $y=2e^{-x}$ lies above $y=e^x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\ln 2}\left(2e^{-x}-e^x+1\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-2e^{-x}-e^x+x\Big]_0^{\ln 2}\\ &=-2e^{-\ln 2}-e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2-\left(-2e^0-e^0+0\right)\\ &=-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-2+\ln 2-(-2-1)\\ &=\ln 2-3+3\\ &=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for the area, or equivalent merit

\exfigure{1367_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Using the trapezoidal rule with 4 function values, find the approximate shaded area in exact form.

dif.r: trapezoidal, three strips, exact logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,(x\ln x)$.

dif.r: direct product rule

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_1^7\ln x\,dx$.

dif.r: reverse differentiation from (b), definite, subtract int 1

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Deduce that $\ln 7\approx\dfrac{1}{3}\,(\ln 3+\ln 5)+1$.

dif.r: equate estimate to exact value, rearrange logs

figures.cap: graph of y = ln x with the region under the curve from x = 1 to x = 7 shaded; x-axis ticks 1 to 7

solutions.latex:
Four function values give three strips:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=\dfrac{7-1}{3}\\ &=2\end{aligned}$$
so $x=1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$:

\extable{Ts1403_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}\left[0+\ln 7+2(\ln 3+\ln 5)\right]\\ &=2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)&=\ln x+\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ &=\ln x+1\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Progress towards the answer, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrating both sides of the result from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^7(\ln x+1)\,dx&=\int_1^7\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)\,dx\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx+\int_1^7dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7\\ &=7\ln 7-0-(7-1)\\ &=7\ln 7-6\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates both sides of the equation in part (b), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The trapezoidal estimate in part (a) approximates the integral in part (c), so
$$\begin{aligned}7\ln 7-6&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\\ 6\ln 7&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+6\\ \ln 7&\approx\dfrac{1}{3}(\ln 3+\ln 5)+1\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot{x}=4\sin 2t$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin moving to the left at 1 metre per second.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$.

dif.r: integrate sine, initial velocity -1 from direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.

dif.r: trig equation cos2t=1/2, smallest positive t

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds.

dif.r: distance with direction change at pi/6, two integrals

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity graph x-dot = 1 - 2cos 2t from t = 0 to π/2, crossing zero at π/6; regions below and above the axis hatched

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int 4\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-2\cos 2t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle moves left at $1$ m/s, so $\dot{x}=-1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&=-2\cos 0+C\\ C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$$
criteria: Integrates the acceleration, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-2\cos 2t&=0\\ \cos 2t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\quad(\text{smallest positive solution})\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Correct expression for the distance, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the perimeter of the rectangle is given by:

$$2x+2\sqrt{25-4x^2}$$

dif.r: sector geometry: tan ratio and Pythagoras to build perimeter

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the maximum perimeter of the rectangle. Leave your answer in exact form.

dif.r: chain rule with root, solve surd equation, exact max

figures.cap: sector OAB of radius 5 m with angle θ at O; rectangle PQRS with R, S on OA, Q on OB, P on the arc; OR = x, RS = y

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $QOR$, with $\tan\theta=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{QR}{x}\\ QR&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$PS=QR=2x$ (opposite sides of the rectangle). Applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle $POS$ (hypotenuse $OP=5$, the radius):
$$\begin{aligned}(x+y)^2+PS^2&=OP^2\\ (x+y)^2+(2x)^2&=5^2\\ (x+y)^2&=25-4x^2\end{aligned}$$
Since $x+y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x+y&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ y&=-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is $2QR+2RS$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2(2x)+2\left(-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\right)\\ &=2x+2\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$

Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2x+2\left(25-4x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dP}{dx}&=2+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(25-4x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-8x)\\ &=2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=0\\ \dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=2\\ 4x&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ 16x^2&=25-4x^2\\ 20x^2&=25\\ x^2&=\dfrac{5}{4}\\ x&=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts1411_1}

$\therefore$ the maximum is at $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}+2\sqrt{25-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{5}+2\sqrt{20}\\ &=5\sqrt{5}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows the maximum at this $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Two independent events $A$ and $B$ are given such that $P(A)=m$ and $P(B)=m+0.4$.

It is known that $P(A\cap B)=0.21$.

What is the value of $P(A\cup B)$?

dif.r: independence gives quadratic in m, then union

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
$$\begin{aligned} m(m+0.4)&=0.21\\ m^2+0.4m-0.21&=0\\ (m+0.7)(m-0.3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
A probability cannot be negative, so $m=0.3$, giving $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.7$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\ &=0.3+0.7-0.21\\ &=0.79 \end{aligned}$$

Let $f(x)$ be a continuous and differentiable function for all real values of $x$.

The following facts are known.

\begin{itemize}
\item $f'(-x)=f'(x)$
\item $f'(x)\neq0$
\item $f(0)=f''(0)=0$
\end{itemize}

Which of the following statements is always true?

dif.r: abstract: even derivative implies odd function, reject POI

solutions.latex:
$f'(-x)=f'(x)$, so $f'$ is even and its primitive can be written $f(x)=g(x)+c$ with $g$ odd.

$f(0)=0$ gives $c=0$, so $f(x)$ is an odd function.

$f''(0)=0$ alone does not guarantee a change in concavity: $f(x)=x$ satisfies all three facts and has no point of inflection, so $(0,0)$ need not be a point of inflection.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+5x$.

Use the definition $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ to find the derivative of $f(x)$.

Expanding $f(x+h)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)&=3(x+h)^2+5(x+h)\\ &=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)-f(x)&=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h-(3x^2+5x)\\ &=6xh+3h^2+5h \end{aligned}$$
Using the definition:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{6xh+3h^2+5h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(6x+3h+5) \end{aligned}$$
Apply the limit by letting $h=0$:
$$\therefore \dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x+5$$
criteria: Finds correct expression for $f(x+h)-f(x)$, or equivalent merit

At $A$, $AC$ makes $30^\circ$ with due south (alternate angles, $BC$ parallel to the north line), so
$$\angle BAC=294^\circ-180^\circ-30^\circ=84^\circ$$
$\angle CBA=180^\circ-84^\circ-30^\circ=66^\circ$ (angle sum of $\triangle ABC$)

Using the sine rule, with $AB=18$ opposite the $30^\circ$ angle:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AC}{\sin66^\circ}&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\\ AC&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\times\sin66^\circ\\ &=32.88763648 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{BC}{\sin84^\circ}&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\times\sin84^\circ\\ &=35.80278823 \end{aligned}$$
Perimeter of the triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=18+32.88763648+35.80278823\\ &=86.6904\ldots\\ &\approx86.7 \text{ (3 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The total length of the race is 86.7 km, correct to three significant figures.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{\ln(x-1)}{x-1}$ at the point $(2,0)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln(x-1) & v&=x-1\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x-1} & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{x-1}\times(x-1)-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\dfrac{1-\ln(2-1)}{(2-1)^2}=1$$
Hence the gradient of the normal is $-1$ (negative reciprocal).

Using the point-gradient formula for the normal through $(2,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-1(x-2)\\ \therefore\ y&=2-x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the equation of the tangent instead of the normal, or finds the gradient of the normal but not the equation of the normal, or equivalent merit

A plane is flying through clouds to drop a water quality monitoring system onto a lake.

solutions.latex:
The rectangle is 450 m wide and 700 m long.

The centre measurement of the lake is
$$450-70-80=300$$
Using the trapezoidal rule with 2 strips along the 700 m length, $h=\dfrac{700}{2}=350$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of lake}&\approx\dfrac{350}{2}(80+2\times300+100)\\ &=136\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of rectangle}=700\times450=315\,000 \text{ m}^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{success})&=\dfrac{\text{Area of lake}}{\text{Area of rectangle}}\\ &=\dfrac{136\,500}{315\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The probability that the monitoring system will drop onto the lake is $\dfrac{13}{30}$, or about $43.3\%$.
criteria: Correctly finds the area of the lake and the rectangle, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the perimeter of the 24th square in this sequence?

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the total perimeter of all the squares after the robot draws the 24th square.

dif.r: direct S_24 times 4

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The amount of ink in the robot's pen can only draw up to a maximum of 12 000 cm. How many complete squares can the robot draw using the one pen?

dif.r: quadratic inequality in n from S_n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: three squares of sides 5 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm joined corner to corner in a staircase; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
The side lengths form the arithmetic sequence $5, 8, 11, \ldots$ with first term $a=5$ and common difference $d=3$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $n=24$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{24}&=5+(24-1)\times3\\ &=74 \end{aligned}$$
The side length of the 24th square is 74 cm, and its perimeter is 4 times the side length:
$$4\times74=296$$
$\therefore$ The perimeter of the 24th square is 296 cm.
criteria: Uses correct formula to get side length of 24th square but does not multiply by 4 to obtain perimeter, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The perimeter of the first square is $4\times5=20$ cm and the perimeter of the 24th square is 296 cm.

Using the arithmetic series formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{24}&=\dfrac{24}{2}(20+296)\\ &=3792 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The total perimeter of the first 24 squares is 3792 cm.

12 000 cm is the total perimeter the robot can draw. Dividing by 4 gives the series in terms of side length instead of perimeter:
$$12\,000\div4=3000$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $S_n=3000$, $a=5$ and $d=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3000&=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times5+(n-1)3\big)\\ 6000&=n(10+3n-3)\\ 6000&=3n^2+7n\\ 0&=3n^2+7n-6000 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$n=-45.9 \text{ or } n=43.6$$
$n>0$, so the negative answer is invalid.

$n=43.6$ means the robot draws 43 complete squares plus part of the 44th square.

$\therefore$ The robot can draw 43 complete squares with one pen.
criteria: Attempts to solve for $n$ using the appropriate sum formula without regard to the perimeter of each square, or correctly forms an arithmetic series based on the perimeter of each successive square and attempts to solve for $n$, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} f(-4)&=10 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(4)&=66 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(-3)&=17 &&\text{stationary point}\\ f(1)&=-15 &&\text{stationary point} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(0)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, hence a point of inflection exists at $x=-1$.

$\therefore$ The point of inflection is at $(-1,1)$.

questions.stem:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation

$$C=100\left(1-2^{-kt}\right).$$

The battery is charged to 35\% capacity after 50 minutes.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 0.01243, correct to 4 significant figures.

dif.r: show k: rearrange and solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
To prolong the service life of the battery, the charger may be set to switch off when the battery reaches 90\% capacity.

For how long will the battery be on charge until it reaches 90\% capacity?

dif.r: rearrange exponential model, solve with logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By considering the first and second derivatives, describe the behaviour of $C$ for $t\ge0$ if the battery is left on charge indefinitely.

dif.r: signs of C prime, C double prime and limit describe behaviour

solutions.latex:
Substituting $C=35$ and $t=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} 35&=100\left(1-2^{-50k}\right)\\ 0.35&=1-2^{-50k}\\ 2^{-50k}&=0.65\\ -50k\ln(2)&=\ln(0.65) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(0.65)}{-50\ln(2)}\\ &=0.0124297\ldots\\ \therefore\ k&=0.01243 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes values for $C$ and $t$ into equation with some manipulation and attempts to use logarithms to solve for $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substituting $C=90$ and $k=0.01243$:
$$\begin{aligned} 90&=100\left(1-2^{-0.01243t}\right)\\ 0.1&=2^{-0.01243t}\\ -0.01243t\ln(2)&=\ln(0.1) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln(0.1)}{-0.01243\ln(2)}\\ &=267.2508\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The battery will be on charge for 267.25 minutes (2 dec. pl.), or 4 hours 27 minutes.
criteria: Attempts to solve for $t$ when $C=90$ with $k=0.01243$ and showing some algebraic manipulation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Initially ($t=0$), $C=0$.

For $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, hence $C\to100$ as $t\to\infty$.

Describing the rate of change using the first and second derivatives:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln(2)\times2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln2)^2\times2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Given $k>0$, for all $t>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&>0 &&\text{capacity increasing}\\ C''&<0 &&\text{rate of increase decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never (theoretically) reach $100\%$ charge.
criteria: Provides a brief description of the behaviour of the function by either considering the rate of change over time OR the behaviour of $C$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{3x+1}} & 1\le x\le5\ (\text{where } A>0)\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $A$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

dif.r: integral of root pdf equals 1, show A

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that $P(X<c)=3P(X>c)$, find the value of $c$.

dif.r: twin of HSC: build CDF, ratio condition to F(c)=0.75

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} A\int_1^5(3x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}\left[\sqrt{3x+1}\right]_1^5&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}(4-2)&=1\\ \dfrac{4A}{3}&=1\\ \therefore\ A&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly sets up integral equation with some progress toward solving equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le5$, using $A=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_1^x\dfrac{3}{4}(3t+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{3t+1}\right]_1^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3x+1}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$P(X<c)=F(c)$ and $P(X>c)=1-F(c)$, so solve
$$\begin{aligned} F(c)&=3\big(1-F(c)\big)\\ F(c)&=3-3F(c)\\ 4F(c)&=3\\ F(c)&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3c+1}-1&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \sqrt{3c+1}&=\dfrac{7}{2}\\ 3c+1&=\dfrac{49}{4}\\ 3c&=\dfrac{45}{4}\\ \therefore\ c&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ and sets up equation with some progress, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $l=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x}$, given that the box is open at the top.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of 1200 cm$^2$.

figures.cap: open rectangular box with length l, height x and width 2x; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
The box is open at the top, so the sheet metal forms the base and the 4 sides, with total area $k$ cm$^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+lx+lx+2x^2+2x^2\\ &=4lx+4x^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ \therefore\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

Let $V$ be the volume of the prism. Using $V=lwh$ and part (a) with $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V'&=600-6x^2\\ V''&=-12x \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2&=600\\ x&=\pm10 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$ since it represents a side length, so $x=10$.

$V''<0$ when $x=10$, hence the volume is maximised when $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2\times(10)^2\times\left(\dfrac{1200-4\times(10)^2}{4\times(10)}\right)\\ &=4000 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The maximum volume of the box is 4000 cm$^3$.

Solve $h(t)=11$ (11 000 km):

For $0\le t\le24$, $-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\le\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)&=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ t-15&=-11,\ -7,\ 1,\ 5\\ t&=4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 20 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{641_q30_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function

$$v_P=3t^2-6t+4,$$

where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times $t=0$ and $t=4$
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the equation for the velocity, $v_Q$, of car $Q$ is given by $v_Q=6t+4$.

dif.r: read intersections from graph, linear velocity from two points

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.

dif.r: equate displacements of two cars from integrated velocities

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: straight line Q and parabola P starting at the same point on the v-axis and crossing again; NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
Car $Q$ has constant acceleration, so its velocity is linear in $t$: $v_Q=mt+c$.

At $t=0$: $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$:
$$v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$$
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6\\ c&=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$
criteria: Finds an equation in the form $y=mx+c$ with correct gradient and incorrect $y$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The signed area between curves $P$ and $Q$ represents the relative displacement between the cars.

The cars are at the same displacement from the start when the displacement between them is zero, so solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a\left(3t^2-12t\right)dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=6$: the cars are the same distance from the start at $t=6$.

The integrand $3t^2-12t$ is the velocity of $P$ relative to $Q$, and $v_P>v_Q$ for $t>4$.

Hence car $P$ passes car $Q$ 6 seconds after the start of the race.
criteria: Finds an integral that represents the area between $P$ and $Q$ and attempts to find a time $t$ $(t>0)$ when relative displacement is zero, or equivalent merit
Understands that relative displacement between both cars is represented by the signed area between $P$ and $Q$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=1-x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\cdots$, where $0<x<1$.

By considering $f'(x)$, show that $f(a)-f(b)=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right)$.

dif.r: f' as GP limiting sum, integrate to log, subtract

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=-1+x-x^2+x^3-\cdots$$
This is a geometric series with first term $-1$ and common ratio $-x$.

Since $0<x<1$, the geometric series has a limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=S_\infty\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1-(-x)}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1+x} \end{aligned}$$
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-\int\dfrac{1}{1+x}\,dx\\ &=-\ln(1+x)+C \end{aligned}$$
The constant $C$ cancels in the difference:
$$\begin{aligned} f(a)-f(b)&=-\ln(1+a)-\big(-\ln(1+b)\big)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\right)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\div\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\times\dfrac{1+b}{1}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $f(x)$ by integrating $S_\infty$, or equivalent merit
Recognises that the expression for $f'(x)$ forms a geometric series with limiting sum with first term $-1$ and common ratio $-x$, or equivalent merit
Finds an expression for $f'(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the common ratio of $-1+x-x^2+\cdots$ is $-x$ (as the working uses), not $x$.

questions.stem: Let $C$ be the circle with equation $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$, and $\ell$ the line given by the equation $y=x+d$ for some real constant $d$.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page images (default review)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$, then $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points.

dif.r: discriminant in d with heavy algebra, surd bounds

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Let $A$ and $B$ be the two points of intersection in part (a).

It is given that the distance between $A$ and $B$ is $2\sqrt{3}$ units.

By determining the coordinates of $A$ and $B$, find a possible value of $d$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: chord length from root difference, solve for d

solutions.latex:
Solve $y=x+d$ and $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$ simultaneously. By substitution:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-1)^2+(x+d-3)^2&=9\\ (x-1)^2+\big(x+(d-3)\big)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2x(d-3)+(d-3)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2dx-6x+d^2-6d+9&=9\\ 2x^2+2dx-8x+d^2-6d+1&=0\\ 2x^2+(2d-8)x+(d^2-6d+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
This non-monic quadratic has 2 distinct real solutions if its discriminant $D>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} D&=(2d-8)^2-4(2)(d^2-6d+1)\\ &=4d^2-32d+64-8d^2+48d-8\\ &=-4d^2+16d+56 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula to find the values of $d$ when $D=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{(16)^2+4(4)(56)}}{2(-4)}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{1152}}{-8}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm24\sqrt{2}}{-8}\\ &=2\pm3\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$D$ is a concave-down quadratic in $d$ with roots $2\pm3\sqrt{2}$, hence $D>0$ for
$$2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$$
$\therefore$ $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$.
criteria: Recognises that discriminant $>0$ for 2 distinct real solutions and attempts to use quadratic formula to find values of $d$, or equivalent merit
Finds an equation involving $x$ and $d$ by solving equation of $\ell$ and $C$ simultaneously, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the square of (d-3) is (d-3)^2, not (d+3)^2; the next line already expands it as d^2-6d+9.

solutions.latex:
Solving the equation from part (a) with the quadratic formula gives the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$:
$$2x^2+(2d-8)x+d^2-6d+1=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_1&=\dfrac{8-2d-\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ x_2&=\dfrac{8-2d+\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Using $y=x+d$ for the corresponding $y$-coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned} y_1&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ y_2&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
So $x_2-x_1=y_2-y_1=\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}$. Using the distance formula with $AB=2\sqrt{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2}&=2\sqrt{3}\\ \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2&=12\\ D&=24 \end{aligned}$$
Solving $-4d^2+16d+56=24$, first dividing all terms by $-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2-4d-8&=0\\ d&=2\pm2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Possible values of $d$ are $2-2\sqrt{3}$ or $2+2\sqrt{3}$.
criteria: Finds the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ in terms of $d$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
An athlete runs for 500 metres around a circular track with radius 200 metres.

How far, in a direct line across the field, is the athlete from her starting position?

dif.r: arc gives radian angle, then cosine rule chord

figures.cap: solution sketch: circle with two radii of 200 enclosing angle theta, chord x, arc 500

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q2_s1}

Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} 500&=200\theta\\ \theta&=2.5 \end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in the triangle formed by the two radii and the direct line $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=200^2+200^2-2\times 200\times 200\times\cos 2.5\\ &=144091.4892\ldots\\ x&=379.59\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The distance is about 380 m.

parts.latex:
A set of scores in a data set has a median of 72, an interquartile range of 14 and a variance of 4.

Each score has 3 added to it and each resulting score is then doubled to form a new set of scores.

What is the median, interquartile range, and variance of the new set of scores?
parts.note: Effect of linear changes on median, IQR and variance of a data set · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
The median is a specific score, so it also has 3 added and is then doubled.

The interquartile range and variance are measures of spread, so they are unaffected by adding 3 to each score; doubling multiplies the IQR by 2 and the variance by $2^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median}&=(72+3)\times 2\\ &=150 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=14\times 2\\ &=28 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Variance}&=4\times 2^2\\ &=16 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: How many solutions does $\sec\theta+\tan\theta=0$ have for $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$?

dif.r: MCQ: solve, then reject solution where cos=0 (excluded domain)

solutions.latex:
Writing $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, for $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=0\\ 1+\sin\theta&=0,\quad \cos\theta\ne 0\\ \sin\theta&=-1\\ \theta&=-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
But $\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$, so $\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is not allowed.

$\therefore$ There are no solutions.

parts.latex: Let $g(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$. What is the domain of the composite function $g(g(x))$?

dif.r: nested root domain: two conditions on g(g(x))

solutions.latex:
$$g(g(x))=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2-x}}$$
The inner square root needs $2-x\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2-x&\ge 0\\ x&\le 2 \end{aligned}$$
The outer square root needs $2-\sqrt{2-x}\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\sqrt{2-x}&\ge 0\\ \sqrt{2-x}&\le 2\\ 0\le 2-x&\le 4 &&(\text{square})\\ -2\le -x&\le 2 &&(\text{subtract } 2)\\ -2\le x&\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } -1) \end{aligned}$$
Both conditions hold for $-2\le x\le 2$.

parts.latex: Which of the following shows the graph of $f(x)=(x+a)^2(b-x)$, if $a>0$ and $b>0$?

dif.r: match double root, single root, leading sign

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

option B: cubic rising from bottom left through a negative x-intercept, maximum on the y-axis, touching the x-axis at a positive x value, then rising

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=(x+a)^2(b-x)$ with $a>0$ and $b>0$:

Double root at $x=-a<0$, so the graph touches the $x$-axis left of the origin.

Single root at $x=b>0$, so the graph crosses the $x$-axis right of the origin.

As $x\to\infty$, $y\to-\infty$ (leading term $-x^3$).

The keyed graph is the one with all three features.

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_1^6 f(x)\,dx=-2$ and $\displaystyle\int_3^6 f(x)\,dx=6$, what is the value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3\big(f(x)+x\big)\,dx$?

parts.latex: $ABC$ is a triangle in which $\cos A=-\dfrac{2}{5}$. Find the exact value of $\tan A$.

dif.r: obtuse angle sign, Pythagoras, exact tan

figures.cap: solution sketch: right-angled triangle with angle A, hypotenuse 5, adjacent side 2, opposite side x

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q11_s1}

$\cos A=-\dfrac{2}{5}$, so the reference triangle has adjacent side 2 and hypotenuse 5.

Using Pythagoras' theorem in the reference triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=5^2-2^2\\ x&=\sqrt{21} \end{aligned}$$
$\cos A<0$, so $A$ is obtuse and $\tan A<0$.
$$\therefore \tan A=-\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$$
criteria: Finds the third side in the triangle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $|3x+2|=4$

dif.r: routine absolute value equation, two cases

solutions.latex:
$|3x+2|=4$ means $3x+2=4$ or $3x+2=-4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x+2&=4\\ 3x&=2\\ x&=\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
or
$$\begin{aligned} 3x+2&=-4\\ 3x&=-6\\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ or } x=-2$$
criteria: Provides one correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\log_2 x$ at the point where $x=4$.

dif.r: log base 2 derivative, point-gradient tangent

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\dfrac{1}{x\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{(\ln 2)x}\\ m_T&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2} &&(x=4) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=4$, $y=\log_2 4=2$.

Using the point-gradient formula:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\ y-2&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}(x-4)\\ y&=\dfrac{x}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}+2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct $y'$ AND either correct gradient or $y$ value, or equivalent merit
Finds correct $y'$ OR correct $y$ value, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{(2x+1)^2}{4+x}$ with respect to $x$

dif.r: quotient rule with chain rule numerator

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(2x+1)^2 & v&=4+x\\ u'&=2(2x+1)\times 2 & v'&=1\\ &=8x+4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{(2x+1)^2}{4+x}\right]&=\dfrac{(4+x)(8x+4)-(2x+1)^2(1)}{(4+x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{32x+16+8x^2+4x-\left(4x^2+4x+1\right)}{(4+x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4x^2+32x+15}{(4+x)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2e^{x^2}\right)=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right)$.

dif.r: show given derivative: product and chain, factorise

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence show that $y=x^2e^{x^2}$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.

dif.r: sign of factors to justify decreasing for x<0

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{x^2}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=2xe^{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2e^{x^2}\right)&=e^{x^2}\times 2x+x^2\times 2xe^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}+2x^3e^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $y'=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right)$. When $x<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&<0\\ e^{x^2}&>0\\ 1+x^2&>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\text{negative}\times\text{positive}\times\text{positive}\\ &=\text{negative} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $y$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x}\,dx$

dif.r: f'/f with factor 1/2

solutions.latex:
The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator, so the integral has the form $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{2x-6}{x^2-6x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|x^2-6x\right|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the integral is of the form $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A bag of potatoes is labelled as having a net weight of 2 kilograms. The packaging process produces bags of potatoes whose weights are normally distributed with a mean of 2.05 kilograms and a standard deviation of 0.05 kilograms.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: In a supermarket selling 2000 of these bags of potatoes, how many bags will contain less than the labelled weight?

dif.r: z=-1, empirical rule, scale to 2000

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b

dif.r: inverse table lookup for top 20%, solve x

figures.cap: standard normal curve with the area to the left of z shaded
solution sketch: normal curve for weight (kg) with mean 2.05 and the area below 2 shaded; 34% between 2 and 2.05

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q19_s1}

The labelled weight is 2 kg:
$$z=\dfrac{2-2.05}{0.05}=-1$$
By the empirical rule, $34\%$ of bags lie between $z=-1$ and the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(z<-1)&=50\%-34\%\\ &=16\% \end{aligned}$$
$$16\%\times 2000=320$$
$\therefore$ 320 bags contain less than the labelled weight.
criteria: Provides correct percentage, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The heaviest $20\%$ lie above the weight with $P(Z<z)=0.8$.

From the table, $z=0.84$.

Converting back using $x=\mu+z\sigma$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2.05+0.84\times 0.05\\ &=2.092\text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The heaviest $20\%$ of bags weigh more than 2.092 kg.
criteria: Identifies the correct probability from the table, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Sixty people visited a swimming pool one afternoon. Thirteen out of the twenty-three people who wore goggles were adults. There were nineteen children.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the two-way table below, showing this information.

\extable{335_q20_t1}

dif.r: complete two-way table by subtraction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If an adult is selected at random, what is the probability they were wearing goggles?

dif.r: conditional from table, adults derived

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
An additional group of adults, not wearing goggles, arrived at the pool.

The probability that a person selected at random is an adult who is not wearing goggles is now 0.6.

How many additional adults arrived?

dif.r: set up linear equation for added adults

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts2175_1}
criteria: Completes the table with up to three errors, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
There are $60-19=41$ adults, 13 of whom wore goggles.
$$P(\text{goggles}\mid\text{adult})=\dfrac{13}{41}$$

Let $x$ be the number of additional adults.

There are $41-13=28$ adults not wearing goggles, and $60+x$ people in total.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{adult not wearing goggles})&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ \dfrac{3}{5}&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ 3(60+x)&=5(28+x)\\ 180+3x&=140+5x\\ 40&=2x\\ x&=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 20 additional adults arrived.
criteria: Finds an expression for $P(\text{adult not wearing goggles})$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine the nature of the stationary points.

dif.r: f' given: factorise, second-derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The curve $y=f(x)$ has a $y$-intercept at $y=-2$.

Find an expression for $f(x)$.

dif.r: integrate quadratic, find C from y-intercept

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve, clearly indicating the stationary points and intercepts on the axes.

dif.r: factor by grouping for x-intercept, sketch cubic

parts.label: d
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is the curve concave down?

dif.r: f''<0 linear inequality

figures.cap: solution sketch: cubic y = (x^2+1)(x-2) with maximum (1/3, -50/27), minimum (1, -2), x-intercept 2 and y-intercept -2

solutions.latex:
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3},\ 1 \end{aligned}$$
For the nature of the stationary points, consider the sign of $f''(x)$.
$$f''(x)=6x-4$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=6\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } x=\dfrac{1}{3}\\ f''(1)&=6(1)-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } x=1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct $x$ coordinates AND correct expression for $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit
Provides correct $x$ coordinates OR correct expression for $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(3x^2-4x+1\right)dx\\ &=x^3-2x^2+x+c \end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept is $-2$, so $f(0)=-2$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x-2$$
criteria: Provides a correct primitive without evaluating $c$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Factorising to find the $x$-intercept:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-2x^2+x-2\\ &=x^2(x-2)+1(x-2)\\ &=\left(x^2+1\right)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$x^2+1>0$, so the only $x$-intercept is $x=2$.

The $y$-values of the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2\\ &=-\dfrac{50}{27} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(1)&=(1)^3-2(1)^2+(1)-2\\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{335_q21_s1}
criteria: Provides a graph with some correct features, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct graph with points indicated as required

solutions.latex:
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$. From part (a), $f''(x)=6x-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-4&<0\\ 6x&<4\\ x&<\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A|B)=0.4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $P(A\cup B)=0.6$

dif.r: intersection from conditional, then addition rule

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)$

dif.r: complement of union

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

req: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events
A.note: Relies on the value from part (a)

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A|B)\times P(B)\\ &=0.4\times 0.5\\ &=0.2 \end{aligned}$$
Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\ &=0.3+0.5-0.2\\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use conditional probability formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the complement of $A\cup B$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)&=1-P(A\cup B)\\ &=1-0.6\\ &=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the expected value $E(X)$

dif.r: direct sum of x P(x)

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} p^2+p+p^2+p+2p^2+p&=1\\ 4p^2+3p-1&=0\\ (4p-1)(p+1)&=0\\ p&=\dfrac{1}{4}\text{ or }-1 \end{aligned}$$
But $p\ge 0$ (it is a probability), thus $p=\dfrac{1}{4}$.
criteria: Provides correct simplified equation involving $p$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $p=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\sum x\cdot p(x)\\ &=0\left(\dfrac{5}{16}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+3\left(2\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{31}{16} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\log_e(1+\sin x)-\log_e(1-\sin x)=2\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)$

dif.r: log laws combined with identities and difference of squares

solutions.latex:
Starting from the right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)&=\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)^2\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)^2\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{\cos^2 x}\right)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{1-\sin^2 x}\right) &&(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{(1+\sin x)(1-\sin x)}\right)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x}\right)\\ &=\log_e(1+\sin x)-\log_e(1-\sin x) \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a

dif.r: trapezoidal, four strips, surd values

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
