dif.r: concave down so trapezia under curve: underestimate

figures.cap: solution sketch: quarter circle of radius 1 in the first quadrant with its area shaded

solutions.latex:
The strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
so the $x$ values are $0,\ \dfrac{1}{4},\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{3}{4},\ 1$.

\extable{Ts2191_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{8}\left[1+0+2\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{15}{16}}+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}}+\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{16}}\right)\right]\\ &\approx 0.748927\ldots \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct function values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q28_s1}

$y=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ for $0\le x\le1$ is the quarter of the unit circle in the first quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx&=\text{area of quadrant}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times 1^2\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Using the estimate from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{4}&\approx 0.748927\ldots\\ \pi&\approx 2.99570\ldots\\ &\approx 2.996 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct exact value of the definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: The curve is concave down, so all trapeziums used to estimate its area sit entirely below the curve, and the estimate of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and hence of $\pi$, is too small.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\equiv\sec^2 x$.

dif.r: reciprocal trig simplification to sec^2 show-that

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx$

dif.r: f'(f)^2 form with tan x via (a), exact

solutions.latex:
Writing $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{1}{\sin x}-\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} &&(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1)\\ &=\sec^2 x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression in terms of $\sin x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using part (a), the integrand is $\tan^2 x\sec^2 x$, which has the form $f'(x)\big[f(x)\big]^2$ with $f(x)=\tan x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\sec^2 x\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^3 x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\tan^3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\tan^3(0)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^3-0\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(3\sqrt{3}\right)\\ &=\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the integral is of the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\big[f(x)\big]^n\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A wire of length $L$ is bent to form a sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\theta=\dfrac{L-2r}{r}$.

dif.r: perimeter of sector, rearrange

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the area $A$ of the sector is maximised when $r=\dfrac{L}{4}$.

dif.r: parametric sector area, maximise quadratic in r

figures.cap: solution sketch: sector with radii r, angle theta and arc length l = r theta

criteria: Provides an expression for $L$ in terms of $r$ and $\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: denominator of the last line is r, not theta.

solutions.latex:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ with $\theta$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{L-2r}{r}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{Lr}{2}-r^2 \end{aligned}$$
For maximum area, need
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=0\\ \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}&<0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=\dfrac{L}{2}-2r\\ 0&=\dfrac{L}{2}-2r\\ 2r&=\dfrac{L}{2}\\ r&=\dfrac{L}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-2<0$$
Thus area is maximised when $r=\dfrac{L}{4}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

dif.r: equate curves, tan^2 x=1/3, choose root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By considering $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $x$ axis between $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

dif.r: split region, two log primitives of tan and cot

figures.cap: graphs of y = 3 tan x (increasing through the origin) and y = cot x (decreasing, crossing the x-axis at pi/2), intersecting at A in the first quadrant

solutions.latex:
At $A$, the curves are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\tan x&=\cot x\\ 3\tan^2 x&=1\\ \tan^2 x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\\ \tan x&=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ \ldots \end{aligned}$$
But at $A$, $x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, thus $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
criteria: Provides a correct equation involving $\tan^2 x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The region lies under $y=3\tan x$ from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and under $y=\cot x$ from $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}3\tan x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,dx\\ &=3\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx\\ &=-3\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx\\ &=-3\Big[\ln|\cos x|\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}+\Big[\ln|\sin x|\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-3\left[\ln\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\ln(\cos 0)\right]+\left[\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]\\ &=-3\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\ln(1)\right]+\left[\ln(1)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\ &=-3\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)+\ln 2\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides an antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Provides an integral expression for the area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A farming company harvests oranges to sell to grocery stores. Oranges that weigh less than 150 grams are rejected and used for juicing instead. Typically, 16% of all oranges are rejected. Also, oranges that are larger than 300 grams are reserved for restaurants. Typically, 2.5% of all oranges are sold to restaurants.

If the weights of the oranges are normally distributed, find the mean and standard deviation of the normal distribution.

dif.r: 16% and 2.5% give z=-1, z=2; simultaneous for mu, sigma

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: solution sketch: normal curve for weight (g) with 68-95-99.7 percentages; 150 g one standard deviation below the mean, 300 g two above, tails shaded

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q34_s1}

Using the empirical rule:

$16\%$ lies below 150 g, so 150 g is one standard deviation below the mean.

$2.5\%$ lies above 300 g, so 300 g is two standard deviations above the mean.

So 150 g to 300 g spans 3 standard deviations:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation}&=(300-150)\div 3\\ &=50\text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean}&=150+50\\ &=200\text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards finding a correct solution, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k(\sin(\pi x)+2x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 3\\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}$.

dif.r: trig plus polynomial integral equals 1, solve k

parts.label: b

dif.r: argue area left of mode exceeds half from graph

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the mode of $X$. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: f'=0 gives inverse cos, choose correct root in domain

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

figures.cap: graph of the density function on [0, 3]: rises from the origin to a local maximum, dips to a local minimum, then rises to a higher maximum near x = 3
solution sketch: density graph with a dashed vertical line at the mode, close to x = 3
solution sketch: ASTC quadrant diagram with S and T starred (cosine negative)

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3 k\big(\sin(\pi x)+2x\big)\,dx&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi x)+x^2\right]_0^3\\ 1&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(3\pi)+3^2-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(0)+0^2\right)\right]\\ 1&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(-1)+9+\dfrac{1}{\pi}(1)-0\right]\\ 1&=k\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}+9\right)\\ 1&=k\left(\dfrac{2+9\pi}{\pi}\right)\\ k&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides a correct equation involving a definite integral equal to 1 AND finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Provides a correct equation involving a definite integral equal to 1 OR finds an antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{335_q35_s1}

The mode occurs at the maximum value on the graph.

The median occurs at the point which divides the area under the curve in half.

From the graph, the area to the left of the mode is clearly greater than half the total area.

Thus the median must be to the left of the mode, i.e. $\text{mode}>\text{median}$.

The mode occurs at a maximum turning point. For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}\big(\sin(\pi x)+2x\big)\\ f'(x)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}\big(\pi\cos(\pi x)+2\big)\\ 0&=\pi\cos(\pi x)+2\\ \cos(\pi x)&=-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\\ \pi x&=\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{335_q35_s2}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Reference }\angle&=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)\\ &=0.88068\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\cos(\pi x)<0$, so $\pi x$ is in the second or third quadrant of each revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} \pi x&=\pi-0.88,\ \pi+0.88,\ 3\pi-0.88,\ 3\pi+0.88,\ \ldots\\ &=2.2609,\ 4.0222,\ 8.5440,\ 10.3054,\ \ldots\\ x&=0.72,\ 1.28,\ 2.72,\ 3.28,\ \ldots \end{aligned}$$
But $0\le x\le 3$, and from the graph the mode is the third stationary point.

$\therefore$ The mode is $x=2.72$.
criteria: Finds $x$ value for at least one stationary point, or equivalent merit
Provides an equation involving $\cos(\pi x)$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to find the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{4}{(5-2x)^3}\,dx$?

dif.r: MCQ: reverse chain with negative power, sign care

solutions.latex:
Writing the integrand as a power and using the reverse chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{4}{(5-2x)^3}\,dx&=\int 4(5-2x)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-2\int -2(5-2x)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-2\times\dfrac{(5-2x)^{-2}}{-2}+C\\&=(5-2x)^{-2}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{(5-2x)^2}+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the series $1+1+1+1+\cdots$

What could NOT be said about the series?

dif.r: MCQ: conceptual check of AP/GP/limiting-sum statements

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

options.label: A
options.latex: This is an arithmetic progression with a common difference of $0$.

options.label: B
options.latex: This is a geometric progression with a common ratio of $1$.

options.label: C
options.latex: This series has a limiting sum of $2n$, where $n$ represents the number of terms.

options.label: D
options.latex: The terms of this series can be described by $T_n=T_{n-1}$, where $T_1=1$.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $r=1$.

A limiting sum exists only when $|r|<1$, so this series has no limiting sum; the statement about a limiting sum of $2n$ cannot be said.

The other statements are true: $d=0$, $r=1$ and $T_n=T_{n-1}$ with $T_1=1$.

solutions.latex:
The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$\int_0^h f(x)\,dx=1$$
\exfigure{1371_q10_s1}

At $x=h$:
$$y=1-\left|\dfrac{h}{2}\right|=1-\dfrac{h}{2}$$
The region is a trapezium with parallel sides $1$ and $1-\dfrac{h}{2}$ and width $h$:

questions.stem: The $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by $T_n=5n-3$.

parts.label: a

dif.r: substitute n=1,2,3

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the sum of the first 50 terms.

dif.r: direct S_50

solutions.latex:
Substituting $n=1,2,3$ into $T_n=5n-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=5\times1-3=2\\T_2&=5\times2-3=7\\T_3&=5\times3-3=12\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first 3 terms are $2,7,12$.

meta.marker_note: No half marks.

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ with $a=2$, $d=5$, $n=50$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{50}&=\dfrac{50}{2}\left[2\times2+(50-1)\times5\right]\\&=25\times(4+245)\\&=6225\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, or into $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+\ell)$ with the correct 50th term, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Determine the following with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$

dif.r: divide by sqrt x, integrate three fractional powers

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int16\cos(2x-1)\,dx$

dif.r: direct cos(ax+b) primitive

solutions.latex:
Dividing each term by $\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ (index laws):
$$\begin{aligned}&\int\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\\&=\int\dfrac{x^2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}-\dfrac{3x}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}+\dfrac{4}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,dx\\&=\int x^{\frac{3}{2}}-3x^{\frac{1}{2}}+4x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{\frac{5}{2}}-\dfrac{3x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+\dfrac{4x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\&=\dfrac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}-2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+8x^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct simplification using index laws, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark deducted only once across Booklet 1 for leaving out the constant of integration. Poorly attempted across the whole cohort; simplify first before integrating.

solutions.latex:
Using
$$\int\cos(ax+b)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{a}\sin(ax+b)+C$$
$$\begin{aligned}&\int16\cos(2x-1)\,dx\\&=16\times\dfrac{1}{2}\int2\cos(2x-1)\,dx\\&=8\sin(2x-1)+C\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer (including $+C$). $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark deducted if answer was $-8\sin(2x-1)+C$; $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark deducted only once across Booklet 1 for leaving out the constant of integration.

questions.stem:
Brendan is sitting in a cabin of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of her cabin is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Brendan's cabin first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1371_q15_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 28 metres and a smallest height of 4 metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $c$ and $k$.

dif.r: centre and amplitude from max and min

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many seconds does it take for one complete revolution of the Ferris wheel?

dif.r: period 2pi/n directly

figures.cap: illustration of a Ferris wheel

solutions.latex:
Rearranging:
$$B(t)=-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right)+c$$
so $c$ is the centre and $k$ is the amplitude.

The centre is midway between the greatest and smallest heights:
$$c=\dfrac{28+4}{2}=16$$
The amplitude is the distance from the centre to the greatest height:
$$k=28-16=12$$
$$\therefore c=16,\ k=12$$

meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark deducted if $k=-12$; 1 mark deducted if the values of $k$ and $c$ are switched. Many students struggled with this question.

solutions.latex:
One complete revolution is one period. Using period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{\pi}{28}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{28}}\\&=2\pi\times\dfrac{28}{\pi}\\&=56\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The probability distribution table for a random variable $X$ is given below.

\extable{1371_q16_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the value of $k$.

dif.r: probabilities sum to 1, linear in k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the standard deviation.

dif.r: E(X^2) minus mean squared, square root

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned}k+2k+3k+4k&=1\\10k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{10}\text{ or }0.1\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer as fraction or decimal
meta.marker_note: Accept a fraction or a decimal.

solutions.latex:
From the calculator, $\sigma=1$.

Or, by hand:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)=\mu&=\sum\left[x\times p(x)\right]\\&=1\times0.1+2\times0.2+3\times0.3+4\times0.4\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma^2=\text{Var}(X)&=\sum\left[x^2p(x)\right]-\mu^2\\&=\left[1^2\times0.1+2^2\times0.2+3^2\times0.3+4^2\times0.4\right]-3^2\\&=10-9\\\sigma^2&=1\\\therefore\sigma&=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}$$
Or, using $\text{Var}(X)=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma^2&=(1-3)^2\times0.1+(2-3)^2\times0.2+(3-3)^2\times0.3+(4-3)^2\times0.4\\\sigma^2&=1\\\therefore\sigma&=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Determine the last term under 100 in the sequence below.

$$-11,\quad-4,\quad3,\quad10,\quad17,\quad\ldots$$

dif.r: linear inequality for n then T_n

solutions.latex:
The sequence is arithmetic with $a=-11$, $d=7$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=-11+7(n-1)\\&=-11+7n-7\\&=7n-18\end{aligned}$$
For the terms under 100:
$$\begin{aligned}7n-18&<100\\7n&<118\\n&<16.857\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The largest whole number is $n=16$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{16}&=7(16)-18\\&=94\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the last term under 100 is the 16th term, $94$.
criteria: Finds the correct value of $n$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $1\dfrac{1}{2}$ marks if students stated the 16th term is the last term under 100 with no mention of 94. Show all working and answer the question completely.

parts.latex: Differentiate $\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)$ with respect to $x$.

dif.r: log law split then two standard derivatives

solutions.latex:
Method 1, using the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\log_e(x+1)-\log_e(x-2)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x+1 & v&=x-2\\u'&=1 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}\times\dfrac{(x-2)\times1-(x+1)\times1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{x-2}{x+1}\times\dfrac{x-2-x-1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-3}{(x+1)(x-2)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses a log law correctly (Method 1), or writes the factor $\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}$ (Method 2), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Method 1: 1: correct use of log law
meta.marker_note: Method 1: 1 mark for the log law, 1 mark for differentiating both terms. Method 2: 1 mark for $\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}$, 1 mark for the quotient rule result $\dfrac{-3}{(x-2)^2}$. This type of question has appeared in many past papers; use Method 1.

parts.latex:
Determine the sum of the geometric series below.

$$2+6+18+\cdots+39\,366$$

dif.r: GP: n from last term then S_n

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=2$, $r=3$.

Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$ to find the number of terms:
$$\begin{aligned}2\times3^{n-1}&=39\,366\\3^{n-1}&=19\,683\\3^{n-1}&=3^9\\\therefore n-1&=9\\n&=10\end{aligned}$$
Or: $n-1=\log_3 19\,683=9$, so $n=10$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{3-1}\\&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{2}\\&=3^{10}-1\\&=59\,048\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The following sequence is geometric.

$$6-x,\qquad x-8,\qquad x+4$$

Determine the possible values of the common ratio.

dif.r: GP condition gives quadratic, two ratios

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x-8}{6-x}&=\dfrac{x+4}{x-8}\\(x-8)^2&=(6-x)(x+4)\\x^2-16x+64&=6x+24-x^2-4x\\x^2-16x+64&=-x^2+2x+24\\2x^2-18x+40&=0\\2(x^2-9x+20)&=0\\2(x-4)(x-5)&=0\\\therefore x&=4\text{ or }5\end{aligned}$$
When $x=4$:
$$r=\dfrac{4-8}{6-4}=-2$$
When $x=5$:
$$r=\dfrac{5-8}{6-5}=-3$$
$\therefore$ the possible common ratios are $-2$ and $-3$.
criteria: Equates the ratios $\dfrac{x-8}{6-x}=\dfrac{x+4}{x-8}$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: CFPE allowed for the common ratios. Only $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the last mark was awarded if $r$ was worked out but it was concluded that $r=4$ or $5$.

dif.r: image point under f(1-x)+2: reflect before shift

solutions.latex:
Writing the function as $y=f\big(-(x-1)\big)+2$, the transformations are:
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{horizontal dilation by factor } -1 &&\text{(reflect in the } y\text{-axis)}\\&\text{horizontal translation 1 unit right}\\&\text{vertical translation 2 units up}\end{aligned}$$
The horizontal dilation must happen before the horizontal translation; the vertical translation can come at any stage:
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{Option 1:} &&\text{dilation, horizontal translation, vertical translation}\\&\text{Option 2:} &&\text{vertical translation, dilation, horizontal translation}\\&\text{Option 3:} &&\text{dilation, vertical translation, horizontal translation}\end{aligned}$$
Using Option 1:
$$\begin{aligned}P(3,-5)&\mapsto(-3,-5) &&\text{reflect in the } y\text{-axis}\\&\mapsto(-2,-5) &&\text{translate 1 unit right}\\&\mapsto(-2,-3) &&\text{translate 2 units up}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the image is $P'(-2,-3)$.

The quick way: $P(x,y)\mapsto P'(1-x,\,y+2)$, so
$$P(3,-5)\mapsto P'(1-3,\,-5+2)=P'(-2,-3)$$
criteria: Finds $(-2,-5)$ after the reflection and the horizontal translation, or equivalent merit
Finds $(-3,-5)$ after the reflection, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The last mark is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $(-2,-3)$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for doing all 3 transformations in the correct order (zero if the reflection order is not demonstrated). The quick way does not show understanding but was still awarded. Many students did not write the function as $y=kf(a(x+b))+c$; some did not do the horizontal dilation before the horizontal translation; many did not use $P'$ notation for the image.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $x\ln x$.

dif.r: direct product rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,dx$.

dif.r: reverse differentiation from (a), isolate int ln x

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\ln x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=x\times\dfrac{1}{x}+1\times\ln x\\&=1+\ln x\end{aligned}$$

Method 1, integrating the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\int(1+\ln x)\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int1\,dx+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\x+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: from part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$, so
$$\ln x=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\ln x\,dx&=\int\left(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\right)dx\\&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some progress, e.g. $\displaystyle\int(1+\ln x)\,dx=x\ln x+C$ or $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,dx=\int\left(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\right)dx$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: some progress, e.g. $\int 1+\ln x\,dx=x\ln x+C$ (or $\int\ln x\,dx=\int\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\,dx$)
meta.marker_note: Lose $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark for forgetting $+C$ (once only in Booklet 1).

parts.latex:
A toy racetrack consists of multiple track pieces which join together.

The first and longest piece of the track is 35 cm long, and each piece of track after the longest is 2 centimetres shorter than the previous piece.

The total length of the completed track is 2.6 metres.

Find the length of the shortest piece of track.

dif.r: quadratic in n from S_n, reject a root, then T_n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The track lengths form an arithmetic sequence with $a=35$, $d=-2$ and $S_n=260$ cm (2.6 m).

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(35)+(n-1)(-2)\big)&=260\\n(70-2n+2)&=520\\n(72-2n)&=520\\72n-2n^2&=520\\2n^2-72n+520&=0\\n^2-36n+260&=0\\n&=\dfrac{36\pm\sqrt{36^2-4(1)(260)}}{2}\\&=26\text{ or }10\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_{26}&=35+(26-1)(-2)\\&=35+25(-2)\\&=-15\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
Lengths cannot be negative, so $n\ne26$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=35+(10-1)(-2)\\&=17\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the length of the shortest piece is 17 cm.
criteria: Forms the correct equation $\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(35)+(n-1)(-2)\big)=260$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The last mark is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $T_{26}=-15$ with a justification for rejecting it and $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for 17 cm. Generally done well; a few did not find the $T_n$ values or did not eliminate the negative $T_n$ with an appropriate justification.

questions.stem: Given $x^2+y^2=14xy$,

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}$ simplifies to $xy$.

dif.r: expand and substitute given relation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, show that $\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)$.

dif.r: log-law proof using part (a) result

solutions.latex:
Expanding and substituting the given $x^2+y^2=14xy$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{x^2+2xy+y^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{14xy+2xy}{16}\\&=\dfrac{16xy}{16}\\&=xy\end{aligned}$$

Using the log laws $\log a+\log b=\log ab$ and $n\log a=\log a^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\right)\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ LHS $=$ RHS, as required.

Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\sqrt{xy}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(x+y)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log16\\&=\log(x+y)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}-\log16^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log(x+y)-\log4\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log x+\dfrac{1}{2}\log y\\&=\log x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\log y^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses any 2 relevant logarithm laws, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The second mark is for substantial progress towards the solution.

parts.latex: Determine the area of the region bounded by $y=x^2-3x-3$ and $y=x+2$.

dif.r: find intersections then standard area between line and parabola

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the line y = x + 2 and parabola y = x^2 - 3x - 3 with the enclosed region hatched; vertex x = 3/2, y = -21/4, x-intercepts -0.79 and 3.79

solutions.latex:
Sketch the two graphs to see the region:

\exfigure{1371_q30_s1}

Points of intersection:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-3&=x+2\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x=5\text{ or }x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
The line $y=x+2$ is above the parabola on $[-1,5]$, so the area is
$$\int_{-1}^{5}(\text{top curve}-\text{bottom curve})\,dx$$
Note: the area between the curves does not change if the region is translated, so no absolute value is needed as long as one graph is above the other throughout the interval, even if some of the region is below the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-1}^{5}\big((x+2)-(x^2-3x-3)\big)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(x+2-x^2+3x+3)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{5^3}{3}+2(5)^2+5(5)\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\&=36\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct integrand $-x^2+4x+5$, or equivalent merit
Finds the points of intersection $x=5$ and $x=-1$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the lower-limit bracket read (+1/3 − 2 + 5); substituting x = −1 gives (1/3 + 2 − 5). Answer 36 units² unchanged.

questions.stem:
Consider the infinite series below.

$$S=\sin^2x\cos^2x+2\sin^2x\cos^4x+4\sin^2x\cos^6x+\cdots$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that the limiting sum of $S$ exists, show that it is $\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}$.

dif.r: identify GP ratio 2cos^2x, limiting sum, Pythagorean rewrite

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, show that $\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x\,(\tan^2x-1)}$ can also be expressed as the limiting sum of $S$.

dif.r: hence: divide by cos^2 x to reach reciprocal-function form

solutions.latex:
Using the limiting sum $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\sin^2x\cos^2x\\r&=\dfrac{2\sin^2x\cos^4x}{\sin^2x\cos^2x}\\&=2\cos^2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore S&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-\cos^2x-\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}&&(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x)\end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Uses the limiting sum formula correctly with an incorrect common ratio, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct steps to show $S$; $1\dfrac{1}{2}$: finding the common ratio $r=2\cos^2x$ and using the limiting sum formula correctly and writing $S=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}$
meta.marker_note: $1\dfrac{1}{2}$ marks for finding the common ratio $r=2\cos^2x$, using the limiting sum formula correctly and writing $S=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}$; $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark for finding the common ratio correctly. Answered well overall, but some students applied Extension 1 trig identities to finish the proof, e.g. $\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-(2\cos^2x-1)}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-\cos2x}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-(\cos^2x-\sin^2x)}$; this was accepted but is not intended in an Advanced paper.

solutions.latex:
Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x\div\cos^2x}{(\sin^2x-\cos^2x)\div\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\tan^2x-1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&&\text{since }\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\frac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\cos^2x}-\frac{1}{\sin^2x}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x\sin^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark each for using $\operatorname{cosec}^2x=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}$ and $\tan^2x=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}$; $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark for incorrect methods with at least one trig identity used correctly. Not well answered: many used $\sec^2x=\tan^2x-1$, which is not correct; the correct identity is $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$.

questions.stem:
Consider $y=x^2e^{-x}$.

This will have the following derivatives (do NOT prove this).

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x}$$

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{x^2-4x+2}{e^x}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine any stationary points and their nature.

dif.r: given derivatives: solve dy/dx=0, test with given second derivative

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Describe what occurs to the function as $x\to\pm\infty$.

dif.r: behaviour at infinity with exponential dominance

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
You are given that $(3.4,0.4)$ and $(0.6,0.2)$ are points of inflection.

Sketch $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: twin of 2025 Q16(b): sketch x^2e^{-x} with given inflections

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = x^2 e^{-x}: minimum (0,0), maximum (2, 4e^{-2}), inflections (0.6, 0.2) and (3.4, 0.4), approaching the x-axis as x increases

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x}=0$$
$e^x>0$, so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$; when $x=2$, $y=4e^{-2}$.

At $(0,0)$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{1}=2>0$$
so the curve is concave up and $(0,0)$ is a local minimum.

At $(2,4e^{-2})$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{4-8+2}{e^2}=-\dfrac{2}{e^2}<0$$
so the curve is concave down and $(2,4e^{-2})$ is a local maximum.
criteria: Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: complete solution; $1\dfrac{1}{2}$: almost the complete solution but not including the stationary points $(0,0)$ and $(2,4e^{-2})$
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: (4 − 8 + 2)/e² = −2/e², not −6/e²; the nature (local maximum) is unchanged.
meta.marker_note: $1\dfrac{1}{2}$ marks for an almost complete solution without stating the stationary points $(0,0)$ and $(2,4e^{-2})$; $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark for finding $x=0$, $x=2$. Well done overall.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{As } x\to-\infty, & y&\to\infty\\&\text{As } x\to\infty, & y&\to0^+\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Gives one of the two limits correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Answered well overall; no marks if students did not separate the two directions and wrote $x\to\pm\infty$, $y\to0$.

questions.stem:
The shape below is made of a sector $OAB$ and equilateral triangle $OBC$.

The sector $OAB$ has a radius $r$ cm.

The arc $AB$ subtends an angle $\theta$ radians at $O$.

\exfigure{1371_q33_1}

Let $A$ represent the area of the shape.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Given that the perimeter of the shape is 10 cm, show that

$$A=5r+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r^2.$$

dif.r: twin of 2025 Q26(a): eliminate theta, sector plus triangle area

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, determine the maximum area of the shape to the nearest cm$^2$.

dif.r: maximise concave-down quadratic area

figures.cap: sector OAB with radius r and angle theta at O, joined along OB to equilateral triangle OBC (tick marks on equal sides)

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $OA+\text{arc }AB+BC+CO$, with arc length $r\theta$ and each side of the equilateral triangle equal to $r$:
$$P=3r+r\theta\qquad(1)$$
Substituting $P=10$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3r+r\theta&=10\\r\theta&=10-3r\\\theta&=\dfrac{10-3r}{r}\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Using the sector area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ and (2):
$$\begin{aligned}A_1=\text{Area of sector}&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{10-3r}{r}\right)\\&=5r-\dfrac{3}{2}r^2\end{aligned}$$
Using $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ for the equilateral triangle (each angle $60^\circ$):
$$\begin{aligned}A_2=\text{Area of triangle}&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin(60^\circ)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore A&=A_1+A_2\\&=5r-\dfrac{3}{2}r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\\&=5r+\dfrac{-6}{4}r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\\A&=5r+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\theta=\dfrac{10-3r}{r}$ and the areas of the sector and the triangle correctly, or equivalent merit
Expresses $\theta$ as $\dfrac{10-3r}{r}$, or finds the areas of the triangle and the sector, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark for $P=3r+r\theta$, or for finding either the area of the triangle or the area of the sector. Review the arc length ($l=r\theta$) and sector area ($A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$) formulas; many wrote $P=3r+AB$ or used $\dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ}\times\pi r^2$ with an angle in radians.

solutions.latex:
$$A=5r+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r^2$$
At the maximum area, $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dr}=5+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{2}r&=0\\\therefore r&=-5\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}-6}\\&=\dfrac{10}{6-\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{2}\approx-2.134<0$$
so the maximum occurs at $r=\dfrac{10}{6-\sqrt{3}}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=5\left(\dfrac{10}{6-\sqrt{3}}\right)+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}\left(\dfrac{10}{6-\sqrt{3}}\right)^2\\&\approx6\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: The last mark is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for the justification (can be a gradient table) and $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for the final answer. $\dfrac{1}{2}$ deducted for minor errors in simplifying after finding $\dfrac{dA}{dr}$ correctly or solving for $r$; lack of units not penalised. Common errors: not substituting back into $A$ correctly; $2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r=(2\sqrt{3}-12)r$; some candidates used $\approx$ incorrectly.

questions.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line such that its velocity in metres per second, $v$, is given by the equation below, where $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

$$v=2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the particle's initial speed?

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why the particle can never be at rest.

dif.r: justify v>=2 so never zero

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction
can_use: Discriminant and the nature of roots

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
What is the particle's change in displacement in the first 4 seconds?

Leave your answer in exact form.

dif.r: integrate f'/f log term with limits

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Determine the particle's exact acceleration at $t=5$.

dif.r: quotient rule then substitute t=5

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2+0\\&=2\text{ ms}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$

$t>0$ and $t^2+1>0$, since square values must be positive.

$\therefore\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$, since the quotient of two positives is positive.

$\therefore 2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge2$

$\therefore v$ is always positive and never equals zero, so the particle is never at rest.

Or, using the discriminant: if the particle is at rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}&=0\\2t^2+2+t&=0\\2t^2+t+2&=0\\\Delta&=1^2-4(2)(2)\\&=-15<0\end{aligned}$$
$\Delta<0$, so there is no solution: the particle is never at rest.
criteria: Shows $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$ with a partial justification, or reaches $2t^2+t+2=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 0.5 for any mention of $t^2\ge0$ or $t^2+1>0$. If $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ is stated: 1 mark if $t^2>0$ stated previously; 1.5 marks if $t^2>0$ AND $t>0$ stated; 0 marks if only $t>0$ stated. 0.5 for observing large values of $t$ (e.g. stating $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ hence $\ne-2$; $\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}=0$). Discriminant method: 1 for reaching $2t^2+t+2=0$; 0.5 for the discriminant or quadratic formula; 0.5 for interpretation of the discriminant. Marker: observing $t\to\infty$ alone does not consider earlier values (e.g. $\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}=\dfrac{1}{5}$ but $\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}=0$ at $t\approx4.10462$ and $4.9063$); practise supporting arguments in explain questions.
meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for any mention of $t^2\ge0$ or $t^2+1>0$. At $t=0$, $x=C$.

$\therefore$ the change in displacement is $8+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln17$ metres.

The position, $x$ metres, of a particle moving in a straight line from a fixed origin $O$ at time, $t$ seconds, is given by

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore a&=(k-1)^2\times(k+1)\\&=(k^2-1)(k-1)\end{aligned}$$

Let $f(x)$ be a continuous odd function.

Given that $f(x-a)$ is an even function, which of the following must be true?

dif.r: abstract parity: odd f, even shift, combine

solutions.latex:
Let $g(x)=f(x-a)$. Since $g$ is even, $g(-x)=g(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x-a)&=f(x-a)\\f\big[-(x+a)\big]&=f(x-a)\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)$ is odd, $-f(x+a)=f(x-a)$.
$$\therefore f(x-a)+f(x+a)=0$$

questions.stem:
The wavelength, $\lambda$ metres, of a musical tone is inversely proportional to its frequency, $f$ vibrations per second.

The frequency of middle C is approximately 260 vibrations per second and its wavelength is approximately 1.32 m.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the frequency, in vibrations per second, of a sound wave with wavelength 0.8 m.

dif.r: one substitution into model from (a)

solutions.latex:
Since $\lambda$ is inversely proportional to $f$:
$$\lambda=\dfrac{k}{f}$$
Substituting $f=260$, $\lambda=1.32$:
$$\begin{aligned}1.32&=\dfrac{k}{260}\\k&=260\times1.32=343.2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\lambda=\dfrac{343.2}{f}$$

From part (a), with $\lambda=0.8$:
$$\begin{aligned}f&=\dfrac{343.2}{\lambda}\\&=\dfrac{343.2}{0.8}\\&=429\text{ vibrations per second}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln\left(e^x\sin x\right)\Big]$.

dif.r: log laws first to x+ln sin x

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws first:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln\left(e^x\sin x\right)\Big]&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln e^x+\ln(\sin x)\Big]\\&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[x+\ln(\sin x)\Big]\\&=1+\cot x\end{aligned}$$
Alternative, using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^x & v&=\sin x\\u'&=e^x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\sin x\right)=e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x$$
Then, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln\left(e^x\sin x\right)\Big]&=\dfrac{e^x(\cos x+\sin x)}{e^x\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x+\sin x}{\sin x}\\&=1+\cot x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\cot 2x+\dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{x}}\,dx$

dif.r: cot as f'/f plus fractional power term

solutions.latex:
Writing $\cot2x=\dfrac{\cos2x}{\sin2x}$ and $\dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{x}}=x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$:
$$\int\dfrac{\cos2x}{\sin2x}\,dx+\int x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,dx$$
Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$ with $f(x)=\sin2x$, $f'(x)=2\cos2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\int\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\cos2x}{\sin2x}\right)dx+\int x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin2x|+\dfrac{x^{-\frac{1}{2}}}{-\frac{1}{2}}+c\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin2x|-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}+c\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin2x|-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}+c\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{16-8x}{3x^2-12x+1}\,dx$.

dif.r: f'/f with negative constant -4/3

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=3x^2-12x+1$, so $f'(x)=6x-12$.
$$\therefore16-8x=-\dfrac{4}{3}(6x-12)$$
Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{16-8x}{3x^2-12x+1}\,dx&=-\dfrac{4}{3}\int\dfrac{6x-12}{3x^2-12x+1}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{4}{3}\ln\left|3x^2-12x+1\right|+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The sum of an infinite geometric series, with positive terms, is 3.

The sum of the cubes of its terms is $\dfrac{27}{19}$. What is the common ratio of the original series?

dif.r: S_inf of cubes; factor 1-r^3, solve quadratic

solutions.latex:
Let the sum of the original geometric series be $S_1$ and the new series (the cubes, first term $a^3$, ratio $r^3$) be $S_2$.
$$S_1=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=3\text{, so }a=3(1-r)\qquad(1)$$
$$S_2=\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}\qquad(2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2) and divide both sides by 27:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\big(3(1-r)\big)^3}{1-r^3}&=\dfrac{27}{19}\\\dfrac{(1-r)^3}{(1-r)(1+r+r^2)}&=\dfrac{1}{19}\\\dfrac{1-2r+r^2}{1+r+r^2}&=\dfrac{1}{19}\\6r^2-13r+6&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore r=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ or }\dfrac{2}{3}$$
Since $|r|<1$ for a limiting sum:
$$\therefore r=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
criteria: Writes $\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}$ for the series of cubes, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x-\sin^3 x}\,dx$.

dif.r: factor, identity, sqrt cos^2, spot reverse chain; non-routine

solutions.latex:
Using $1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x-\sin^3x}\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x\left(1-\sin^2x\right)}\,dx\\&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x\cos^2x}\,dx\end{aligned}$$
Since $x\in\left[0,\,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\cos x\ge0$, so $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{2}\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}-(\sin0)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(1-0)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive $\dfrac{2}{3}(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}$, or equivalent merit
Simplifies the integrand to $\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Method 1 (integrating with respect to $y$): from $y=20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$,
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^{10}\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}\,dy\\&=\int_0^{10}\sqrt{100-5y}\,dy\\&=\left[-\dfrac{2}{15}(100-5y)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^{10}\\&=-\dfrac{2}{15}\left(50^{\frac{3}{2}}-100^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
The volume of the prism is the cross-sectional area times the width:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=Ah\\&=\left(\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\times4\\&=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (rectangle plus side regions): at $y=10$,
$$20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2=10\text{, so }x=\pm\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\times\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\times10+2\int_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(100-\dfrac{100}{3}-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{25}{3}\sqrt{2}\right)\right)\\&=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(\dfrac{200}{3}-\dfrac{125\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
Method 3 (whole parabola minus the unshaded cap):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-5}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx-\int_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2-10\right)dx\\&=\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-5}^{5}-\left[10x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\\&=\left(200-\dfrac{200}{3}\right)-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{50\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
In each method:
$$V=4A=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$$

$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^h\dfrac{\sqrt{5y}}{2}\,dy\\&=\sqrt{5}\int_0^h\sqrt{y}\,dy\\&=\sqrt{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[y^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^h\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}\left(h^{\frac{3}{2}}-0\right)\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The table below shows the future value of annuity with a contribution of \$1 at the end of each period.

\extable{1372_q33_t1}

Kevin opened an account and deposited \$15 000 at the end of each year for 6 years.

At the end of the 7th year, he deposited \$20 000 in the same account and continued to deposit \$20 000 at end of each year until the end of the 10th year.

He made no more deposits after the end of the 10th year.

The money in his account was earning interest at 2.5% per annum compounded annually.

How much money will Kevin have in his account at the end of 15 years?
parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up is removed (annuities by GP formula only) · Standard: MST-12-S2-03

solutions.latex:
Using the 2.50% column of the table: the balance at the end of the first 6 years is the future value factor for 6 periods times the deposit of \$15 000:
$$6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10$$
This amount continues to earn interest for the remaining 9 years at 2.50% per annum, so it is multiplied by $1.025^9$.

Similarly, the four \$20 000 deposits (end of years 7 to 10) are worth $4.15252\times\$20\,000$ at the end of year 10, and earn interest for 5 more years:
$$4.15252\times\$20\,000\times1.025^5$$
Thus the final account balance at the end of 15 years is:
$$\begin{aligned}&6.38774\times\$15\,000\times1.025^9+4.15252\times\$20\,000\times1.025^5\\&=\$213\,625.08\text{ (nearest cent)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternate method (in stages, rounding to the nearest cent):
$$\begin{aligned}\text{End of 6 years: }&6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10\\\text{End of 10 years: }&4.15252\times\$20\,000+\$95\,816.10\times1.025^4=\$188\,813.45\\\text{End of 15 years: }&\$188\,813.45\times1.025^5=\$213\,625.09\end{aligned}$$
Depending on how the stages are rounded, the final result differs by a few cents.
criteria: Applies the interest rate in the years after deposits have stopped, or equivalent merit
Takes the appropriate products of deposit amount and future value, or equivalent merit

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)&=1\times e^{-x}+x\times\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $xe^{-x}=e^{-x}-\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)$.

Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}\int xe^{-x}\,dx&=\int\left(e^{-x}-\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}\right)\right)dx\\&=\int e^{-x}\,dx-xe^{-x}\\&=-e^{-x}-xe^{-x}+c\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{e}&=xe^{-x}\\ xe^{-1}&=xe^{-x} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $e^{-1}=e^{-x}$, giving $x=1$.

Using the primitive of $xe^{-x}$ from part (b), the shaded area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \left(xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x}{e}\right)dx&=\left[-e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x^2}{2e}\right]_0^1\\ &=\left(-e^{-1}-e^{-1}-\dfrac{1}{2e}\right)-(-1-0-0)\\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{2e} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}, & 0\le x\le 2\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$.

dif.r: log-form integral equals 1, show k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.

dif.r: integrate log-form pdf to piecewise CDF

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, show that the median of $X$ is $\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$.

dif.r: F(m)=1/2, solve log equation exactly

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so $\displaystyle\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx=1$.

The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $5-x^2$, which is $-2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{-2}\int_0^2\dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{-2}\Big[\ln\left(5-x^2\right)\Big]_0^2&=1\\ k(\ln 1-\ln 5)&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k=\dfrac{-2}{-\ln 5}=\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$$

For $0\le x\le 2$, $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$; below $0$ no probability has accumulated and above $2$ all of it has:
$$F(x)=\begin{cases} 0, & x<0\\ p(x), & 0\le x\le 2\\ 1, & x>2 \end{cases}$$
where
$$\begin{aligned} p(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{kt}{5-t^2}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{k}{-2}\int_0^x\dfrac{-2t}{5-t^2}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{k}{-2}\Big[\ln\left(5-t^2\right)\Big]_0^x\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\Big(\ln\left(5-x^2\right)-\ln 5\Big)\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-x^2\right)+1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-x^2\right)+1$ for $0\le x\le 2$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct piecewise $F(x)$ including the pieces for $x<0$ and $x>2$
meta.marker_note: Full marks need the pieces for $x<0$ and $x>2$.

solutions.latex:
The median, $m$, is given by $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, where $0\le m\le 2$.

Method 1:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)+1&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5\\ &=\ln\sqrt{5}\\ 5-m^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ m^2&=5-\sqrt{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore m=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\quad(\text{since }0\le m\le 2)$$
Method 2: using $\ln\sqrt{5}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5$,
$$\begin{aligned} p\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)^2\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(5-\sqrt{5}\right)\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\sqrt{5}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the median is $\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$.
criteria: Sets $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ using the expression from part (b), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has a cumulative distribution function given by:

$$F(x)=\dfrac{1}{16}x^2\left(5-2\sqrt{x}\right)\text{ for }0\le x\le 4.$$

Find the (exact) mode of $X$.

dif.r: differentiate CDF to pdf, then f'=0 with fractional powers

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{16}x^2\left(5-2\sqrt{x}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(5x^2-2x^{2.5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The pdf is $F'(x)$:
$$F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10x-5x^{1.5}\right)$$
The mode is where the pdf takes its greatest value in $0\le x\le 4$, so solve $F''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} F''(x)=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10-7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)&=0\\ 7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=10\\ x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=\dfrac{10}{7.5}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\\ x&=\dfrac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Testing with the third derivative:
$$F'''(x)=\dfrac{1}{32}\left(-7.5x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$$
$F'''\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)<0$, so the pdf has a global maximum there.
$$\therefore \text{mode}=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Finds the pdf $F'(x)$, or equivalent merit

Find the value of $\mu$ such that

$$n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)=\left(n^2+\mu n\right)\left(n^2+\mu n+2\right).$$

dif.r: pair outer and inner factors to find mu

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Let $n$ be an integer.

Deduce that $2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1$ is a perfect square.

dif.r: deduce perfect square: substitute k, k(k+2)+1

solutions.latex:
Pairing the outer and inner factors:
$$\begin{aligned} n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)&=n(n+3)\times(n+1)(n+2)\\ &=\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \mu=3$$

Let $n=2022$. Using part (a):
$$2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1=\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$$
Let $k=n^2+3n$ (an integer):
$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=k(k+2)+1\\ &=k^2+2k+1\\ &=(k+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
where $k+1$ is an integer.

$\therefore 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1$ is a perfect square.

Alternate method: let $n=2022$ and $k=n^2+3n+1$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=(k-1)(k+1)+1\\ &=k^2\\ &=\left(n^2+3n+1\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the expression as $\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$ with $n=2022$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$y=9x+2$ is a non-vertical line: one-to-one.

$x=4y^2$ is a parabola opening sideways: one-to-many.

parts.latex: If A and B are two independent events such that $P(A)=0.5$ and $P(B)=0.4$, what is is the value of $P(A\cup B)$?
skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
For independent events, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\&=0.5+0.4-P(A)\times P(B)\\&=0.9-0.5\times 0.4\\&=0.9-0.2\\&=0.7\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: MCQ: equal areas means integral 0 to a is zero

figures.cap: parabola h(x)=3x^2-6 with shaded regions A below the x-axis from 0 and B above the x-axis up to x=a

solutions.latex:
The curve cuts the $x$-axis where $h(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6&=0\\x^2&=2\\x&=\pm\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
Region $A$ (below the axis, $0\le x\le\sqrt{2}$) has the same area as region $B$ (above the axis, $\sqrt{2}\le x\le a$):
$$\left|\int_0^{\sqrt{2}}\left(3x^2-6\right)dx\right|=\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{a}\left(3x^2-6\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned}\Big[x^3-6x\Big]_{\sqrt{2}}^{0}&=\Big[x^3-6x\Big]_{\sqrt{2}}^{a}\\-2\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{2}&=a^3-6a-\left(2\sqrt{2}-6\sqrt{2}\right)\\a^3-6a&=0\\a(a^2-6)&=0\\a=0\ &\text{ or }\ a=\pm\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}$$
Since $a>0$, $a=\sqrt{6}$.

parts.latex:
Let $h(x)=f\big(g(x)\big)$, with $f(-1)=3,\ f'(-1)=5,\ g(4)=-1$ and $g'(4)=3$.

What is the equation of the tangent to the graph of $y=h(x)$ at $x=4$?

dif.r: MCQ: chain rule with given values, then tangent

solutions.latex:
When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}h(4)&=f\big(g(4)\big)\\&=f(-1)\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
so the point of contact is $(4,3)$.

By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}h'(x)&=f'\big(g(x)\big)\times g'(x)\\h'(4)&=f'\big(g(4)\big)\times g'(4)\\&=f'(-1)\times g'(4)\\&=5\times 3\\&=15\end{aligned}$$
Substituting $(4,3)$ and $m=15$ into $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3&=15(x-4)\\y&=15x-60+3\\y&=15x-57\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The expression $\dfrac{1}{\log_a(b)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_b(c)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_c(a)}$ is equal to

dif.r: reciprocal change-of-base on three terms

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a}$, to each term:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\log_a(b)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_b(c)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_c(a)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_b(b)}{\log_b(a)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_c(c)}{\log_c(b)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_a(a)}{\log_a(c)}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_b(a)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_c(b)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_a(c)}}\\&=\log_b(a)+\log_c(b)+\log_a(c)\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: perpendicular condition plus intercept distance gives quadratic in b

figures.cap: perpendicular lines through (0,3) and (0,2) cutting the x-axis at L and M, LM = 5 [diagram not to scale]

solutions.latex:
$L$ is where $y=ax+3$ meets the $x$-axis: $ax+3=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{3}{a}$.

$M$ is where $y=bx+2$ meets the $x$-axis: $bx+2=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{2}{b}$.
$$\begin{aligned}LM&=-\dfrac{2}{b}-\left(-\dfrac{3}{a}\right)\\&=-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}\end{aligned}$$
$LM=5$, and the lines are perpendicular, so $ab=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}&=5\\3b-2a&=5ab &&(\text{multiply by } ab)\\3b-2a&=-5 &&\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$a=-\dfrac{1}{b}\quad\ldots(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3b-2\left(-\dfrac{1}{b}\right)&=-5\\3b+\dfrac{2}{b}&=-5\\3b^2+5b+2&=0\\(b+1)(3b+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$b=-1$ or $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so
$$\begin{cases}a=1\\b=-1\end{cases}\text{ or }\begin{cases}a=\dfrac{3}{2}\\[6pt]b=-\dfrac{2}{3}\end{cases}$$
Since $a>1$, $a=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$$a+b=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{5}{6}$$

parts.latex:
The points $P(1,-2)$ and $Q(7,1)$ lie on the circumference of a circle.

Show that the centre of the circle lies on the line $4x+2y=15$.

dif.r: show-that: equal distances from centre give line; circle geometry

solutions.latex:
A circle with centre $(a,b)$ has equation $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$.

$P(1,-2)$ and $Q(7,1)$ lie on the circle:
$$\begin{aligned}(1-a)^2+(-2-b)^2&=r^2 &&\ldots(1)\\(7-a)^2+(1-b)^2&=r^2 &&\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$$
Expanding (1):
$$\begin{aligned}1-2a+a^2+4+4b+b^2&=r^2\\a^2-2a+b^2+4b+5&=r^2\end{aligned}$$
Expanding (2):
$$\begin{aligned}49-14a+a^2+1-2b+b^2&=r^2\\a^2-14a+b^2-2b+50&=r^2\end{aligned}$$
$(1)-(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}12a+6b-45&=0\\4a+2b&=15 &&(\div 3)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the centre $(a,b)$ satisfies $4x+2y=15$, so it lies on the line.
criteria: Expands and simplifies, or equivalent merit
Forms the circle equations, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Substituting the midpoint $\left(4,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ of $PQ$ into $4x+2y=15$ does not prove the midpoint is the centre and was awarded 2 marks.

questions.stem: Consider the arithmetic progression $-7,\,2,\,11,\,20,\,\ldots,\,713$.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the number of terms.

dif.r: solve T_n=713 (linear)

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, find the sum of terms.

dif.r: direct S_n with n known

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a=T_1=-7$.

The common difference is $d=T_2-T_1=2-(-7)=9$ (also $T_3-T_2=11-2=9$).
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=a+(n-1)d\\&=-7+(n-1)9\\&=-7+9n-9\\&=9n-16\end{aligned}$$
The last term is $713$:
$$\begin{aligned}713&=9n-16\\729&=9n\\n&=\dfrac{729}{9}\\&=81\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the general term $T_n$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows a sector, $EOG$, of a circle, with centre $O$ and radius $r$ cm. The line $GF$ is a tangent to the circle at $G$. Point $E$ is the midpoint of $OF$.

\exfigure{1373_q19_1}

parts.latex: Find the expression for the exact area of the shaded region.

dif.r: tangent perpendicular, Pythagoras, find angle, triangle minus sector

figures.cap: right triangle OGF with sector EOG of radius r cm and shaded region between arc GE and GF, EF

solutions.latex:
$OG=OE=r$ (radii of the circle) and $OE=EF$ ($E$ is the midpoint of $OF$), so $OF=2r$.

$\angle OGF=90^\circ$ (tangent is perpendicular to the radius). By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle OGF$:
$$\begin{aligned}GF&=\sqrt{OF^2-OG^2}\\&=\sqrt{(2r)^2-r^2}\\&=\sqrt{3}\,r\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine ratio in $\triangle OGF$:
$$\cos\angle GOE=\dfrac{r}{2r}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\therefore\angle GOE=60^\circ=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle OGF&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{3}\,r\times r\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,r^2}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of sector }OGE&=\dfrac{60}{360}\pi r^2\quad\left(\text{or }\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{\pi r^2}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of shaded region}&=\triangle OGF-\text{sector }OGE\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,r^2}{2}-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{6}\\&=\dfrac{(3\sqrt{3}-\pi)r^2}{6}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the sector area, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct area. 2/3 for not finding the angle.
meta.marker_note: $2$ out of $3$ for not finding the angle.

parts.latex: Find an approximation for $\displaystyle\int_2^6\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x-5}}\,dx$ correct to 2 decimal places, using 3 applications of the trapezoidal rule.

dif.r: trapezoidal, three strips, fractional x values

solutions.latex:
Three applications use $n=3$ strips of width
$$h=\dfrac{6-2}{3}=\dfrac{4}{3}$$
so the $x$ values are $2$, $\dfrac{10}{3}$, $\dfrac{14}{3}$ and $6$, with $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x-5}}$.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\Big[f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\big(f(x_1)+\cdots+f(x_{n-1})\big)\Big]$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&\approx\dfrac{6-2}{2(3)}\left\{f(2)+f(6)+2\left[f\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)+f\left(\dfrac{14}{3}\right)\right]\right\}\\&\approx\dfrac{2}{3}\left\{1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}+2\left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}+\dfrac{1}{3}\right]\right\}\\&\approx 1.89\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer. Zero for incorrect substitution into first line.
meta.marker_note: Zero for incorrect substitution into the first line.

questions.stem: Consider functions $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x-5}}$.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the rule for the composite function $g\big(f(x)\big)$.

dif.r: direct substitution into composite rule

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the domain of $g\big(f(x)\big)$.

dif.r: radicand in denominator strictly positive, one inequality

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}g\big(f(x)\big)&=g(x+1)\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3(x+1)-5}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+3-5}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x-2}}\end{aligned}$$

The square root is in the denominator, so it must be positive:
$$\begin{aligned}3x-2&>0\\3x&>2\\x&>\dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the domain is $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\infty\right)$.

meta.marker_note: Zero marks for $x\ge\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem: The time from Amber getting out of bed until her arrival at her office is normally distributed with a mean of 43 minutes and a standard deviation of 7 minutes. Amber's arrival at her office is classified as being late if it occurs after 9:20 am.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: If Amber gets out of bed at 8:16 am, find the $z$-score for the number of minutes she has to get to the office.

dif.r: time difference then z-score formula

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: If Amber gets out bed at 8:16 am, find the probability that she will arrive late using the Empirical Rule.

dif.r: empirical rule tail beyond 3 sd

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
From 8:16 am to 9:20 am is 64 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\&=\dfrac{64-43}{7}\\&=3\end{aligned}$$

Amber is late if the trip takes more than 64 minutes, that is $z>3$. By the empirical rule, $99.7\%$ of scores lie within 3 standard deviations of the mean, and the rest is split equally between the two tails:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{arriving late})&=P(z>3)\\&=1-P(z<3)\\&=\dfrac{1-0.997}{2}\\&=0.15\%\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer without supporting working, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer with working (any of: $1-P(z<3)$, $\dfrac{1-0.997}{2}$, or a sketch of the normal curve shaded beyond $z=3$)
meta.marker_note: Accepted working: any of $1-P(z<3)$, $\dfrac{1-0.997}{2}$, or a sketch of the normal curve shaded beyond $z=3$.

parts.latex: Given that $f(x)=-2x^3+k^3x^2$ where $k$ is a positive constant. Find the complete set of values of $x$ for which the graph of $f(x)$ is concave up, using interval notation.

dif.r: second derivative inequality with parameter k

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is concave up where $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=-2x^3+k^3x^2\\f'(x)&=-6x^2+2k^3x\\f''(x)&=-12x+2k^3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}-12x+2k^3&>0\\-12x&>-2k^3\\6x&<k^3\\x&<\dfrac{k^3}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave up for $x\in\left(-\infty,\dfrac{k^3}{6}\right)$.

meta.marker_note: The line $-12x+2k^3>0$ must be shown for the second mark.

questions.stem: A ship departs from point $A$ and sails 12 kilometres on a bearing of $156^\circ$ to reach point $B$. It then changes direction and sails 16 kilometres on a bearing of $123^\circ$ to reach point C.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the distance $AC$, correct to the nearest kilometre.

dif.r: angle from bearings, cosine rule

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the true bearing that the ship should follow to return directly to point $A$ from point $C$. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

dif.r: sine rule for angle, convert to return bearing

figures.cap: solution sketch: bearing diagram of A, B, C with 12 km, 16 km, angles 24, 123, 57 degrees

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1373_q24_s1}

At $B$, $BA$ makes $180^\circ-156^\circ=24^\circ$ with the north line (co-interior angles), and $BC$ is on a bearing of $123^\circ$:
$$\angle ABC=24^\circ+123^\circ=147^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned}AC^2&=12^2+16^2-2\times 12\times 16\cos 147^\circ\\&=722.049\ldots\\AC&=26.8\ldots\\&\approx 27\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule with angle $147^\circ$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: AC = 27 km. Comment: generally well done.
meta.marker_note: Generally well done.

solutions.latex:
Let $\alpha=\angle ACB$. Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{12}&=\dfrac{\sin 147^\circ}{27}\\\alpha&=14.008\ldots^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$CB$ is on a bearing of $123^\circ+180^\circ=303^\circ$, which is $57^\circ$ west of north, and $CA$ is $\alpha$ closer to north:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=57^\circ-\alpha\\&=42.9917\ldots^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Required bearing}&=360^\circ-\theta\\&\approx 317^\circ\text{T}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle ACB$ using the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct bearing 317 degrees T. Comment: students with a clear diagram were generally more successful.
meta.marker_note: Students with a clear diagram were generally more successful.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^{\sqrt{3}}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{1}{3x^2}\right)dx$, giving your answer in the form $a+b\sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be determined.

dif.r: negative power primitive, surd evaluation to a+b sqrt3

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^{\sqrt{3}}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{1}{3x^2}\right)dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{24}-\dfrac{1}{3x}\right]_1^{\sqrt{3}}\\&=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3})^4}{24}-\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}-\left(\dfrac{1}{24}-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{9}{24}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{9}+\dfrac{7}{24}\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{9}\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{9}\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore a=\dfrac{2}{3},\ b=-\dfrac{1}{9}$$
criteria: Correct progress substituting the limits, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve the equation $3\sin^2 x+1=4\cos x$ for $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$.

Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

dif.r: convert sin^2 to cos, quadratic, reject root, solve on [-pi,pi]

solutions.latex:
Using $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(1-\cos^2x)+1&=4\cos x\\0&=3\cos^2x+4\cos x-4\\0&=(3\cos x-2)(\cos x+2)\end{aligned}$$
$\cos x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $\cos x=-2$.

$-1\le\cos x\le 1$, so $\cos x\ne -2$ and $\cos x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

In $[-\pi,\pi]$, $\cos x$ is positive in the first and fourth quadrants:
$$\therefore x\approx\pm 0.841$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the quadratic read $0=3\cos^2x+4\cos x-3$; it is $3\cos^2x+4\cos x-4=0$, which matches the factorisation $(3\cos x-2)(\cos x+2)$. Answer unchanged.

questions.stem:
The table below shows the future values of an annuity of \$1 for different rates of interest and different numbers of compounding periods. The contribution is made at the end of each time period.

\extable{1373_q27_t1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Kelly opens an annuity account and makes contributions of \$3500 at the end of each quarter over a period of 18 months at an interest rate of 8% per annum, compounding quarterly. Find the total amount in Kelly's account after 18 months.
parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up: Standard (2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only) · Standard: MST-12-S2-03

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
Julie deposits \$10 000 into a saving account at the end of each year for 9 years.

For the first 4 years, the interest rate is 3% per annum, compounding annually. From the 5th year, the interest rate increases to 5% per annum, compounding annually.

Find the amount of money in Julie's account at the end of nine years.
parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up: Standard (2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only) · Standard: MST-12-S2-03

solutions.latex:
$8\%$ p.a. compounding quarterly is $2\%$ per quarter, and 18 months is 6 quarters.

From the table, the future value of \$1 at $2\%$ for 6 periods is $6.3081$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Amount}&=3500\times 6.3081\\&=\$22\,078.35\end{aligned}$$

First 4 years: the table value at $3\%$ for 4 periods is $4.1836$:
$$10\,000\times 4.1836=\$41\,836$$
This amount then earns $5\%$ for 5 years, and the next 5 deposits form an annuity at $5\%$ (table value $5.5256$ for 5 periods):
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Amount}&=41\,836(1.05)^5+10\,000\times 5.5256\\&=\$108\,650.52\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds either $41\,836(1.05)^5$ or $10\,000\times 5.5256$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The curve $y=2\sqrt{(x-1)}$ is shown below. Find the shaded area.

\exfigure{1373_q29_1}

dif.r: area to y-axis: rectangle minus area under curve

can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: curve y=2sqrt(x-1) with region between the y-axis, the curve and the horizontal line through the point at x=10 shaded
solution sketch: question graph annotated with y=6 and x-intercept 1

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1373_q29_s1}

The curve meets the $x$-axis where $2\sqrt{x-1}=0$, so $x=1$.

When $x=10$, $y=2\sqrt{9}=6$.

The shaded area is the $10\times 6$ rectangle minus the area under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=10$:
$$\text{Area of rectangle}=10\times 6=60$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=60-2\int_1^{10}\sqrt{x-1}\,dx\\&=60-2\int_1^{10}(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=60-2\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(x-1)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_1^{10}\\&=60-\dfrac{4}{3}(27-0)\\&=24\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: write $x$ as a function of $y$ and integrate along the $y$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{y}{2}&=\sqrt{x-1}\\x-1&=\dfrac{y^2}{4}\\x&=\dfrac{y^2}{4}+1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^6\left(\dfrac{y^2}{4}+1\right)dy\\&=\left[\dfrac{y^3}{12}+y\right]_0^6\\&=24\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct area expression (rectangle minus integral, or $x$ as a function of $y$), or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Given that $f(x)=5x\cos(5x)$,

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find $f'(x)$.

dif.r: direct product rule

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence find the antiderivative of $x\sin(5x)$.

dif.r: rearrange (i) for x sin5x and integrate, scale 1/25

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5x & v&=\cos(5x)\\ u'&=5 & v'&=-5\sin(5x)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=5\cos(5x)-5x\times 5\sin(5x)\\&=5\cos(5x)-25x\sin(5x)\end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the last line printed $5\cos(5x)-25\sin(5x)$, missing the factor $x$; it is $5\cos(5x)-25x\sin(5x)$ (as used in part (ii)).

solutions.latex:
From part (i), rearrange to make $x\sin(5x)$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=5\cos(5x)-25x\sin(5x)\\25x\sin(5x)&=5\cos(5x)-f'(x)\\x\sin(5x)&=\dfrac{1}{25}\big(5\cos(5x)-f'(x)\big)\end{aligned}$$
Integrating both sides, with $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,dx=f(x)=5x\cos(5x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\sin(5x)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{25}\int\big(5\cos(5x)-f'(x)\big)\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{25}\big(\sin(5x)-f(x)\big)+C\\&=\dfrac{\sin(5x)-5x\cos(5x)}{25}+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress with correct integrand, or equivalent merit
Correctly expresses $x\sin(5x)$ using the derivative from part (i), or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows graphs of the functions $f(x)=e^x-5$ and $g(x)=-e^{2x}+4$.

\exfigure{1373_q35_1}

parts.latex: Find the exact area enclosed by curves, the line $x=-\ln(6)$ and the line $x=\ln(2)$.

dif.r: area between exponentials, exact evaluation at ln6, ln2

figures.cap: graphs of f(x)=e^x-5 and g(x)=-e^{2x}+4 with region between them shaded from x=-ln(6) to x=ln(2)

solutions.latex:
Between $x=-\ln 6$ and $x=\ln 2$, $g(x)=-e^{2x}+4$ lies above $f(x)=e^x-5$, so the area is the integral of $g(x)-f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\left(-e^{2x}+4-e^x+5\right)dx\\&=\int_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\left(-e^{2x}-e^x+9\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-e^{2x}}{2}-e^x+9x\right]_{-\ln 6}^{\ln 2}\\&=\dfrac{-e^{2\ln 2}}{2}-e^{\ln 2}+9\ln 2-\left(\dfrac{-e^{-2\ln 6}}{2}-e^{-\ln 6}-9\ln 6\right)\\&=\dfrac{-4}{2}-2+9\ln 2-\left(\dfrac{-6^{-2}}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}-9\ln 6\right)\\&=9\ln 2+9\ln 6-\dfrac{275}{72}\\&=9\ln 12-\dfrac{275}{72}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly evaluates to get the constant term or the $\ln$ term, or equivalent merit
Provides a correct expression for the area and correctly integrates it before substituting the boundaries, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle moves along a line with velocity

$$v(t)=6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),$$

where time $t$ is measured in seconds.

Given that the displacement at $t=0$ is 2 metres. Find:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: the displacement function $s(t)$.

dif.r: integrate trig velocity, find constant from initial condition

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: the acceleration function $a(t)$.

dif.r: differentiate cos with chain rule

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: the time at which the particle changes direction within the interval $0<t<1$.

dif.r: solve v=0 trig equation within interval

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}s(t)&=\int 6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)dt\\&=3\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $s(0)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}2&=3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+C\\C&=2-3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=2-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore s(t)=3\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+2-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides the correct answer using the initial condition
meta.marker_note: Answered well.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the integral was written with $dx$; the variable is $t$, so $dt$.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}a(t)&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\&=-12\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct answer. Comment: answered well.
meta.marker_note: Answered well.

solutions.latex:
The particle can change direction only where $v(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature: the acceleration there is non-zero, so $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)&=-12\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=-12\\&<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle changes direction at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ seconds.

questions.stem: For the function $y=(4x-1)e^{-\frac{x}{2}}$:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: product rule with exponential, one stationary point, nature

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Using part i), sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, showing all key features.

dif.r: sketch using turning point, intercepts, asymptote

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=(4x-1)e^{-x/2}: max (9/4, 8e^{-9/8}), x-intercept 1/4, y-intercept -1, approaching the x-axis as x increases

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x-1 & v&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=4e^{-\frac{x}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}(4x-1)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(4-\dfrac{1}{2}(4x-1)\right)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(4-2x+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{9}{2}-2x\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$. $e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\ne 0$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{9}{2}-2x&=0\\x&=\dfrac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{9}{4}$, $y=8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}$, so the stationary point is $\left(\dfrac{9}{4},8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}\right)$.

Testing the sign of $y'$ either side ($e^{-\frac{x}{2}}>0$, so the sign is that of $\dfrac{9}{2}-2x$):

\extable{Ts1575_1}

$\therefore$ maximum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{9}{4},8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}\right)$.
