questions.stem:
A lake contains an initial population of 500 000 fish at the beginning of 2025. Each year, the fish population increases by 7% due to natural reproduction. After this increase, a fishing company catches fish from the lake. In 2025, 2000 fish are caught. In each subsequent year, the number of fish caught increases by 9% compared to the previous year.

Let $F_n$ be the number of fish remaining in the lake after the nth year's catch.

dif.r: same structure as 2026 Q33(a): two growth rates

req: Recurrence relations for loans and annuities
A.note: growth then removal each period; recurrence skill is the loan pattern in a non-financial context

B.note: Recurrence for a non-financial quantity (growth then growing catch); 'Recurrence relations for loans and annuities' is finance-only, so no recurrence skill fits

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: If the fishing was allowed to continue at this rate, find the year which there will be no fish in this lake.

dif.r: two-GP model to zero; heavy algebra/logs or trial

meta.top_criterion_original: all steps shown ($F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$). Just putting $F_1$ or $F_2$ was not accepted.
meta.marker_note: All steps ($F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$) must be shown; just putting $F_1$ or $F_2$ was not accepted.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern from part (i):
$$F_n=500000(1.07)^n-2000\left(1.07^{n-1}+1.07^{n-2}(1.09)+1.07^{n-3}(1.09)^2+\cdots+1.09^{n-1}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with first term $1.07^{n-1}$, ratio $\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}$ and $n$ terms. There are no fish left when $F_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}500000(1.07)^n&=2000\left(\dfrac{1.07^{n-1}\left(\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{1.09}{1.07}-1}\right)\\500000(1.07)^n&=2000\left(\dfrac{\frac{1.07^n}{1.07}\left(\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{1.09-1.07}{1.07}}\right)\\500(1.07)^n&=100\left(1.07^n\left(\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)\right)\\5(1.07)^n&=1.07^n\left(\dfrac{1.09^n}{1.07^n}\right)-1.07^n\\6(1.07)^n&=1.09^n\\6&=\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n\\\ln 6&=n\ln\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)\\n&=\dfrac{\ln 6}{\ln\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)}\\&=96.75\end{aligned}$$
The fish run out during the 97th year, and $n=1$ is 2025.

$\therefore$ Year 2121
criteria: Writes the expression for $F_n$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A water trough is to be made from a 21m long strip of tin by bending up by the angle $\theta$ with a 7m strip at each side, as shown in the diagram. Find the size of angle $\theta$ that would maximize the cross-sectional area, and thus the volume, of the trough.

\exfigure{1373_q39_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the cross-sectional area is given by $A=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)$.

dif.r: trapezium cross-section with trig ratios, simplify to form

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, find the size of angle $\theta$ that would maximise the cross-sectional area of the trough.

dif.r: derivative gives quadratic in cos theta, then test maximum

figures.cap: trough from a strip of tin with 7 m sides bent up at angle theta
solution sketch: trapezium cross-section with sides 7, base 7, top a, height h, overhang x, angle theta

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1373_q39_s1}

In each right-angled triangle at the sides (hypotenuse $7$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\dfrac{h}{7} & h&=7\sin\theta\\\cos\theta&=\dfrac{x}{7} & x&=7\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
The cross-section is a trapezium with parallel sides $7$ and $7+2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)(7+7+2x)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)\big(14+2(7\cos\theta)\big)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)(14+14\cos\theta)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)\,14(1+\cos\theta)\\&=49\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\\&=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: All steps must be shown properly.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)\\A'&=49(\cos\theta+\cos\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta\sin\theta)\\&=49(\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)\\A''&=49(-\sin\theta-2\cos\theta\sin\theta-2\sin\theta\cos\theta)\\&=49(-\sin\theta-4\sin\theta\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum or minimum, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta&=0\\\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-(1-\cos^2\theta)&=0\\2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos^2\theta+2\cos\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos\theta(\cos\theta+1)-(\cos\theta+1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\theta$ must be acute, so $\theta\ne\pi$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Testing with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}A''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=49\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}-4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=49\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\&=49\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\&=-\dfrac{147\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cross-sectional area is a maximum when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

meta.top_criterion_original: correct angle with nature tested. Lost 1 mark if not tested by $A''$ or table. Radian measure must be used in calculus.
meta.marker_note: Lost 1 mark if the nature was not tested by $A''$ or a table. Radian measure must be used in calculus.

parts.latex: The population of a country town is given by the equation $P=30000e^{-0.06t}$, where t is taken in years from 2025. The time taken for the population to reach a critical 25% of its current population is closest to:

dif.r: solve exponential equation with logs, 25% given directly

solutions.latex:
The population reaches $25\%$ of its current value when $P=0.25\times 30000$:
$$\begin{aligned}0.25&=e^{-0.06t}\\-0.06t&=\ln 0.25\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.06}\\&\approx 23.1\text{ years}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Twelve students sit in a lecture theatre, with exactly twelve seats. Five in the front row and seven in the second row. Two students are chosen at random from the group to go and present to the rest of the class. What is the probability that they are from different rows?

dif.r: count cross-row pairs over C(12,2)

can_use: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
There are $\displaystyle\binom{12}{2}=66$ equally likely pairs, and $5\times 7=35$ of them have one student from each row:
$$P=\dfrac{5\times 7}{\binom{12}{2}}=\dfrac{35}{66}$$

parts.latex: $\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx=-5$ and $\int_4^{10} f(x)\,dx=3$, then $\int_6^{10}[2f(x)+1]\,dx$ is equal to:

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=(2x^2-x+1)^5$ at the point $(0,1)$.

dif.r: chain rule at x=0, perpendicular gradient, normal

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$y'=5(2x^2-x+1)^4\times(4x-1)$$
At $x=0$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=5\times(1)^4(-1)\\&=-5\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent ($m_T\times m_N=-1$):
$$m_N=\dfrac{1}{5}$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ at $(0,1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=\dfrac{1}{5}(x-0)\\5y-5&=x\\x-5y+5&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The equation of the normal may be given in any form.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $|2x-7|=9$

dif.r: absolute value equation, two linear cases

solutions.latex:
$|2x-7|=9$ means $2x-7=9$ or $-(2x-7)=9$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x-7&=9 &&\text{or} & -2x+7&=9\\2x&=16 &&\text{or} & -2x&=2\\x&=8 &&\text{or} & x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=-1\text{ or }x=8$$

questions.stem:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given in the table below.

\extable{1375_q17_t1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the values of $A$ and $B$ given the expected value of the distribution is 6.3.

dif.r: sum to 1 and E(X) give simultaneous equations

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Using the formula $Var(X)=E(x^2)-\mu^2$ to show that that the standard deviation of the distribution is $\sqrt{2.11}$

dif.r: E(X^2) minus mean squared, show sd

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)=6.3$:
$$0.8+5A+1.8+7B+2.4=6.3\quad\ldots(1)$$
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$A+B=0.2\quad\ldots(2)$$
From (1):
$$5A+7B=1.3$$
$(2)\times 7$:
$$7A+7B=1.4$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned}2A&=0.1\\A&=0.05\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore B=0.15$$

$$\begin{aligned}E(X^2)&=4^2\times 0.2+5^2\times 0.05+6^2\times 0.3+7^2\times 0.15+8^2\times 0.3\\&=41.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}Var(X)&=E(X^2)-\mu^2\\&=41.8-6.3^2\\&=2.11\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{Var(X)}\\&=\sqrt{2.11}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A marine ship leaves port O and travels 120 km on a bearing of $057^\circ$ to a research buoy to collect a sample of water after an oil spill 4 months previously. It then travels a further 150 km to another research buoy on a bearing of $165^\circ$ to collect another sample, before returning to port.

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
Complete the diagram showing the journey of the marine ship.

\exfigure{1375_q18_1}

dif.r: mark journey and 72 degree angle on diagram

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the distance the ship travels, and, on what bearing, from the second sample site back to port O.

dif.r: cosine rule, sine rule, return bearing

figures.cap: axes with North arrow and east arrow through Port O
solution sketch: completed bearing diagram: 120 km on 057 degrees, 150 km on 165 degrees, angle 72 degrees at first buoy; triangle sketch with d and bearing angle alpha

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule with the $72^\circ$ angle at the first buoy:
$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=120^2+150^2-2(120)(150)\cos 72^\circ\\d&=160.547\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule for the angle $\alpha$ at the second buoy:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{120}&=\dfrac{\sin 72^\circ}{160.547}\\\alpha&=\sin^{-1}(0.71\ldots)\\&=45.3^\circ\ (1\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$
At the second buoy, the first buoy is on a bearing of $345^\circ$, which is $15^\circ$ west of north, and port $O$ is a further $\alpha$ round:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-(15^\circ+45^\circ)\\&=300^\circ\text{T}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angle $\alpha$, or equivalent merit
Finds the distance, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $3\tan(\pi x)=\sqrt{3}\qquad 0\le x\le 2$

dif.r: solve tan with scaled domain

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}3\tan(\pi x)&=\sqrt{3}\\\tan(\pi x)&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$0\le x\le 2$ gives $0\le\pi x\le 2\pi$, and $\tan$ is positive in the first and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\pi x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\x&=\dfrac{1}{6},\ \dfrac{7}{6}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\tan(\pi x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ and the related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Differentiate:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: $\ln\left(\sqrt{2x-1}\right)$

dif.r: log law for root then f prime over f
recognise e^{ln x^2}=x^2 before differentiating
log base 5 formula with chain

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\ln\sqrt{a}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln a$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x-1)$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\times 2}{2x-1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2x-1}\end{aligned}$$

Since $e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^2+e^{-x}+3\\y'&=2x-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_a f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{(\ln a)\,f(x)}$ (reference sheet) with $a=5$, $f(x)=3x-5$ and $f'(x)=3$:
$$y'=\dfrac{3}{(\ln 5)(3x-5)}$$

questions.stem: Find

parts.label: i
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int(4x+7)^5\,dx$

dif.r: direct (ax+b)^n formula

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x}{3x^2+1}\,dx$

dif.r: f'/f with constant adjustment

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int 2+2\tan^2 x\,dx$

dif.r: 1+tan^2=sec^2 then sec^2 primitive

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$:
$$\int(4x+7)^5\,dx=\dfrac{1}{24}(4x+7)^6+C$$

The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $3x^2+1$, which is $6x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{2x}{3x^2+1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{6x}{3x^2+1}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln|3x^2+1|+C\end{aligned}$$

Using $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\left(2+2\tan^2 x\right)dx&=2\int\left(1+\tan^2 x\right)dx\\&=2\int\sec^2 x\,dx\\&=2\tan x+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the line through the midpoint of the interval from $A(3,2)$ to $B(-7,8)$ perpendicular to the line $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$.

dif.r: midpoint, gradient from intercept form, perpendicular line

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Midpoint of }AB&=\left(\dfrac{3+(-7)}{2},\dfrac{2+8}{2}\right)\\&=(-2,5)\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$ by 6:
$$\begin{aligned}x+3y&=6\\3y&=6-x\end{aligned}$$
so its gradient is $m=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Perpendicular lines have $m_1\times m_2=-1$:
$$m_\perp=3$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ at $(-2,5)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-5&=3(x+2)\\y&=3x+11\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the midpoint $(-2,5)$ AND the perpendicular gradient $3$, or equivalent merit
Finds the midpoint $(-2,5)$ OR the gradient $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the given line, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In the diagram APB is an arc of a circle with centre O, and radius 8 cm, such that the chord AB bisects the line OP at right angles.

\exfigure{1375_q23_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the angle AOB is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

dif.r: cos ratio gives pi/3, double by symmetry

B.note: 1-mark show: cos = 4/8 gives pi/3; exact ratio in radians is the content of the mark

Exact trigonometric ratios.reason: Assumed-algebra skill used only as a side step.

Radian measure.evidence: cos theta = 4/8, theta = pi/3; angle AOB = 2pi/3
Radian measure.reason: Result must be shown in radians.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the shaded area in simplest exact form.

dif.r: sector minus rhombus of two triangles, exact

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: arc APB of circle centre O, rhombus-like figure with chord AB bisecting OP at M at right angles; segments on AP and PB shaded
solution sketch: right triangle OMB with OM = 4, OB = 8, angle theta at O

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1375_q23_s1}

$AB$ bisects $OP$ at right angles at $M$, so $OM=4$; $OA=8$ (radius).

Using the cosine ratio in right-angled $\triangle AOM$, with $\theta=\angle AOM$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{4}{8}\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$\triangle AOM\equiv\triangle BOM$ (RHS), so $\angle AOM=\angle MOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle AOB&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

$OAPB$ is a rhombus (all sides $8$ cm), made of two triangles congruent to $\triangle AOB$, so the shaded area is the sector minus twice the triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Shaded area}&=\text{sector}-2\times\triangle AOB\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C\times 2\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8^2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 8\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times 2\\&=\dfrac{64\pi}{3}-32\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\times 2\\&=\dfrac{64\pi}{3}-32\sqrt{3}\ \text{cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A and B are two events such that P(A)= 0.25, P(B)=0.3 and $P(A|B)=0.7$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find $P(A\cup B)$

dif.r: intersection from conditional, then union

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find in simplest form P(not A and not B )

dif.r: complement of union

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram of overlapping events A and B

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1375_q24_s1}

Using $P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}0.7&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.3}\\P(A\cap B)&=0.21\end{aligned}$$
From the Venn diagram, $P(A\text{ only})=0.25-0.21=0.04$ and $P(B\text{ only})=0.3-0.21=0.09$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B)&=0.04+0.21+0.09\\&=0.34\end{aligned}$$

"Not $A$ and not $B$" is the complement of $A\cup B$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B})&=1-P(A\cup B)\\&=1-0.34\\&=0.66\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ and $b$ if $\left(2\sqrt{3}+3\right)^2+\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}=a+b\sqrt{3}$

dif.r: expand surd square and rationalise denominator, equate parts

solutions.latex:
Rationalising the denominator with $\dfrac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2+\sqrt{3}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(2\sqrt{3}+3\right)^2+\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\&=12+12\sqrt{3}+9+2+\sqrt{3}\\&=23+13\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore a=23,\ b=13$$
criteria: Expands and rationalises, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The curves $y=\dfrac{5}{4}|x-8|$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{12}(3x-6)(14-x)$ intersect at two points as shown in the diagram below

\exfigure{1375_q26_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the point A has coordinates $(4,5)$ and hence write down the coordinates of point B.

dif.r: verify point on both curves, symmetry about x=8 for B

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Calculate the shaded area between the two curves.

dif.r: parabola area minus two triangles, choose decomposition

figures.cap: graph of y = 5/4|x - 8| and the parabola y = 1/12(3x-6)(14-x) meeting at A and B, region between shaded

solutions.latex:
When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{5}{4}|4-8|=5\\y&=\dfrac{1}{12}(3\times 4-6)(14-4)=\dfrac{1}{12}(6)(10)=5\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the curves meet at $A(4,5)$.

Both curves are symmetric about $x=8$ (the vertex of $y=\dfrac{5}{4}|x-8|$ and the axis of the parabola, midway between its roots $2$ and $14$), so $B=(12,5)$.

The shaded area is the area under the parabola from $x=4$ to $x=12$ minus the two triangles under $y=\dfrac{5}{4}|x-8|$ (each with base $4$ and height $5$):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_4^{12}\dfrac{1}{12}(3x-6)(14-x)\,dx-2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\times 4\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\int_4^{12}\left(42x-3x^2-84+6x\right)dx-20\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\int_4^{12}\left(48x-3x^2-84\right)dx-20\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left[24x^2-x^3-84x\right]_4^{12}-20\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left[24\times 12^2-12^3-84\times 12-\left(24\times 16-4^3-84\times 4\right)\right]-20\\&=41\dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{u}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: What is the standard deviation for the age of the population of the town.

dif.r: 2.5% tail means mu+2sigma, solve sigma

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

req: Normal distribution and the empirical rule
Normal distribution and the empirical rule

Inverse normal problems.reason: Starts from a percentage to find σ.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: What is the probability that a person in the town is aged between 48 and 66?

dif.r: empirical rule regions combined from z=-1 to 2

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: By using the values in the table on page 35, find the probability that a resident of the town is aged between 40 and 45.

dif.r: two negative z-scores, table and symmetry, subtract

figures.cap: standard normal curve with area to the left of z shaded
solution sketch: normal curve sketch with z = -1 and z = 2 marked

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of ages lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so $2.5\%$ lie above $\mu+2\sigma$:
$$\begin{aligned}54+2\sigma&=66\\2\sigma&=12\\\sigma&=6\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}x&=66: & z&=2\\x&=48: & z&=-1\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1375_q27_s1}

By the empirical rule, $34\%$ lie between $z=-1$ and $z=0$, and $50\%-2.5\%$ between $z=0$ and $z=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(48\le X\le 66)&=P(-1\le Z\le 2)\\&=34\%+(50\%-2.5\%)\\&=81.5\%\end{aligned}$$

Standardising with $\mu=54$, $\sigma=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=40: & z_1&\approx -2.33\\x&=45: & z_2&=-1.5\end{aligned}$$
By symmetry, $P(Z\le -z)=1-P(Z\le z)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(Z\le -2.33)&=1-0.9901\\&=0.0099\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(Z\le -1.5)&=1-0.9332\\&=0.0668\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(40\le X\le 45)&=0.0668-0.0099\\&=0.0569\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
An indoor surf pool models the movement of their waves according to the rule

$h=30-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{36}t\right)$, where $h$ is the height of the wave above the pool floor, in centimetres and $t$ is the time measured in seconds, from 12 noon.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Sketch the motion of the pool for $0\le t\le 72$. Indicate the co-ordinates of any turning points.

dif.r: sketch reflected cosine with turning points

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
A surfer arrives at the pool at noon and wants to enter the pool as the wave is increasing yet wants to have at the height of the wave to be least 30 cm to feel safe.

How many seconds must he wait for the conditions to be ideal?

dif.r: solve cos=0, choose increasing branch from graph

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of h = 30 - 20cos(pi t/36) on the grid: minimum (0,10), maximum (36,50), minimum (72,10), h = 30 at t = 18 and 54

meta.top_criterion_original: correct sketch with turning points (no breakdown given)

solutions.latex:
The height is $30$ cm when
$$\begin{aligned}30&=30-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{36}t\right)\\0&=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{36}t\right)\end{aligned}$$
Let $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{36}t$, so $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

From the graph in part (i), the wave is increasing at the first of these:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{36}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\t&=18\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
At an airport, luggage is weighed at check-in to ensure that it meets the airlines strict requirements.

The mass of each piece of luggage, in kilograms, is modelled by a continuous random variable X, whose probability density function is

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} kx^2(30-x) & 0\le x\le 30\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

dif.r: polynomial integral equals 1, solve k

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
An airline allows each passenger one piece of luggage free of charge if it weighs 23 kg or less and refuses to carry a bag if the single bag weighs more than 30kg.

They charge \$40 excess fee for every kilogram, or part thereof, a bag is over the 23kg.

What is the probability that a passenger will not have to pay for excess luggage?

dif.r: one definite integral, interpret no excess as X<=23

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: What is the probability that a passenger will need to pay \$200, or more, in excess luggage fees?

dif.r: translate $200 and part-thereof rule to X>27, integrate

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^{30}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx&=1\\k\left[10x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4\right]_0^{30}&=1\\k\left[10(30)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(30^4)-0\right]&=1\\k(67500)&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\end{aligned}$$

No excess is paid if the bag weighs $23$ kg or less:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\le 23)&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\int_0^{23}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4\right]_0^{23}\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10(23)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(23)^4-0\right]\\&\approx 0.766\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

$\$200=5\times\$40$, so the bag is more than $27$ kg (up to the $30$ kg limit):
$$\begin{aligned}P(27<X\le 30)&=\int_{27}^{30}\dfrac{1}{67500}\left(30x^2-x^3\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{67500}\left[10(30)^3-\dfrac{30^4}{4}-\left[10(27)^3-\dfrac{1}{4}(27)^4\right]\right]\\&=0.0523\ldots\ (4\text{ sig fig})\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Sketch the curve $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2-12x+10$ by first finding the coordinates of all the stationary points, checking their nature, and finding the point of inflection.

dif.r: routine cubic: stationary points, nature, inflection, sketch

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
A new curve with equation $g(x)=10-f(x+2)$ is to be drawn.

What is the minimum value of this curve in the domain $-5\le x\le 1$?

dif.r: transformations move max to min, check domain and endpoints

A.note: min of g on a domain via transformed f; endpoint check

B.note: Image of f's maximum turning point under g(x)=10-f(x+2); minimum on a closed domain (endpoints should be checked)

Translations of graphs.evidence: Translating 2 units left: (-3,-17). Translating 10 units up: (-3,-7)

Combined transformations.evidence: reflected in the x-axis, translated 2 units left, then 10 units up

figures.cap: solution sketch: cubic sketch: max (-1,17), y-intercept 10, inflexion, min (2,-10)

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)=6x^2-6x-12&=0\\6(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\x=2\ &\text{ or }\ x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$f(2)=-10$ and $f(-1)=17$.

Testing the nature with the first derivative:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -2 & -1 & 0\\ \hline f'(x) & + & 0 & -12 \end{array}\qquad\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & 2 & 3\\ \hline f'(x) & - & 0 & + \end{array}$$
$\therefore$ $(-1,17)$ is a local maximum turning point.

$\therefore$ $(2,-10)$ is a local minimum turning point.

Possible inflexion where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)=12x-6&=0\\x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\y&=\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(0)&=-6 &&\text{concave down}\\f''\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=0\\f''(1)&=6 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ point of inflexion at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{7}{2}\right)$ (concavity changes).

\exfigure{1375_q30_s1}
criteria: No test of inflexion, or equivalent merit
Errors in points or missing steps for inflexion and two turning points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$g(x)=-f(x+2)+10$: the graph of $f$ is reflected in the $x$-axis, translated 2 units left, then translated 10 units up.

For $-5\le x\le 1$, $x+2$ runs over $-3\le x+2\le 3$, which contains the maximum turning point $(-1,17)$ of $f$; the reflection turns this maximum into the minimum of $g$.

Reflecting in the $x$-axis: $(-1,17)$ becomes $(-1,-17)$.

Translating 2 units left: $(-3,-17)$.

Translating 10 units up: $(-3,-7)$.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum value}=-7$$
criteria: Finds the point $(-3,-7)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Use the trapezoidal rule with three function values to evaluate the integral $\int_0^1 3e^x\sin x\,dx$.

Answer to 3 significant figures.

dif.r: trapezoidal, two strips, calculator values

solutions.latex:
The trapezoidal rule with three function values uses $n=2$ strips on $[0,1]$, so $h=\dfrac{1-0}{2}=0.5$ (radians used):

\extable{Ts1627_1}

With $a=0$, $b=1$, $n=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 3e^x\sin x\,dx&\approx\dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left[f(a)+f(b)+2f(0.5)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1-0}{2(2)}\left[0+3e\sin 1+2\times 3e^{\frac{1}{2}}\sin\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\\&=2.901\ldots\\&\approx 2.90\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the trapezoidal rule correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: full marks at $2.901\ldots$ (no deduction if rounding not done)
meta.marker_note: Full marks at $2.901\ldots$ (no deduction if rounding not done).
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the middle function value in the rule was left blank, $2\times f(\ )$; it is $2f(0.5)$. Answer unchanged.

parts.latex:
Daniel grows tomatoes.

Some are grown inside a greenhouse while others are grown outside the greenhouse in the garden, with the other vegetables he grows.

The box and whisker plots shown below show the distribution of the heights of the tomato plants inside and outside the greenhouse.

\exfigure{1375_q32_1}

Write down two comparisons, supported with mathematical reasoning, about the heights of the plants grown inside the greenhouse to those grown outside the greenhouse and make a justified recommendation for future plantings.
parts.note: Box plots / comparing data sets (medians, ranges) have no 2024 Advanced dot point · Standard: MST-11-08

figures.cap: box and whisker plots of plant heights (cm): Inside Greenhouse and Outside Greenhouse, scale 100 to 200

solutions.latex:
Comparing the box plots.

Inside the greenhouse:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{median}&=148\text{ cm}\\ \text{range}&=190-114=76\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
Outside the greenhouse:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{median}&=138\text{ cm}\\ \text{range}&=194-102=92\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
The median is higher inside, so the plants inside are taller.

The range is larger outside, so there is more variation in heights outside.

$\therefore$ the recommendation for future plantings is to grow them inside.

meta.top_criterion_original: two supported comparisons and a justified recommendation (no breakdown given)
meta.marker_note: Full marks need two supported comparisons and a justified recommendation (no breakdown given).

parts.latex:
A particle moves along the $x$-axis with the acceleration at time $t$ equal to $a=12(t+3)^2$.

If the particle is initially at rest at the origin find the position of the particle after one second of motion.

dif.r: integrate acceleration twice using initial conditions

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$v=\int 12(t+3)^2\,dt=4(t+3)^3+C$$
Initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(3)^3+C\\C&=-108\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=4(t+3)^3-108$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$x=\int\left(4(t+3)^3-108\right)dt=(t+3)^4-108t+C_2$$
Starting at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=81-0+C_2\\C_2&=-81\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=(t+3)^4-108t-81$$
When $t=1$:
$$x=67$$
criteria: Finds the displacement $x=(t+3)^4-108t-81$, or equivalent merit
Finds the velocity $v=4(t+3)^3-108$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A die is loaded such that in a roll of a single die the chance of rolling a 1 is $\dfrac{x}{4}$, the chance of rolling a 2 is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the chance of rolling a 6 is $\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)$. The chance of rolling the other numbers (3,4 or 5) remain one in 6.

Two such dice are rolled together and the numbers on the uppermost faces are added to obtain a total score for the roll.

The probability of the total score of the two dice being 7 can be expressed as $y=f(x)$

Find the probability of rolling a 1 in a single roll of a die if the probability of rolling a total of 7 with two dice is $\dfrac{5}{36}$.

dif.r: model P(sum 7) with parameter, solve x(1-x)=0

solutions.latex:
A total of 7 comes from $(1,6)$, $(6,1)$, $(2,5)$, $(5,2)$, $(3,4)$ or $(4,3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=2\times\dfrac{x}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2\\&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{18}\end{aligned}$$
Setting $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{36}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{5}{36}&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{5}{36}\\ \dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

$x\ne 0$, as $P(1)$ exists.
$$\therefore x=1$$
$$\therefore P(1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$

questions.stem:
A drain is made by folding up a rectangular sheet of metal, with cross- sectional length of 6 m, to form a cross-sectional area in the shape of an isosceles trapezium, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1375_q35_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
Show that the area of the trapezoidal cross section of the drain can be expressed as

$A=\sin\vartheta(4+4\cos\vartheta)$ where $\vartheta$ is the angle in radians that the metal sheet is bent to form the drain.

dif.r: trapezium area from diagram with trig height and width

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the angle $\vartheta$ that maximizes the cross-sectional area.

dif.r: derivative gives quadratic in cos theta, then test maximum

figures.cap: cross-section of drain: isosceles trapezium, base and sloping sides 2 m each (tick marks), sides inclined at angle theta to the horizontal
solution sketch: drain diagram annotated: sloping sides 2, base 2, height 2 sin theta, horizontal 2 cos theta

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1375_q35_s1}

From the diagram, the base and each sloping side are $2$ m, so the height is $2\sin\theta$ and each side adds $2\cos\theta$ to the top width.

Using the area of a trapezium, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)$ (or a rectangle plus two triangles):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(2+2+4\cos\theta)\\&=\sin\theta(4+4\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the height $2\sin\theta$ and the width $2\cos\theta$ (may be shown on the diagram), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The area must be explicitly shown.

solutions.latex:
Expanding the area from part (i):
$$A=4\sin\theta+4\sin\theta\cos\theta$$
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on $4\sin\theta\cos\theta$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=4\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\u'&=4\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=4\cos\theta+4\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)+4\cos\theta\cos\theta\\&=4\cos\theta-4(1-\cos^2\theta)+4\cos^2\theta\\&=8\cos^2\theta+4\cos\theta-4\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum or minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\theta$ is an angle in a right-angled triangle, so $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ only:
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
Testing with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=16\cos\theta(-\sin\theta)-4\sin\theta$$
At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\times\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=16\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-4\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=-4\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}\\&=-6\sqrt{3}<0\end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\therefore$ the angle that maximises the area is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (or $60^\circ$).

meta.top_criterion_original: correct angle with test (no breakdown given)
meta.marker_note: Full marks need the correct angle with a test of its nature. As it is a trig function, $\theta$ is in radians; this should be reflected in the students' solutions.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ was substituted as $4\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$, giving $-4\sqrt{3}+2\sqrt{3}=-2\sqrt{3}$; it is $-4\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}=-6\sqrt{3}$. Conclusion (maximum) unchanged.

The first and last terms are known, so use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[a+l\right]$:

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, the 3rd, 7th and 16th terms are $a+2d$, $a+6d$ and $a+15d$.

They are the first three terms of a GP, so the ratios of consecutive terms are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}&=\dfrac{a+15d}{a+6d}\\(a+6d)(a+6d)&=(a+2d)(a+15d)\\a^2+6ad+6ad+36d^2&=a^2+15ad+2ad+30d^2\\a^2+12ad+36d^2&=a^2+17ad+30d^2\\6d^2&=5ad\end{aligned}$$
$d\ne 0$, so dividing by $d$:
$$6d=5a\text{ as required}$$

The common ratio is the 7th term divided by the 3rd term:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}\\&=\dfrac{a+6d}{\frac{1}{3}(3a+6d)}\\&=3\times\dfrac{a+6d}{3a+6d}\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $6d=5a$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=3\times\dfrac{a+5a}{3a+5a}\\&=3\times\dfrac{6a}{8a}\\&=\dfrac{18}{8}\\&=\dfrac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$

The following transformations were applied to the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the order shown below.

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal translation to the right by 4 units.
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Vertical translation down by 3 units

\end{itemize}

solutions.latex:
Horizontal transformations first.

Translation right 4 units:
$$y=(x+1-4)^2=(x-3)^2$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$:
$$y=\left(\dfrac{x}{\frac{4}{3}}-3\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2$$
Then the vertical transformations.

Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2$$
Translation down 3 units:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2-3$$
Reflection in the $x$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2-3\right)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2+3\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{163_q10_s1}

Writing the function from part (a) in vertex form:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}(x-4)\right)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3\end{aligned}$$
So the vertex is $(4,3)$.

$x$-intercepts, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3\\-3&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2\\16&=(x-4)^2\\x-4&=\pm 4\\x&=0\text{ or }x=8\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x+\log_e(4x-3)$ at the point where $x=1$.

dif.r: tangent with e^x and ln(4x-3)

solutions.latex:
$$y=e^x+\ln(4x-3)$$
Differentiating, with the chain rule for $\ln(4x-3)$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x+\dfrac{1}{4x-3}\times4$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e+\ln(4-3)\\&=e\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e+\dfrac{4}{4-3}\\&=e+4\end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through $(1,e)$ with gradient $m=e+4$. Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=(e+4)(x-1)\\y&=(e+4)x-e-4+e\\&=(e+4)x-4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the point $(1,e)$ or the gradient $e+4$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2(\ln x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\&=\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\ln x^2=2\ln x$, then part (a): $\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}$ is the derivative of $(\ln x)^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln x^2}{2x}\,dx&=\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{2x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(\ln x)^2\Big]_1^e\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left((\ln e)^2-(\ln1)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1^2-0^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites the integral as $\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $y=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$, show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

dif.r: quotient rule, trig identity simplification, second derivative, verify identity

Chain rule.reason: Second derivative of -1/(1+sin x) can equally be done by the quotient rule (agreed); method is free.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\cos x & v&=1+\sin x\\u'&=-\sin x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Simplifying with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)(-\sin x)-\cos x(\cos x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-\sin x-\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Writing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-(1+\sin x)^{-1}$ and using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-(-(1+\sin x)^{-2})\cdot(\cos x)\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into the left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}+\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\cdot\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x-\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct second derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle travels on a straight line such that its displacement is given by the function

$$x(t)=\begin{cases}5t & 0\le t\le1\\[4pt]6\sqrt{t}-\dfrac{1}{t} & t>1\end{cases}$$

where $x$ is the particle's displacement from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time, in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the particle begins its journey at the origin.

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the particle is never at rest.

dif.r: continuity of piecewise plus positive derivative argument

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction
Velocity as a rate of change

req: Particles at rest and changing direction
Particles at rest and changing direction
Velocity as a rate of change

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: not_when: powers-of-t displacement with no acceleration/integration belongs to Velocity as a rate of change.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds of the particle's journey.

dif.r: use monotonicity from (b), evaluate x(4)

solutions.latex:
For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5(0)\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ at $t=0$, $x=0$: the particle starts at the origin.

For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$, so the displacement increases linearly (at $5$ m/s).

At $t=1$, the second piece gives
$$\begin{aligned}x(1)&=6\sqrt{1}-\dfrac{1}{1}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
which matches $5t$, so the displacement is continuous at $t=1$.

For $t>1$:
$$x'(t)=3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\dfrac{1}{t^2}$$
Both terms are positive, so $x'(t)>0$ and $x(t)$ is increasing for $t>1$.

$\therefore$ the displacement is increasing for $t>0$.

$\therefore$ the particle never comes to rest.

Alternatively, as $t\to\infty$, $x'(t)\to0^+$ (an asymptote), so $x'(t)$ is never $0$.
criteria: Velocity $5$ m/s for $0\le t\le1$ and $x(1)=5$ (continuity), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{\sec^23x}{\tan3x}=\sec3x\ \text{cosec}\,3x.$$

dif.r: trig ratio simplification show-that

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\sec3x\ \text{cosec}\,3x\,dx$.

dif.r: use (a) then f'/f with tan 3x

solutions.latex:
Writing $\sec 3x=\dfrac{1}{\cos 3x}$ and $\tan 3x=\dfrac{\sin 3x}{\cos 3x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec3x\sec3x}{\tan3x}\\&=\sec3x\times\dfrac{1}{\cos3x}\times\dfrac{\cos3x}{\sin3x}\\&=\sec3x\times\dfrac{1}{\sin3x}\\&=\sec3x\,\text{cosec}\,3x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses in terms of $\sin3x$ and $\cos3x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using part (a); the numerator $3\sec^23x$ is the derivative of $\tan3x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\sec3x\,\text{cosec}\,3x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{\sec^23x}{\tan3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3\sec^23x}{\tan3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|\tan3x\right|+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows the graphs of the functions $y=2\cos x$ and $y=\cot x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.

\exfigure{165_q13_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, and solve this equation.

dif.r: equate, factorise cos x, solve over 0 to 2pi

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$.

dif.r: direct chain rule on ln(sin x)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find, in simplest form, the total area of the region enclosed by the two curves for $0\le x\le\pi$.

dif.r: two regions by symmetry, log primitive of cot, exact

figures.cap: graphs of y=2cos x and y=cot x for 0 to 2pi

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where $2\cos x=\cot x$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos x&=\cot x\\2\cos x&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\2\sin x\cos x&=\cos x\\2\sin x\cos x-\cos x&=0\\\cos x(2\sin x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Either $\cos x=0$:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
or $2\sin x-1=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Shows $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$ and finds one pair of solutions, or equivalent merit
Shows $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)&=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\times\cos x\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\end{aligned}$$

For $0\le x\le\pi$ the curves enclose two regions between $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, equal in area by symmetry about $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$.

On $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $2\cos x\ge\cot x$. Using part (b) for the primitive of $\cot x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(2\cos x-\cot x\right)dx\\&=2\Big[2\sin x-\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=2\left[2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\right]\\&=2\left[2-\ln1-1+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\&=2+2\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=2-2\ln2\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral expression, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Full marks need the answer in simplest form.

parts.latex:
Ian is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven in $^\circ C$ at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the initial temperature of the oven?

dif.r: substitute t=0 into given model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: evaluate model twice, average rate of change

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Ian can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ C$ per minute.

After turning on the oven, how long must Ian wait before he can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute?

dif.r: differentiate a^(kt), solve derivative inequality with logs

solutions.latex:
The oven is switched on at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^0\\&=25^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$

At $t=25$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(25)}\\&=86.4265\end{aligned}$$
At $t=75$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(75)}\\&=144.1163\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The average rate of change is the change in $T$ divided by the change in $t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Average rate}&=\dfrac{144.1163\ldots-86.4265}{75-25}\\&=1.15\ ^\circ\text{C/min (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

The instantaneous rate is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt}=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-150\times0.2\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\\&=-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\end{aligned}$$
Require $\dfrac{dT}{dt}<1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}&<1\\(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\\\ln(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by $\ln(0.9)<0$ reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}0.2t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)}{\ln(0.9)}\\0.2t&>10.9227\\t&>54.6\\t&>55\text{ min (nearest min)}\end{aligned}$$
Ian must wait 55 minutes.

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on a straight line with acceleration given by

$$\ddot{x}=12e^{-2t}+e^{-t}$$

where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds.

Initially the particle's velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 8 m.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by

$$x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4.$$

dif.r: integrate exponentials twice with two initial conditions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the particle comes to rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

dif.r: quadratic in e^t, reject negative root

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Find the displacement when the particle comes to rest.

Give a simplified, exact answer.

dif.r: exact simplification of e^(-2ln3) terms

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int\ddot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{12e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+C\\&=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $\dot{x}=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6&=-6-1+C\\C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-6e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+t+C_2\\&=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+C_2\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $x=8$:
$$\begin{aligned}8&=3+1+0+C_2\\C_2&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1=0$$
Multiplying by $e^{2t}$ gives a quadratic in $e^t$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6-e^t+e^{2t}&=0\\(e^t)^2-e^t-6&=0\\(e^t+2)(e^t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-2$ or $e^t=3$.

$e^t>0$, so $e^t=-2$ has no solution.
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=3\\t&=\ln3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

meta.marker_note: Full marks need $t=\ln3$ with $e^t=-2$ rejected.

dif.r: difference of sectors, linear equation for r

figures.cap: two sectors OAB and OCD with centre O, angle 3pi/4 at O, AC = 6 cm, region ACDB shaded; not to scale

solutions.latex:
Let $OA=r$, so $OC=r+6$.

Using the sector area $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, the shaded area is the large sector minus the small sector:
$$\begin{aligned}99\pi&=\dfrac{1}{2}(r+6)^2\times\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\\ 99\pi&=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}(r+6)^2-\dfrac{3\pi}{8}r^2\\ 264&=r^2+12r+36-r^2\\ 264&=12r+36\\ r&=19\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore OA=19\text{ cm}$.

parts.latex:
Characteristics of the cubic function $f(x)$ are given.

\begin{itemize}
\item $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$.
\item $x=2$ is a repeated root of $f(x)$.
\item $f'(-2)=0$
\item $f'(x)>0$ where the graph with equation $y=f(x)$ crosses the $y$-axis.
\end{itemize}

Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)$?

option B: cubic touching x-axis at -4, minimum at x=2, crossing at 4

parts.latex: Differentiate the function $f(x)=\ln\left(\sqrt[3]{x^3+3}\right)$ to find $f'(x)$.

dif.r: log law on cube root then f prime over f

solutions.latex:
Writing the cube root as a power, and using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\ln\left(\left(x^3+3\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)\\ f'(x)&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{3}\left(x^3+3\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\times 3x^2}{\left(x^3+3\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}}\\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{\left(x^3+3\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\times\left(x^3+3\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}}\\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{x^3+3}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:

Period $=\pi$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=\pi\\ n&=2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore y=3\sin 2x$.

solutions.latex:

dif.r: MCQ: inverse table lookup for 90th percentile

figures.cap: standard normal table, z = 0.00 to 1.39, probabilities 0.5000 to 0.9177

solutions.latex:
$\mu=37$ and $\sigma=11$.

The $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile has $P(Z<z)\approx 0.9$; from the table, $z\approx 1.28$.

Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, so $x=z\sigma+\mu$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=1.28\times 11+37\\ &=51.08\end{aligned}$$
which is approximately 51 minutes.

dif.r: near-twin of 2020 Q10: stationary points of composite from graphs

figures.cap: parabola f(x) = x^2 and concave-down parabola g(x) through the origin and (4, 0) with maximum near (2, 3)

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $g$ is a parabola with its turning point at $x=2$, so $g(x)=-a(x-2)^2+k$; and $f(x)=x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}g(f(x))&=-a\left(x^2-2\right)^2+k\\ \dfrac{d}{dx}g(f(x))&=-2a\left(x^2-2\right)\times 2x\\ &=-4ax\left(x^2-2\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where the derivative is $0$:
$$0=-4ax\left(x^2-2\right)$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{2}$: 3 solutions.

$\therefore$ there are 3 stationary points.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the derivative of $g(f(x))$ was written $g'(f(x))$, which means $g'$ evaluated at $f(x)$ and has no factor $2x$; it is $\dfrac{d}{dx}g(f(x))$. Answer unchanged.

parts.latex: Solve $\log_2 9=5\log_2 3-\log_2 x$.

dif.r: power and quotient laws then solve for x

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $n\log_a b=\log_a b^n$ and $\log_a b-\log_a c=\log_a\dfrac{b}{c}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 9&=\log_2 3^5-\log_2 x\\ \log_2 9&=\log_2\dfrac{243}{x}\\ 9&=\dfrac{243}{x}\\ x&=27\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses log laws to combine the right-hand side, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{5}{13}$ and $\tan\alpha<0$, find the exact value of $\cos\alpha$.

dif.r: quadrant from signs, 5-12-13 triangle, negative cos

figures.cap: solution sketch: right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13, opposite 5, adjacent 12, angle theta

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{166_q11_s1}

From the right-angled triangle with sides $5$, $12$, $13$ (Pythagoras' theorem), the related acute angle $\theta$ has
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{13}$$
$\sin\alpha>0$ and $\tan\alpha<0$, so $\alpha$ is in the 2nd quadrant, where cosine is negative.
$$\therefore\ \cos\alpha=-\dfrac{12}{13}$$

solutions.latex:
By the angle sum of a triangle, $\angle C=180^\circ-45^\circ-75^\circ=60^\circ$.

Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{BC}{\sin 45^\circ}&=\dfrac{12}{\sin 60^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{12\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 60^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{12\times\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=6\sqrt{2}\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{12\sqrt{6}}{3}\\ &=4\sqrt{6}\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the sine rule, or equivalent merit

Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with $AB=12$, $BC=4\sqrt{6}$ and the included angle $\angle B=75^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 4\sqrt{6}\times\sin 75^\circ\\ &\approx 56.78\text{ cm}^2\ (2\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $f(x)=(1-\cos x)^5$, find $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned}f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)&=5\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(1-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^4\\ &=5\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the derivative of the function $f(x)=x^2e^{5x}$. Give your answer in factorised form.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $(\sin x+3)(2\sin x+1)=0$ in the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: factorised already; reject sin=-3, solve sin=-1/2

figures.cap: solution sketch: ASTC quadrant diagram with the third and fourth quadrants marked

solutions.latex:
Either $\sin x+3=0$ or $2\sin x+1=0$.

$\sin x+3=0$ gives $\sin x=-3$: no solutions, as $-1\le\sin x\le 1$.

$2\sin x+1=0$ gives $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

\exfigure{166_q11_s2}

Sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants, and the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Explains $\sin x=-3$ has no solutions, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3\dfrac{27x^2-21}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx$, leaving your answer in exact simplified form.

dif.r: f'/f with factor 3, exact log evaluation

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^3-7x+8\right)=9x^2-7$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^3\dfrac{27x^2-21}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx&=3\int_1^3\dfrac{9x^2-7}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx\\ &=3\Big[\ln\left|3x^3-7x+8\right|\Big]_1^3\\ &=3\left[\ln\left|3(3)^3-7(3)+8\right|-\ln\left|3(1)^3-7(1)+8\right|\right]\\ &=3\left[\ln 68-\ln 4\right]\\ &=3\ln 17\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Full marks for $3\ln 17$ in either the substituted or the simplified form.

parts.latex:
Consider the geometric series

$$1+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)^3+\ldots$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the exact value of the limiting sum. Express your answer with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
Each term is the previous term multiplied by $\sqrt{11}-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\sqrt{11}-3\\ &=0.31662\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$-1<0.31662\ldots<1$, so $|r|<1$.

$\therefore$ the GP has a limiting sum.

meta.top_criterion_original: concludes $|r|<1$ so the limiting sum exists

solutions.latex:
Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{11}-3$, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt{11}}\times\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{4+\sqrt{11}}\\ &=\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{5}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Determine the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)$ at the point $(2,\ \ln 14)$. Express your answer in general form $ax+by+c=0$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)\\ y'&=\dfrac{6x}{3x^2+2}\end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{6(2)}{3(2)^2+2}\\ &=\dfrac{6}{7}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{6}{7}$ at $(2,\ln 14)$.

Using the point-gradient form $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\ln 14&=\dfrac{6}{7}(x-2)\\ 7y-7\ln 14&=6x-12\\ 6x-7y+7\ln 14-12&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient $\dfrac{6}{7}$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Any equivalent general form is accepted.

parts.latex: It is given that $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When $x=9$, $y=3$. Determine the equation relating $x$ in terms of $y$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: decreasing curve y = 27/x through (2, 27/2), (9, 3) and (18, 3/2)

solutions.latex:
For inverse proportion, $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.

Substituting $x=9$, $y=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}3&=\dfrac{k}{9}\\ k&=27\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{27}{x}$$

At $x=2$, $y=\dfrac{27}{2}$.

At $x=18$, $y=\dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{change in }y&=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{27}{2}\\ &=-12\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{166_q12_s1}

parts.latex: Ava is managing the growth of a population of bacteria in a laboratory. The population can be modelled by the exponential equation $P(t)=500e^{kt}$ where the initial population is 500 bacteria, $k$ is the growth constant, and $t$ is time in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ correct to 1 significant figure, given that there are 1660 bacteria present after 2 hours.

dif.r: solve for k with logs, convert hours to minutes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the rate of change of the population with respect to time after 2 hours. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: differentiate exponential and substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Ava is concerned about the growth of the bacteria and wants to determine if she needs to introduce a control mechanism.

Interpret the nature of the population growth with reference to the derivatives $P'(t)$ and $P''(t)$, and hence determine if a control would be needed.

dif.r: interpret signs of P' and P'' in context

solutions.latex:
Substituting $P(120)=1660$ ($t=120$ minutes):
$$\begin{aligned}1660&=500e^{120k}\\ \dfrac{83}{25}&=e^{120k}\\ 120k&=\ln\dfrac{83}{25}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}\\ &\approx 0.01\ (1\text{ sig. fig.})\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Either the exact or the rounded value of $k$ is accepted.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P'(120)&=500ke^{k\times 120}\\ &=16.6\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the population is increasing at approximately 17 bacteria/min at $t=120$.

meta.marker_note: Also accept 16 or 16.6 bacteria/min.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P''(t)&=500k^2e^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
$e^{kt}>0$ for all $t$, so
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P(t)\text{ is increasing}\\ P''(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P'(t)\text{ is increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ P(t)$ is increasing at an increasing rate, so a control mechanism should be introduced.
criteria: Shows $P'(t)$ and $P''(t)$ are both positive for all $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: increasing at an increasing rate, so a control is needed

parts.latex:
Lara works as a sales representative for a company that sells laboratory equipment. The number of sales she makes in a day is given by the probability distribution table.

\extable{166_q13_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the expected value of the number of sales that Lara makes on a particular day.

dif.r: direct sum of x P(x)

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Another sales representative, Rebecca, has an expected number of sales of 2.5 and a standard deviation in the number of sales of 1.2.

The CEO of the company would like to promote a sales representative to be the leader of the sales team.

If the CEO bases her decision on sales performance, are they more likely to promote Lara or Rebecca? Justify your answer with appropriate statistical reasoning.

dif.r: compute sd then compare mean and spread, justify

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=0\times 0.14+1\times 0.15+2\times 0.25+3\times 0.3+4\times 0.11+5\times 0.05\\ &=2.24\end{aligned}$$

Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=2.24$:
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=0^2\times 0.14+1^2\times 0.15+2^2\times 0.25+3^2\times 0.3+4^2\times 0.11+5^2\times 0.05-2.24^2\\ &=1.8424\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{1.8424}\\ &\approx 1.36\ (2\text{ dp})\end{aligned}$$
Rebecca has a higher mean and a smaller standard deviation, so she has higher sales on average and is more consistent.

$\therefore$ Rebecca is more likely to be promoted.
criteria: Finds the standard deviation $\approx 1.36$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Rebecca, justified by higher mean and smaller standard deviation

parts.latex:
Find all the values of $\theta$ where $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$ such that

$$\cos\left(\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$

dif.r: shifted domain; boundary solutions -pi and pi easily missed

solutions.latex:
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned}-\pi&\le\theta\le\pi\\ -\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&\left(\text{subtract }\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\\ -\dfrac{7\pi}{6}&\le\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=-\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ \theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=-\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ \theta&=-\pi,\ -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \pi\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the values of $\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, or equivalent merit
Adjusts the domain or finds the acute angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The first three terms of a series are 3, 9, 15, ……

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the fifteenth term in this series.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The sum of the first $n$ consecutive terms of the series is 243.

What is the value of $n$?

dif.r: quadratic in n but collapses to 3n^2=243

solutions.latex:
The series is arithmetic with $a=3$, $d=6$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=a+(n-1)d\\ T_{15}&=3+14\times 6\\ &=87\end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=3$, $d=6$ and $S_n=243$:
$$\begin{aligned}243&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(6+6(n-1)\right)\\ 243&=\dfrac{n}{2}(6n)\\ 243&=3n^2\\ n^2&=81\\ n&=9\quad(n>0)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A bag contains eight cards that are each printed with one of the following sets of characters.

$$\text{aaa}\qquad\text{aab}\qquad\text{aba}\qquad\text{baa}\qquad\text{abb}\qquad\text{bab}\qquad\text{bba}\qquad\text{bbb}$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first character printed on the card is an ‘a’ and $N_2$ be the event that the first and second characters printed on the card are both an ‘a’.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.

dif.r: test independence by product of probabilities

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
$N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent if $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)&=\dfrac{4}{8}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ P(N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1\cap N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{8}\end{aligned}$$
$P(N_1)\times P(N_2)\ne P(N_1\cap N_2)$

$\therefore\ N_1$ and $N_2$ are not independent.
criteria: Finds $P(N_1\cap N_2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}3\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)dx$. Express your answer with a rational denominator.

dif.r: sin(x/4) primitive, exact value, rationalise

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sin(ax)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos(ax)+C$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi}3\sin\dfrac{x}{4}\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{-3\cos\frac{x}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right]_0^{\pi}\\ &=\left[-12\cos\dfrac{x}{4}\right]_0^{\pi}\\ &=-12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\left(-12\cos 0\right)\\ &=-12\times\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+12\\ &=12-6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Either form of the primitive is accepted.

parts.latex: A 40-centimetre length of wire is cut into three pieces. Two pieces are bent to form two congruent circles and the final piece is bent to form a square.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If the radius of each congruent circle is $r$ centimetres, show that the total area of the three shapes is given by $A=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2$

dif.r: wire-length constraint, eliminate x, two area formulas

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the length of the side of the square and the value of $r$ that will minimise the total area of the three shapes.

dif.r: chain rule with pi terms, solve for r, find square side

Chain rule.reason: (10 - pi r)^2 could be expanded first; chain rule is one valid method.

Second derivative.reason: Nature of the minimum may be shown by any method (e.g. table of slopes).

solutions.latex:
Let the side length of the square be $x$. The wire forms two circles (circumference $2\pi r$ each) and the square (perimeter $4x$):
$$\begin{aligned}40&=2\pi r+2\pi r+4x\\ 40&=4\pi r+4x\\ 10&=\pi r+x\\ x&=10-\pi r\end{aligned}$$
The total area is two circles ($\pi r^2$ each) and the square ($x^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ A&=2\pi r^2+(10-\pi r)^2\\ &=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $40=2\pi r+2\pi r+4x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (chain rule on $(10-\pi r)^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\\ \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=2(10-\pi r)\times(-\pi)+4\pi r\\ &=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 20\pi&=2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 10&=\pi r+2r\\ 10&=r(\pi+2)\\ r&=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature using $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi^2+4\pi>0\text{ for all }r$$
$\therefore\ A$ is always concave up, so there is a minimum at $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$.

At $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10-\pi\left(\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{10(\pi+2)-10\pi}{\pi+2}\\ &=\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the area is minimised when $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$ cm and the side of the square is $\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}$ cm.
criteria: Finds $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$ and verifies the minimum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A jelly baby is a lolly.

A bag of jelly babies is labelled as having a net weight of 220 grams. The production process produces bags whose weights are normally distributed with a mean of 224.7 grams and a standard deviation of 2.35 grams.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If 1200 bags of jelly babies are produced, how many bags would be expected to contain less than the labelled weight?

dif.r: z=-2, empirical rule tail, scale to 1200

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b

dif.r: z-score, table, complement, scale to 1200

figures.cap: normal curve shaded to the left of z
solution sketch: normal curve with mean 224.7, region below 220 shaded

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{166_q16_s1}

Standardising, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{220-224.7}{2.35}\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of weights lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<220)&=0.5\times(1-0.95)\\ &=0.025\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Expected number}&=1200\times 0.025\\ &=30\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 30 bags would be expected to be below 220 g.

Standardising, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{231-224.7}{2.35}\\ &=2.68\end{aligned}$$
Using the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>231)&=1-P(X\le 231)\\ &=1-\Phi(2.68)\\ &=1-0.9963\\ &=0.0037\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Expected number}&=0.0037\times 1200\\ &=4.44\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 4 bags would be expected to be over 231 g.

meta.marker_note: Also accept 4.44 or 5 bags.

The diagram shows the graph of $y=p^x$, where $p>1$. Also shown on the diagram are 4 inner rectangles of width 1 unit.

\exfigure{166_q16_2}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area of the 4 rectangles is $\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}$ square units.

dif.r: rectangle heights form GP, sum formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By finding the area under the curve $y=p^x$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$, and using the result in part (a), prove that $\ln p<p-1$.

dif.r: compare rectangles with integral, rearrange to log inequality

figures.cap: curve y = p^x with 4 inner rectangles of width 1 from x = 0 to x = 4; not to scale

solutions.latex:
Each rectangle has width 1 and height $p^x$ at its left end ($x=0,1,2,3$):
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{rect}}&=1\times p^0+1\times p^1+1\times p^2+1\times p^3\\ &=1+p+p^2+p^3\end{aligned}$$
This is a GP with $a=1$, $r=p$, $n=4$, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{rect}}&=\dfrac{1\left(p^4-1\right)}{p-1}\\ &=\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}\text{ u}^2\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area as $1+p+p^2+p^3$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: sums the GP, or equivalent algebra
meta.marker_note: Summing the GP or equivalent algebra is accepted.

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{curve}}&=\int_0^4 p^x\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{p^x}{\ln p}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{p^4}{\ln p}-\dfrac{p^0}{\ln p}\\ &=\dfrac{p^4-1}{\ln p}\end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, the rectangles lie under the curve, so $A_{\text{rect}}<A_{\text{curve}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}&<\dfrac{p^4-1}{\ln p}\\ \dfrac{1}{p-1}&<\dfrac{1}{\ln p}\\ \ln p&<p-1\quad\text{as }p>1\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Since $f(t)$ is a PDF, the total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^6 f(t)\,dt&=1\\ k\int_0^6 \left(36t-t^3\right)dt&=1\\ k\left[18t^2-\dfrac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^6&=1\\ k\left(18(6)^2-\dfrac{6^4}{4}-0\right)&=1\\ 648k-324k&=1\\ 324k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{324}\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

The mode is where $f(t)$ is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}f(t)&=36kt-kt^3\\ &=\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\\ f'(t)&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $f'(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\\ \dfrac{3t^2}{324}&=\dfrac{1}{9}\\ t^2&=12\\ t&=\sqrt{12}\quad(t>0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(t)&=-\dfrac{6t}{324}\\ f''(2\sqrt{3})&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{27}\end{aligned}$$
$f''(2\sqrt{3})<0$, so there is a maximum at $t=2\sqrt{3}$.

$\therefore$ the mode is $2\sqrt{3}$ minutes.

meta.top_criterion_original: checks nature to show a maximum (must show for 2/2)
meta.marker_note: The nature must be checked to show a maximum for 2 marks.

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, $P(A\,|\,B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>3\,|\,X\ge 1)&=\dfrac{P(X>3)}{P(X\ge 1)}\\ &=\dfrac{1-P(X\le 3)}{1-P(X<1)}\end{aligned}$$
With $f(t)=\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<3)&=\int_0^3\left(\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\right)dt\\ &=\left[\dfrac{t^2}{18}-\dfrac{t^4}{1296}\right]_0^3\\ &=\dfrac{3^2}{18}-\dfrac{3^4}{1296}-0\\ &=\dfrac{7}{16}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<1)&=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\right)dt\\ &=\left[\dfrac{t^2}{18}-\dfrac{t^4}{1296}\right]_0^1\\ &=\dfrac{1^2}{18}-\dfrac{1^4}{1296}-0\\ &=\dfrac{71}{1296}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ P(X>3\,|\,X\ge 1)&=\dfrac{1-\frac{7}{16}}{1-\frac{71}{1296}}\\ &=\dfrac{729}{1225}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the conditional probability, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: An amount of \$6000 is invested at an interest rate of 6.5% p.a. compounded annually. How much interest, to the nearest dollar, has been earned after 15 years?

solutions.latex:
Compound interest formula:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= P(1+r)^n \\ &= 6000(1.065)^{15} \\ &= 15431.0\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Interest earned:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= A-P \\ &= 15431.0\ldots-6000 \\ &= 9431.0\ldots \\ &\approx \$9431 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following formulas could be used to calculate the sum of the first $n$ positive \textbf{even} numbers?

dif.r: MCQ: general S_n algebra for evens

solutions.latex:
The even numbers $2,4,6,8,\ldots$ form an arithmetic series with $a=2$, $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big) \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(2)+(n-1)\times 2\big) \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(4+2n-2) \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(2+2n) \\ &= n(1+n) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The following transformations are applied to the function $f(x)=x^2-3$:

\begin{itemize}
\item A vertical dilation with scale factor 3.
\item Then a horizontal dilation with scale factor 2.
\item Then a vertical translation down 1 unit.
\end{itemize}

Which of the following is the equation of the transformed function $g(x)$?

dif.r: three transformations applied in order to quadratic

solutions.latex:
Vertical dilation by 3: $3(x^2-3)=3x^2-9$.

Horizontal dilation by 2 (replace $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{2}$):
$$3\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2-9=\dfrac{3}{4}x^2-9$$
Translation down 1:
$$g(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}x^2-10$$

dif.r: MCQ: even symmetry halves integral, then split intervals

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: even function y=f(x) with x-intercepts x1, x2, x3, x4

solutions.latex:
Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_0^{x_3} f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{x_3}^{x_4} f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^{x_4} f(x)\,dx-\int_0^{x_3} f(x)\,dx \\ &= -1-1 \\ &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{x_2}^{x_4} f(x)\,dx &= 2+(-2) \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For which values of $k$ is the parabola $y=kx^2-2x+3k+2$ always positive?

dif.r: positive definite: a>0 and discriminant<0 in parameter combined

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the discriminant as a function of k, zeros at -1 and 1/3

solutions.latex:
Always positive requires $a>0$ (so $k>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= b^2-4ac \\ &= (-2)^2-4k(3k+2) \\ &= -12k^2-8k+4 \\ &= -4(3k^2+2k-1) \\ &= -4(3k-1)(k+1) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{309_q10_s1}

$\Delta<0$ when $k<-1$ or $k>\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Combined with $k>0$:
$$k>\dfrac{1}{3}$$

parts.latex: A parabola with vertex $(2,-5)$ has a $y$-intercept of 11. Find the equation of the parabola.

dif.r: vertex form then solve for a from intercept

solutions.latex:
Vertex form with vertex $(2,-5)$:
$$y=a(x-2)^2-5$$
When $x=0$, $y=11$:
$$\begin{aligned} 11 &= a(0-2)^2-5 \\ 11 &= 4a-5 \\ 16 &= 4a \\ a &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4(x-2)^2-5$$
(Expanded form $y=4x^2-16x+11$ is also acceptable.)

parts.latex: If $3+\dfrac{1}{x}=\sqrt{15}$, find the exact value of $x$. Express your answer with a rational denominator.

dif.r: rearrange then rationalise conjugate surd denominator

solutions.latex:
Subtracting 3, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{x} &= \sqrt{15}-3 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{15}-3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{15-9} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{6} \end{aligned}$$

A discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution as shown in the table below, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $E(X)=2.2$.

dif.r: sum to 1 gives a, E(X) gives b

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

dif.r: E(X^2) minus mean squared with parameters known

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 0.15+(3a+b)+0+(a-b)+0.05 \\ &= 0.2+4a \\ 4a &= 0.8 \\ a &= 0.2 \end{aligned}$$
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)=2.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2.2 &= 0.15+2(3\times 0.2+b)+4(0.2-b)+5\times 0.05 \\ &= 2.4+2b-4b \\ -0.2 &= -2b \\ b &= 0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.2 \text{ and } b=0.1$$

A function $y=f(x)$ undergoes the following transformations:

\begin{itemize}
\item A reflection in the $x$ axis
\item Then a horizontal dilation with scale factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Then a horizontal translation 7 units left

$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{1}{a}x-b \\ -2 &= \dfrac{1}{3}x-7 \\ 5 &= \dfrac{1}{3}x \\ x &= 15 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y_2 &= ky \\ 1 &= -y \\ y &= -1 \end{aligned}$$

In the diagram below, the length of minor arc $XY$ is $\dfrac{5\pi}{2}$ cm, $\theta$ is the angle subtended by that arc, and the area of shaded sector $XOY$ is $\dfrac{15\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2$. Find the exact value of $\theta$ in radians.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{2} &= r\theta \\ r &= \dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta} \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{x-1}}{x^2}$ at the point where $x=2$.

dif.r: quotient with chain rule, exact substitution at x=2

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}} & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}x^2(x-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2x(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(2)^2(2-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2(2)(2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2^4} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m_T=-\dfrac{1}{8}$$
criteria: Correct derivative using the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: May has a mango orchard with 20 trees that each produce 400 mangoes per year. For every additional tree that May plants in the orchard, the output of every tree decreases by 10 mangoes per year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the number of mangoes, $M$, produced by May’s orchard each year is given by $M=-10x^2+200x+8000$ where $x$ is the number of additional trees planted.

dif.r: build product of trees and yield, expand

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the number of additional trees May should plant in order to maximise the number of mangoes grown each year.

dif.r: maximise given quadratic by derivative

solutions.latex:
Number of trees $=20+x$; mangoes per tree $=400-10x$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= (20+x)(400-10x) \\ &= 8000-200x+400x-10x^2 \\ &= -10x^2+200x+8000 \end{aligned}$$

$$M'=-20x+200$$
Stationary points when $M'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -20x+200 \\ 20x &= 200 \\ x &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$M''=-20<0$ for all $x$, so there is a local maximum at $x=10$.

$\therefore$ May should plant 10 more trees.

At the beginning of January 2025, Hannah starts her trip and stops contributing to the account. Instead, she withdraws \$400 from the account \textbf{at the start} of each month to cover expenses. The account continues to earn interest at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. Show that Hannah’s account balance, $A_n$, at the end of the $n$th month of her trip is given by:

$$A_n=3776.76(1.005)^n-80400(1.005^n-1)$$

parts.latex: How many \$400 withdrawals can Hannah make from her travel fund?

solutions.latex:
$n=1$ year $=12$ months, $r=6\%$ p.a. $=0.5\%$ per month, so the factor is $12.3356$.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= M\times\text{factor} \\ &= 100\times 12.3356 \\ &= 1233.56 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Hannah has \$1233.56.

The 2023 balance grows for 12 months at $0.5\%$ per month, plus the new annuity ($n=12$, $r=0.5\%$):
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= FV_{\text{lump}}+FV_{\text{instal}} \\ &= P(1+r)^n+M\times\text{factor} \\ &= 1233.56(1+0.5\%)^{12}+200\times 12.3356 \\ &= 3776.763\ldots \\ &\approx 3776.76 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Hannah has \$3776.76.

criteria: Writes $A_n$ with the geometric series $400(1.005+\cdots+1.005^n)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The fund runs out when $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3776.76(1.005)^n-80400(1.005)^n+80400 \\ &= -76623.24(1.005)^n+80400 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 76623.24(1.005)^n &= 80400 \\ (1.005)^n &= 1.049\ldots \\ n\ln 1.005 &= \ln 1.049\ldots \\ n &= 9.64\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Hannah can make 9 withdrawals.
criteria: Sets $A_n=0$ and simplifies to $-76623.24(1.005)^n+80400=0$, or equivalent merit
