questions.stem:
Last Sunday, 45 people were surveyed about three types of restaurants that they prefer to attend on their next birthday.

Of them, 26 chose French, 22 chose Italian, 18 Japanese.

It is also found that 11 chose French and Italian, 10 chose French and Japanese and 7 chose Italian and Japanese.

Only 4 people chose all three types of restaurants.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Represent this information in the Venn Diagram below.

\exfigure{402_q27_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: A person from those who were surveyed last Sunday is to be selected at random. What is the probability that this person chose French or Italian but not Japanese?

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Two people are chosen at random, what is the probability of both chose French only?

figures.cap: blank three-set Venn diagram (French, Italian, Japanese) in a rectangle
solution sketch: Venn diagram filled in: 9, 7, 8, 6, 4, 3, 5 and 3 outside

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct Venn diagram (including the 3 outside the circles)

solutions.latex:
French or Italian but not Japanese: the regions $F$ only, $I$ only and $F\cap I$ only, so $9+7+8=24$ people.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{9+7+8}{45}\\ &=\dfrac{24}{45}\\ &=\dfrac{8}{15}\end{aligned}$$

Two people are chosen without replacement and $9$ of the $45$ chose French only:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{9}{45}\cdot\dfrac{8}{44}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{55}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\left(\cot\theta+\operatorname{cosec}\theta\right)^2=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}$.

solutions.latex:
Write $\cot\theta$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta+1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{1-\cos^2\theta} &&\left(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{(1-\cos\theta)(1+\cos\theta)} &&(\text{difference of two squares})\\ &=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta} &&(\text{cancel }1+\cos\theta)\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Consider the following diagram with the cone inscribed in a sphere.

\exfigure{402_q29_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: If $r$ is the radius of the cone show that $r^2=2hR-h^2$.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the cone that can be inscribed in a sphere of radius $R$ is given by $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ where $h$ is the height of the inscribed cone.

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

figures.cap: cone ABC inscribed in a sphere with centre O, radius R, base radius r, height h
solution sketch: cone-in-sphere diagram with OA = R and OD = h - R marked

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Substitute $r^2=2hR-h^2$ from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2hR-h^2\right)h\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)\end{aligned}$$

Let $V_C=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ be the volume of the cone and $V_S=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3$ the volume of the sphere. Differentiate with respect to $h$:
$$\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4Rh-3h^2\right),\qquad\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6h\right)$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4Rh-3h^2&=0\\ h\left(4R-3h\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$h=0$ is rejected since $h>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$.

Second derivative test at $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6\cdot\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(4R-8R)\\ &=-\dfrac{4\pi R}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This is negative since $R>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$ gives a maximum.

The maximum volume of the cone is
$$\begin{aligned}V_C&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2R\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^2-\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^3\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{32R^3}{9}-\dfrac{64R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\cdot\dfrac{96R^3-64R^3}{27}\\ &=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\end{aligned}$$
Compare with the sphere:
$$\dfrac{V_C}{V_S}=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\cdot\dfrac{3}{4\pi R^3}=\dfrac{8}{27}$$
Therefore the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

meta.top_criterion_original: 4 marks for the full solution (the second derivative test must be shown)
meta.marker_note: The second derivative test must be shown.

questions.stem:
(The table on page 27 can be used for this question)

Madelyn is a long jumper training for the national age championships. To be able to compete at the national age championships her longest jump must be able to be beaten by less than 0.17% of the general population.

The distance jumped by the general population is normally distributed with a mean of 3.48 metres and standard deviation of 1.08 metres.

\extable{402_q30_t1}

parts.latex: What is the minimum distance that Madelyn needs to jump, correct to the nearest centimetre?

solutions.latex:
Madelyn's jump $D$ must be beaten by less than $0.17\%$ of the population, so $P(X>D)<0.0017$. Standardise with $z=\dfrac{D-3.48}{1.08}$:
$$P(Z<z)>1-0.0017=0.9983$$
From the table, $P(Z\le2.93)=0.9983$, so $z=2.93$.
$$\begin{aligned}D&=\mu+z\sigma\\ &=3.48+2.93\times1.08\\ &=6.6444\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is }6.64\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct $z$ score, or finds the distance correctly using an incorrect $z$ score

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct distance (1 mark for using an incorrect $z$ score to find the distance correctly)

questions.stem: \exfigure{402_q31_1}

parts.latex: Determine the area of the region enclosed by $y^2=2x+6$ and $y=x-1$.
can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: parabola y^2=2x+6 and line y=x-1 with the enclosed region shaded, vertical lines at x=-1 and x=5

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $(x-1)^2=2x+6$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-2x+1&=2x+6\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=-1$ or $x=5$, giving the points $(-1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.

Method 1 (integrate with respect to $x$). From $x=-3$ to $x=-1$ the region lies between $y=-\sqrt{2x+6}$ and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$. From $x=-1$ to $x=5$ it lies between the line and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_{-3}^{-1}(2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}dx+\int_{-1}^{5}\left((2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}-x+1\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{-3}^{-1}+\left[\dfrac{1}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{2}{3}(0)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(16)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{25}{2}+5\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}-1\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{16}{3}+\dfrac{38}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (integrate with respect to $y$). The line is $x=y+1$ and the parabola is $x=\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3$; between $y=-2$ and $y=4$ the line is to the right of the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-2}^{4}\left((y+1)-\left(\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3\right)\right)dy\\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}\left(y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4\right)dy\\ &=\left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4}\\ &=\left(8-\dfrac{32}{3}+16\right)-\left(2+\dfrac{4}{3}-8\right)\\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}+\dfrac{14}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is }18\text{ units}^2$$

questions.stem: Madison is learning to drive. Her first lesson is 10 minutes long. Her second lesson is 15 minutes long. Each subsequent lesson is 5 minutes longer than the previous lesson.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: How long will Madison's fifteenth lesson be?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: How many hours of lessons will Madison have completed after her fifteenth lesson?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: During which lesson will Madison have completed a total of 40 hours of driving lessons?
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The lesson lengths $10+15+20+25+\ldots$ form an arithmetic series with first term $a=10$ and common difference $d=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{15}&=a+(15-1)d\\ &=10+14\times5\\ &=80\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$

Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, with $a=10$, $d=5$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{15}&=\dfrac{15}{2}\left[2(10)+(15-1)\times5\right]\\ &=\dfrac{15}{2}\times90\\ &=675\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
Convert to hours: $675\div60=11.25$.
$$\therefore\ 11.25\text{ hours}=11\text{ hours }15\text{ minutes}$$

meta.format_note: Checker 17 Nov: "Change the multiplication dots into the normal x" (this question only).

solutions.latex:
$40$ hours $=40\times60=2400$ minutes. Find $n$ with $S_n=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(10)+(n-1)\times5\right]\\ 4800&=n(15+5n)\\ 5n^2+15n-4800&=0\\ n^2+3n-960&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{3^2-4(1)(-960)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{3849}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{3849}}{2}\approx29.5$.

Check with whole lessons: $S_{29}=2320<2400$ and $S_{30}=2475>2400$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Madison completes 40 hours during her 30th lesson}$$

meta.format_note: Checker 17 Nov: "Change the multiplication dots into the normal x" (this question only).

why: Checker got a different answer — Final answers right (80 min; 11.25 h; 30th lesson), but working lines are mistyped: (i) '$10+14.5$' should be $10+14\cdot5$ (as printed it equals 24.5, not 80); (iii) '$40.60$' should be $40\times60$.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2\left(2-2x\right)=\log_{\sqrt{2}}\left(1-x\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need $1-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Method 1 (change of base to $\ln$). Using $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$ and $\ln\sqrt{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\ln(2-2x)}{\ln2}&=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\ln\sqrt{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\frac{1}{2}\ln2}\\ &=\dfrac{2\ln(1-x)}{\ln2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(2-2x)&=2\ln(1-x)\\ 2-2x&=(1-x)^2\\ 2-2x&=1-2x+x^2\\ x^2&=1\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
Since $x<1$, $x=1$ is rejected. Check $x=-1$: $\log_2 4=2$ and $\log_{\sqrt{2}}2=2$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$
Method 2. Let $y$ be the common value, so $2-2x=2^y$, that is $1-x=2^{y-1}$, and $1-x=\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^y=2^{\frac{y}{2}}$. Equating the two expressions for $1-x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2^{y-1}&=2^{\frac{1}{2}y}\\ y-1&=\dfrac{1}{2}y\\ y&=2\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $1-x=2^{y-1}$ gives $1-x=2$, so $x=-1$.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\left(\sin^3 2x^\circ\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $\pi$ radians $=180^\circ$, so $1^\circ=\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ and $2x^\circ=\dfrac{2\pi x}{180}=\dfrac{\pi x}{90}$ radians.
$$y=\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^3$$
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^2\cdot\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{90}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{30}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^2\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Marge borrows \$50 000 in order to buy a car. The loan attracts an interest of just 0.5% per month. The company also offers an interest free period for the first six months. However, the first payment is due at the end of the first month. Marge agrees to repay the loan over 10 years, by making 120 equal monthly repayments of \$$M$. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing at the end of $n$th repayment, then

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $A_6=50\,000-6M$

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Hence derive the expression for $A_{120}$ in simplest form.

parts.label: iv
parts.latex: Find the value of the monthly repayment to the nearest cent.

solutions.latex:
During the interest-free period each repayment of $M$ simply reduces the amount owing:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=50\,000-M\\ A_2&=A_1-M=50\,000-2M\\ A_3&=A_2-M=50\,000-3M\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_6&=50\,000-6M\end{aligned}$$

After the interest-free period, $0.5\%$ interest is added each month, so the balance is multiplied by $1.005$ before each repayment of $M$ is taken off:
$$\begin{aligned}A_7&=A_6\times1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005-M\\ A_8&=A_7\times1.005-M\\ &=\left[(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005-M\right]\cdot1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005^2-M\cdot1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005^2-M(1.005+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $A_7$ in terms of $M$ only

solutions.latex:
Each month the balance is multiplied by $1.005$ and $M$ is subtracted, so the pattern of part (ii) continues up to $A_{120}$, with $114$ months of interest after $A_6$. The terms multiplying $M$ form a geometric series with first term $1$, common ratio $1.005$ and $114$ terms, so $S_n=\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1}$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}A_{120}&=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-\left(1.005^{113}+1.005^{112}+\cdots+1.005+1\right)M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-\dfrac{1.005^{114}-1}{1.005-1}M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-200\left(1.005^{114}-1\right)M\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds expression for $A_{120}$ in terms of $M$ only
Sets $A_{120}=0$ and attempts to solve for $M$

why: Checker got a different answer — Answers right (A120=(50000-6M)1.005^114-200(1.005^114-1)M; M=$539.18), but (ii) working writes '$A_6.1.005$' and '$A_7.1.005$' (period used for multiplication); should be $A_6\times1.005$, $A_7\times1.005$.

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. It’s displacement, $x$ metres, from the origin, $O$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t\ge0$, is given by $x=4+3te^{-2t}$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show the velocity of the particle is given by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3e^{-2t}\left(1-2t\right)$.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Find the greatest possible total distance the particle could travel.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the constant $4$ is $0$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(3te^{-2t}\right)$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=e^{-2t}\\ u'&=3 & v'&=-2e^{-2t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=3e^{-2t}+3t\cdot\left(-2e^{-2t}\right)\\ &=3e^{-2t}-6te^{-2t}\\ &=3e^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to differentiate using the product rule

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$. At $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=3e^{-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}\left(1-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=3e^{-1}(1-1)\\ &=0\end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The particle starts at $x=4$. Since $3e^{-2t}\ne0$, $v=0$ only when $1-2t=0$, that is at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for }t>\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
At the turning point:
$$x=4+3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-1}=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $x=4+\dfrac{3t}{e^{2t}}\to4+0=4$, approached from above but never reached.

Distance travelled moving right: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.

Distance travelled moving left, back towards $x=4$: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest total distance}=\dfrac{3}{2e}+\dfrac{3}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Calculates distance travelled in first half of journey, namely $\dfrac{3}{2e}$ metres

parts.latex:
Sally contributes \$7200 each year into a superannuation fund for the first 15 years of her working life. For the next 20 years until retirement, she decides to increase this, and invest a total of \$10000 each year. Each contribution is paid at the beginning of the year.

If the investment earns 7% per annum paid yearly over whole period, how much will her investment be upon retiring? (Show all your working)

solutions.latex:
Each contribution is paid at the start of the year, so the first contribution earns interest for the whole $15$ years. After $15$ years the amount is a geometric series with first term $7200(1.07)$, common ratio $1.07$ and $15$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=7200(1.07)\\ A_2&=\left(A_1+7200\right)(1.07)=7200(1.07)^2+7200(1.07)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_{15}&=7200(1.07)^{15}+7200(1.07)^{14}+\cdots+7200(1.07)^2+7200(1.07)\\ &=\dfrac{7200(1.07)\left(1.07^{15}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &=193\,593.9855\ldots\end{aligned}$$
From then on the contributions are $\$10\,000$ at the start of each year. The new contributions form a geometric series with first term $10\,000(1.07)$, common ratio $1.07$ and $20$ terms, and $A_{15}$ grows for a further $20$ years:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{16}&=\left(A_{15}+10\,000\right)(1.07)=A_{15}(1.07)+10\,000(1.07)\\ A_{17}&=\left(A_{16}+10\,000\right)(1.07)=A_{15}(1.07)^2+10\,000(1.07)^2+10\,000(1.07)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_{35}&=A_{15}(1.07)^{20}+10\,000(1.07)^{20}+10\,000(1.07)^{19}+\cdots+10\,000(1.07)\\ &=A_{15}(1.07)^{20}+\dfrac{10\,000(1.07)\left(1.07^{20}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &\approx\$1\,187\,799.41\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{her investment on retiring is }\$1\,187\,799.41\text{ (nearest cent)}$$
criteria: Successively finds $A_{16}$ and $A_{17}$ or an expression for $A_{35}$ with working

solutions.latex:
Make $y$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3y+1 &= 0 \\ 3y &= 2x+1 \\ y &= \dfrac{2}{3}x+\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The graph of a function $y=\dfrac{4}{x+1}$ is translated 3 units left, and dilated vertically by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Which of the following gives the equation of the new function?

solutions.latex:
Translating $3$ units left replaces $x$ with $x+3$:
$$y=\dfrac{4}{(x+3)+1}=\dfrac{4}{x+4}$$
A vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $y$ with $2y$ (that is, $y$ becomes half as large):
$$2y=\dfrac{4}{x+4}$$

parts.latex:
Three chess players are chosen from 3 males and 7 females.

What is the probability that they are all the same gender?

solutions.latex:
Choose $3$ from $10$ people: $\binom{10}{3}=120$ ways.

All male: $\binom{3}{3}=1$ way. All female: $\binom{7}{3}=35$ ways.
$$P=\dfrac{1+35}{120}=\dfrac{36}{120}=\dfrac{3}{10}$$

parts.latex:
What is the domain of the function:

$$y=-\sqrt{1+3x}$$

solutions.latex:
The square root needs a non-negative number under it:
$$\begin{aligned} 1+3x &\ge 0 \\ 3x &\ge -1 \\ x &\ge -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So the domain is $\left[-\dfrac{1}{3},\infty\right)$. The endpoint is included, and infinity is never a bracketed endpoint.

parts.latex: Prove that $(\tan x+\cot x-1)(\sin x+\cos x)=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}$

solutions.latex:
Expand the left side, using $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\tan x\sin x+\tan x\cos x+\cot x\sin x+\cot x\cos x-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\sin x+\cos x+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Now the right side, using $\sec x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\\ &=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands the left side correctly, or equivalent merit
Writes $\tan x$ and $\cot x$ in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$

parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{2e}{3x^3}$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $f(x)=x^3\log_e 4x$

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{-\ln x}{x}$

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a power of $x$ ($2e$ is a constant):
$$y=\dfrac{2e}{3}x^{-3}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2ex^{-4}=-\dfrac{2e}{x^4}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=\ln4x\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=\dfrac{4}{4x}=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2\ln4x+x^3\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=3x^2\ln4x+x^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule with one of $u'$, $v'$ correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-\ln x & v&=x\\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{x\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right)-(-\ln x)}{x^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule with one of $u'$, $v'$ correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\sin(2x+1)$, so $y=u^3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\sin^2(2x+1)\cdot2\cos(2x+1)\\ &=6\sin^2(2x+1)\cos(2x+1)\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows a sketch of the curve $y=6x^2-x^3$. The curve cuts the x axis at $A$, has a local maximum at $B$, and a point of inflexion at $C$.

\exfigure{416_q21_1}
questions.review_note: scan path: every question defaults to review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of $A$.
skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of $B$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of $C$.

figures.cap: sketch of y=6x^2-x^3 with points A, B and C

solutions.latex:
$A$ is where the curve meets the $x$-axis, so put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=6x^2-x^3\\ 0&=x^2(6-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ (the origin) or $x=6$. $A$ is the intercept to the right of the origin.
$$\therefore\ A=(6,0)$$

$B$ is a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12x-3x^2\\ 12x-3x^2&=0\\ 3x(4-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=4$. Test with $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12-6x$:
$$\begin{aligned}x=0:&\quad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12>0 &&\text{minimum (the origin)}\\ x=4:&\quad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-12<0 &&\text{maximum}\end{aligned}$$
$B$ is the local maximum, so $x=4$ and $y=6(4)^2-4^3=32$.
$$\therefore\ B=(4,32)$$

$C$ is a point of inflexion, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ there and the concavity changes:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12-6x\\ 12-6x&=0\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ for $x<2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ for $x>2$, so the concavity changes. When $x=2$, $y=6(2)^2-2^3=16$.
$$\therefore\ C=(2,16)$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ using the Trapezoidal Rule with five function values. Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Calculate the same area by evaluating $\displaystyle\int_2^6\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Explain why the Trapezoidal Rule overestimates the area.

figures.cap: graph of y=1/x with area shaded between x=2 and x=6

solutions.latex:
Five function values at $x=2,3,4,5,6$ means $4$ strips, each of width $h=\dfrac{6-2}{4}=1$. With $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(2)+f(6)+2\left[f(3)+f(4)+f(5)\right]\right\}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{6}+2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\right]\\ &\approx1.117\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct trapezoidal rule expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\int_2^6\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx&=\Big[\ln x\Big]_2^6\\ &=\ln6-\ln2\\ &=\ln3\\ &\approx1.099\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

For $x>0$, $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ has $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{x^3}>0$, so the curve is concave up. Each trapezium's top edge is a chord, which lies above a concave up curve, so the Trapezoidal Rule overestimates the area (as $1.117>1.099$).

questions.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v\,ms^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.
questions.review_note: scan path: every question defaults to review; Q25(a) is 3 marks in the final copy; the clean copy prints 2

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is

$(8-2\sqrt{3})$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$; the first time after $t=0$ is the smallest positive solution:
$$\begin{aligned}-4\cos t&=0\\ \cos t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
For the position, integrate the velocity and use $x=1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int-4\cos t\,dt\\ &=-4\sin t+C\\ 1&=0+C\\ x&=-4\sin t+1\end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=-4+1=-3$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest at }t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s, at }x=-3\text{ (3 m to the left of the origin)}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and an expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v=-4\cos t$ changes sign at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so find the distance in each part separately:
$$\begin{aligned}v&<0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for }\dfrac{\pi}{2}<t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &&\text{moving right}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-4\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left, so the distance travelled in this part is $4$ m.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\\ &=-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\\ &=4-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total distance}=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)=\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in one of the two intervals, or equivalent merit
Identifies that the direction changes at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of $y=3x^4-4x^3+2$ in the space provided showing all:

\begin{itemize}
\item turning points
\item points of inflexion
\item y-intercept
\end{itemize}

There is no need to find the x-intercept(s).

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=3x^4-4x^3+2 with y-intercept 2, point of inflexion (2/3,38/27) and minimum (1,1)

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=12x^3-12x^2,\qquad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=36x^2-24x$$
For turning points, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12x^3-12x^2&=0\\ 12x^2(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

At $x=1$: $y=3-4+2=1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=36-24=12>0$, so $(1,1)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$, so the second derivative test fails and the concavity is tested below.

For points of inflexion, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}36x^2-24x&=0\\ 12x(3x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$. When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $y=3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4-4\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3+2=\dfrac{38}{27}$.

Test the concavity either side of each value:

\extable{Ts2888_1}

The concavity changes at both values. At $x=0$ the gradient is also $0$, so $(0,2)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion, not a turning point. $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)$ is also a point of inflexion.

The $y$-intercept is $(0,2)$.

\exfigure{416_q26_s1}

questions.stem:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a teacher waiting on the phone with a government department has a probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3}{32}x(k-x), & 0\le x\le k\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.
questions.review_note: scan path: every question defaults to review

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=4$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the mode of the probability density function.
skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the probability that the phone will be answered within the first minute.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^k\dfrac{3}{32}x(k-x)\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\left[\dfrac{kx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\left(\dfrac{k^3}{2}-\dfrac{k^3}{3}\right)&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\cdot\dfrac{k^3}{6}&=1\\ k^3&=64\\ k&=4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to $1$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

meta.edited_from_original: Owner 17 Nov: "all ok, just for these" (the checker's rename requests on 2024 Sydney Tech Q5, Q27, Q29; not a standing rule). "Department of Education" is now "a government department".

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{3}{32}t(4-t)\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{3}{32}\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{3}{32}\left(2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3x^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{32}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for }x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac{3x^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{32} & \text{for }0\le x\le4\\[6pt] 1 & \text{for }x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral for $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=\dfrac{3}{32}x(4-x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $0$ and $4$, so its maximum is on the axis of symmetry, halfway between them:
$$\text{mode}=\dfrac{0+4}{2}=2$$

The phone is answered within the first minute when $X<1$, so use the cumulative distribution function from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<1)&=F(1)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{16}-\dfrac{1}{32}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{32}\end{aligned}$$

How far south of the port will the speed boat be when it is directly west of the yacht?

figures.cap: diagram with Port A, due south Island B, and yacht destination Y to the south-east of A, North arrow
solution sketch: diagram of triangle ABY with 60 degree angle at A, right angle and 30 degree angles marked

solutions.latex:
The yacht sails $3\times15=45$ km, so $AY=45$ km. Also $AB=30$ km, and the bearing $120^\circ$ is $60^\circ$ from due south, so $\angle YAB=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$. Use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABY$:
$$\begin{aligned}YB^2&=30^2+45^2-2\times30\times45\cos60^\circ\\ &=900+2025-1350\\ &=1575\\ YB&\approx39.7\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ YB\approx40\text{ km}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule with the correct sides and angle, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: a labelled triangle $ABY$ ($AB=30$, $AY=45$, $60^\circ$ at $A$, north line) at the top.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{416_q28_s1}

Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABY$, with the unrounded $YB=\sqrt{1575}\approx39.69$ km:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle YBA}{45}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{39.69}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle YBA&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{45\sin60^\circ}{39.69}\right)\\ &\approx79.1^\circ\end{aligned}$$
($\angle YBA$ is acute: by the cosine rule, $\cos\angle YBA=\dfrac{30^2+39.69^2-45^2}{2\times30\times39.69}\approx0.19>0$.)

The north-south lines through $A$, $B$ and $Y$ are parallel, so by alternate angles the angle between $YB$ and due south at $Y$ is $\angle YBA=79.1^\circ$. $B$ lies west of south from $Y$:
$$\text{bearing of }B\text{ from }Y=180^\circ+79.1^\circ\approx259^\circ\text{T}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $YB\approx40$ was substituted into the sine rule, which gives $77^\circ$, but the answer $79^\circ$ comes from the unrounded $YB=39.69$; now worked with $39.69$. The bearing $259^\circ$T is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
The boat is directly west of the yacht when it is level with it, so its distance south of $A$ equals the yacht's distance south of $A$. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $AY=45$ km and $60^\circ$ at $A$, let $x$ be the southward distance, the side adjacent to the $60^\circ$ angle:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos60^\circ&=\dfrac{x}{45}\\ x&=22.5\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the speed boat is }22.5\text{ km south of the port}$$

parts.latex:
A small group of students were surveyed to determine whether they were part of the local baseball or tennis team.

\begin{itemize}
\item 16 people played tennis only.
\item 20 people played baseball only.
\item 5 people played neither.
\item $k$ people played both.
\end{itemize}

Let B be the event that a person plays baseball and let $T$ be the event that a person plays tennis.

Determine the value of $k$ such that the events B and $T$ are independent.

solutions.latex:
The total number of people is $16+20+5+k=41+k$. $B$ and $T$ are independent when $P(B\mid T)=P(B)$. Here $T$ has $16+k$ people and $B$ has $20+k$ people:
$$\dfrac{k}{16+k}=\dfrac{20+k}{41+k}$$
$$\begin{aligned}k(41+k)&=(16+k)(20+k)\\ 41k+k^2&=320+36k+k^2\\ 5k&=320\\ k&=64\end{aligned}$$
Check: $P(B\cap T)=\dfrac{64}{105}$ and $P(B)P(T)=\dfrac{84}{105}\cdot\dfrac{80}{105}=\dfrac{64}{105}$.
$$\therefore\ k=64$$
criteria: Sets up $P(B\mid T)=P(B)$ with correct expressions, or equivalent merit
States the condition for independence, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use the Empirical rule to determine the probability that the weight of one packet of coffee beans is less than the advertised weight of 300g.
skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In a shipment of 40 boxes, each with 100 packets of coffee beans, how many packets would be expected to be underweight?

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Manufacturers aim to ensure that the expected number of underweight packets in the shipment will be less than 20. The machine is adjusted to give a mean weight of 308g, with the standard deviation of 3g remaining the same. Will they meet their target? Justify your answer.

figures.cap: table of values P(Z<=z) for the normal distribution N(0,1), z from 0.0 to 3.2

solutions.latex:
$300$ g is $\dfrac{306-300}{3}=2$ standard deviations below the mean. By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of packets lie within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ lie outside, half of them below:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<300)&=\dfrac{0.05}{2}\\ &=0.025=2.5\%\end{aligned}$$

The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets, and $2.5\%$ of them are expected to be underweight:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{expected number}&=0.025\times4000\\ &=100\text{ packets}\end{aligned}$$

With mean $308$ g, the $z$-score of $300$ g is
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{300-308}{3}\\ &\approx-2.67\end{aligned}$$
From the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(Z<-2.67)&=1-P(Z\le2.67)\\ &=1-0.9962\\ &=0.0038\end{aligned}$$
$$0.0038\times4000=15.2\text{ packets}$$
Since $15.2<20$, they meet their target.
criteria: Finds the probability that a packet is underweight, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground. It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0\le t\le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\,ms^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t)=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$
questions.review_note: scan path: every question defaults to review

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground.

Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The rocket rises while $v>0$ and begins to descend when $v$ returns to $0$ after take-off:
$$0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ \ldots$$
$t=0$ is the take-off, and for $0<t<10$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)>0$ so $v>0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket begins to descend at }t=10\text{ s}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and finds $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For maximum velocity, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & v'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ &=0.5e^t\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=0\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}\end{aligned}$$
The rocket is rising for $0<t<10$, so $0<\dfrac{\pi t}{10}<\pi$. Tangent is negative in the second quadrant, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\approx2.837$$
$$t\approx2.837\cdot\dfrac{10}{\pi}\approx9.03\text{ s}$$
$v=0$ at $t=0$ and at $t=10$ and $v>0$ between them, so this stationary point is the maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket reaches its maximum velocity after }9.03\text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Differentiates and forms $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates using the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many solutions does the equation $(\cos x-1)(2\sin x+1)=0$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ have?

solutions.latex:
A product is zero when one of its factors is zero.

$\cos x-1=0$ gives $\cos x=1$, so $x=0$ or $x=2\pi$ (2 solutions).

$2\sin x+1=0$ gives $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$. The acute angle is $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
(2 solutions). The four values are different, so the equation has $4$ solutions.

The count of $4$ is unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $y=e^{2x}\cos 5x$

parts.latex: $g(x)=\sqrt{\ln 7+e^{x}}$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\sin2x$, so $y=u^3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\sin^2(2x)\cdot2\cos2x\\ &=6\sin^22x\cos2x\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=\cos5x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-5\sin5x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2e^{2x}\cos5x+e^{2x}(-5\sin5x)\\ &=e^{2x}(2\cos5x-5\sin5x)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows attempt at product rule, gets $u'$ OR $v'$ correct

meta.marker_note: Also accept the non-factorised form $-5e^{2x}\sin5x+2e^{2x}\cos5x$.

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=\left(\ln7+e^x\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The term $\ln7$ is a constant. Using the chain rule, with inner function $\ln7+e^x$ whose derivative is $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}g'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln7+e^x\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot e^x\\ &=\dfrac{e^x}{2\sqrt{\ln7+e^x}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows attempt at differentiation using chain rule

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=2-\ln x$ for $x>0$.
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{1}{x}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{x}>0$ for $x>0$, $f'(x)<0$, so $f(x)$ is decreasing for all $x>0$.
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}>0\text{ for all }x>0$$
So $f'(x)$ is increasing: the gradient is negative and rising towards $0$, so the decrease gets slower. Hence $f(x)$ is decreasing at a decreasing rate (the graph is concave up).

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $f''(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}>0$ was labelled 'concave down'; it is concave up (this is what 'decreasing at a decreasing rate' means).

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{995_q12_s1}

$x$-intercept: put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\ln x&=0\\ \ln x&=2\\ x&=e^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=2-\ln1=2$. As $x\to0^{+}$, $y\to\infty$, so $x=0$ is a vertical asymptote.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=5x^4-20x^3\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=20x^3-60x^2\end{aligned}$$
For a point of inflexion, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes:
$$\begin{aligned}20x^3-60x^2&=0\\ 20x^2(x-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=1$, giving $(0,1)$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2920_1}

The concavity does not change, so $(0,1)$ is not a point of inflexion.

When $x=3$, $y=3^5-5(3)^4+1=-161$, giving $(3,-161)$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2920_2}

The concavity changes, so $(3,-161)$ is a point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ \text{the only point of inflexion is }(3,-161)$$

questions.stem:
The predicted number of cases, $C$ of Capona virus strain present in country X, $n$ days after it was first detected is predicted by the model:

$$C=5e^{3n}+1$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How many cases were present when the virus strain was first detected?

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the rate at which the number of cases is predicted to be increasing on the 10th day.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: State when is the number of cases predicted to first exceed 2 000.

solutions.latex:
When the strain is first detected, $n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}C&=5e^0+1\\ &=6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 6\text{ cases}$$

The rate of increase is $\dfrac{dC}{dn}$ (cases per day):
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dC}{dn}&=5e^{3n}\cdot3\\ &=15e^{3n}\end{aligned}$$
The first day is $n=0$, so the $10$th day is $n=9$:
$$\dfrac{dC}{dn}=15e^{27}\text{ cases/day}$$

$$\begin{aligned}5e^{3n}+1&=2000\\ 5e^{3n}&=1999\\ e^{3n}&=\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ 3n&=\ln\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ n&\approx1.997\end{aligned}$$
The number of cases exceeds $2000$ when $n>1.997$, so this first happens at $n=2$, the $3$rd day.

questions.stem:
A buoy is suspended in the ocean. At its lowest point, the buoy is at a height of 16 metres above the sea floor. At its maximum height, it reaches 28 metres above the sea floor.

The tide mimics a sinusoidal wave, such that one full cycle of the tide going both in and out occurs in 30 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
If the buoy is initially at its highest point, show that the buoy follows an equation above sea level of

$$h(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)+22$$

where $h(t)$ is the height of the buoy above the sea floor in metres after $t$ hours.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: State the number of times the buoy reaches a level of 20 metres above the sea floor in the first 60 hours.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If the buoy was at its highest point above the sea floor at 2 a.m on Monday, at what times does the buoy reach 20 metres above the sea floor within the next 60 hours. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of h(t) cosine curve with levels 28, 22, 16
solution sketch: sketch of h(t) over 60 hours with line at 20 metres and four intersections

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{995_q14_s1}

The buoy moves between $16$ m and $28$ m:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{28-16}{2}=6\\ \text{rest position}&=28-6=22\end{aligned}$$
One cycle takes $30$ hours, so $n=\dfrac{2\pi}{30}=\dfrac{\pi}{15}$. The buoy starts at its highest point, so the curve is a cosine curve, $h=a\cos(nt)+22$ with $a=6$:
$$h(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)+22$$
criteria: At least 1 correct solution for $a$, $n$, or rest position

meta.top_criterion_original: Full correct proof of all terms (cannot award A1 if cosine curve is not stated)
meta.marker_note: The full mark cannot be awarded if the cosine curve is not stated.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}20&=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)+22\\ -2&=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{15}t$. For $0\le t\le60$, $0\le\theta\le4\pi$. The acute angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}=1.231$ rad, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\pi-1.231,\ \pi+1.231,\ 3\pi-1.231,\ 3\pi+1.231\\ &=1.911,\ 4.373,\ 8.194,\ 10.656\end{aligned}$$
Using $t=\dfrac{15\theta}{\pi}$:
$$t=9\text{ h }7\text{ min},\ 20\text{ h }53\text{ min},\ 39\text{ h }7\text{ min},\ 50\text{ h }53\text{ min}$$
Adding these to $2$ a.m. Monday, the buoy is at $20$ m at
$$\begin{aligned}&11{:}07\text{ am Monday}\\ &10{:}53\text{ pm Monday}\\ &5{:}07\text{ pm Tuesday}\\ &4{:}53\text{ am Wednesday}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: To simplify equation and arrive at $-\dfrac{1}{3}=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)$

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
For the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1+x}{e^{x}}$, $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ .

Sketch $y=f(x)$ showing all key features including any stationary points and points of inflexion.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=(1+x)e^(-x) with maximum (0,1) and inflexion (1,2/e)

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=t^2-8t+12\\ t^2-8t+12&=0\\ (t-2)(t-6)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2\text{ s or }t=6\text{ s}$$

\exfigure{995_q15_s1}

$f(x)=e^{-x}(1+x)$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-x} & v&=1+x\\ u'&=-e^{-x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=-e^{-x}(1+x)+e^{-x}\\ &=e^{-x}\left(1-(1+x)\right)\\ &=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$: $-xe^{-x}=0$ gives $x=0$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(0)=\dfrac{1+0}{e^0}=1$, giving $(0,1)$.

To find the nature, differentiate $f'(x)=-xe^{-x}$ with the product rule, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=-e^{-x}+(-x)\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\ &=e^{-x}(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$f''(0)=e^0(-1)=-1<0$, so $(0,1)$ is a local maximum.

For points of inflexion, $f''(x)=0$: $e^{-x}(x-1)=0$ gives $x=1$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(1)=\dfrac{2}{e}$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2928_1}

$f''(0)=-1<0$ and $f''(2)=e^{-2}(2-1)=\dfrac{1}{e^2}>0$, so the concavity changes and $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to0$, so the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.
criteria: Determines POI (not awarded if concavity change not tested)
Determines nature of stationary point through $f''(x)$ and sub $x$ value
Attempts differentiation using product or quotient rule

parts.latex:
Let $A$ and $B$ be independent events where $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.58$

What is the value of $P(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B})$?

solutions.latex:
Since $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$.
$$P(A\cap B)=0.3\times 0.58=0.174$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &= 0.3+0.58-0.174 \\ &= 0.706 \end{aligned}$$
$\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$ is the event that neither $A$ nor $B$ happens, the complement of $A\cup B$.
$$P(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B})=1-0.706=0.294$$

parts.latex: If $f(x)=|x|$ and $g(x)$ is the new function after $f(x)$ is dilated horizontally by factor $\dfrac{1}{5}$ and shifted down 2 units, what is the range of $g(x)$?

solutions.latex:
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{5}$ replaces $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{5}}=5x$; a shift down 2 replaces $y$ by $y+2$.
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)+2 &= |5x| \\ g(x) &= |5x|-2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $|5x|\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &\ge 0-2 \\ g(x) &\ge -2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the range is $g(x)\ge-2$.

parts.label: a

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By considering the symmetry of the table in (a) show that the probability that Barbie and Ken obtain the same score is $\dfrac{73}{648}$.
skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes
Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Calculate the probability that Barbie’s score exceeds Ken’s score.

solutions.latex:
Sums of 8 on the table: $(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)$, which is 5 of the 36 equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{score }8)=\dfrac{5}{36}$$

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
The two throws are independent.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both score }8) &= \dfrac{5}{36}\cdot\dfrac{5}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{1296} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
The table is symmetric about the sum 7, so $P(2)=P(12)$, $P(3)=P(11)$, and so on. The sums $2$ to $6$ each have a matching sum from $12$ down to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= 2\left[P(2\ \&\ 2)+P(3\ \&\ 3)+P(4\ \&\ 4)+P(5\ \&\ 5)+P(6\ \&\ 6)\right]+P(7\ \&\ 7) \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{1^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{2^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{3^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{4^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{5^2}{36^2}\right]+\dfrac{6^2}{36^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(55)+36}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{146}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{73}{648} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $P(\text{same})$ as a sum of the products $P(s)\cdot P(s)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
Barbie's score is greater than, less than, or equal to Ken's, so these probabilities sum to 1.
$$P(B>K)+P(K>B)+P(B=K)=1$$
The game is fair, so $P(B>K)=P(K>B)$ and $P(B=K)=\dfrac{73}{648}$ from part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} 2P(B>K)+\dfrac{73}{648} &= 1 \\ 2P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{648} \\ P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{1296} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $P(B>K)=P(K>B)$ with the sum of probabilities equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Describe a set of transformations to convert $f(x)=x^2$ into $g(x)=12+12x-3x^2$.

solutions.latex:
Reflect in the $x$-axis: replace $y$ by $-y$.
$$y=-x^2$$
Dilate vertically by a factor of 3: replace $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{3}$.
$$\dfrac{y}{3}=-x^2,\qquad y=-3x^2$$
Translate 2 units right: replace $x$ by $x-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -3(x-2)^2 \\ &= -3x^2+12x-12 \end{aligned}$$
Translate 24 units up: replace $y$ by $y-24$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-24 &= -3x^2+12x-12 \\ y &= 12+12x-3x^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ reflect in the $x$-axis, dilate vertically by a factor of 3, translate 2 units right, then 24 units up.

parts.latex: Using a graph or otherwise determine how many real solutions there are to the equation $\sqrt{x}=(x-3)(x-1)(x+2)$.
skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

solutions.latex:
The solutions are the intersections of $y=\sqrt{x}$ (for $x\ge0$) and $y=(x-3)(x-1)(x+2)$.

The cubic has $x$-intercepts $-2,\ 1,\ 3$ and, at $x=0$, $y=(-3)(-1)(2)=6$.

For $0\le x\le1$: at $x=0$ the cubic ($6$) is above $\sqrt{x}$ ($0$), and at $x=1$ it is below ($0<1$), so the graphs cross once.

For $1\le x\le3$: the cubic is $\le0$, below $\sqrt{x}$, so they do not meet.

For $x>3$: the cubic is below $\sqrt{x}$ at $x=3$ ($0<\sqrt{3}$) and above it at $x=4$ ($18>2$), so the graphs cross once.

Two points of intersection, therefore two solutions.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $e^x(x^2-5x)$?

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=x^2-5x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=2x-5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= (x^2-5x)e^x+e^x(2x-5) \\ &= e^x(x^2-5x+2x-5) \\ &= e^x(x^2-3x-5) \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) crossing the x-axis at -3, 0 and 4 with the area between curve and axis shaded on [-3,0] and [0,4]

solutions.latex:
From $x=-3$ to $x=0$ the curve is below the $x$-axis, so $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,dx<0$ and the shaded area there is $-\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,dx$.

From $x=0$ to $x=4$ the curve is above the $x$-axis, so the shaded area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}f(x)\,dx$.
$$\text{Shaded area}=\int_{0}^{4}f(x)\,dx-\int_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,dx$$
This is option C. Options A and D give the net signed area, and B assumes symmetry.

parts.latex: The value of $\log_8 4$ is

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$ with $c=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_8 4 &= \dfrac{\log_2 4}{\log_2 8} \\ &= \dfrac{\log_2 2^2}{\log_2 2^3} \\ &= \dfrac{2\log_2 2}{3\log_2 2} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $(x^3+\ln 2)^4$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[g(x)\right]^4=4\left[g(x)\right]^3\cdot g'(x)$, where $g(x)=x^3+\ln 2$ and $g'(x)=3x^2$ ($\ln 2$ is a constant).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+\ln 2)^4 &= 4(x^3+\ln 2)^3\cdot 3x^2 \\ &= 12x^2\left(x^3+\ln 2\right)^3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What values of $k$ result in $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin(kx)\,dx=0$, where $k$ is an integer?

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of one cycle of sin(kx) with period 2pi/k

solutions.latex:
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$$
\exfigure{161_q8_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}\sin(kx)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{\cos(kx)}{k}\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{1-\cos(k\pi)}{k} \end{aligned}$$

Let $u=e^x$, so $2e^{2x}-7e^x+3=0$ becomes a quadratic in $u$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= 2x\ln x+x \end{aligned}$$
When $x=e$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2e\ln e+e \\ &= 2e\cdot 1+e \\ &= 3e \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the gradient is $m=3e$.

figures.cap: graphs of y=sin x and y=sqrt3 cos x on [0,2pi] meeting at A and B with region between them shaded

solutions.latex:
Dividing both sides by $\cos x$ (which is not $0$ at a solution):
$$\tan x=\sqrt{3}$$
The acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\tan x>0$ in the first and third quadrants.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$

Both points lie on $y=\sin x$.

When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$y=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$\therefore A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

When $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &= -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore B\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
criteria: Finds one point correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Between $A$ and $B$ the graph of $y=\sin x$ is above $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left(-\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)-\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a power and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \\ y' &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot 4x \\ &= 6x\sqrt{2x^2+1} \end{aligned}$$

From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}$, so $\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}$ is a primitive of $6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\int_0^2 x\sqrt{2x^2+1}\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{6}\int_0^2 6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\left\{9^{\frac{3}{2}}-1^{\frac{3}{2}}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\{27-1\} \\ &= \dfrac{26}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: i

figures.cap: region bounded by y=sec^2 x, y=2cot x and the axes, shaded, with intercepts 1 and pi/2

solutions.latex:
For $y=\sec^2 x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sec^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
For $y=2\cot x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{1} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Both give $y=2$, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$ lies on both curves.
criteria: Verifies one curve, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \cot x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. The upper boundary of the region is $y=\sec^2 x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $y=2\cot x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^2 x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cot x\,dx$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$ from part (ii):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+2\Big[\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan 0+2\left[\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= 1-0+2\left[\ln 1-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right] \\ &= 1+2\left[0-\ln 2^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right] \\ &= 1+\ln 2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Second integral was $\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,dx$ (curve $y=\cot x$), giving $1+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2$; the curve is $y=2\cot x$, so it is now $\int 2\cot x\,dx$ and the area is $1+\ln 2$.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the second integral omitted the factor 2 of $y=2\cot x$; the area is $1+\ln 2$, not $1+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2$.

Consider the function $y=\left(x^2+1\right)e^{-x}$.

The first derivative and second derivatives of this function are:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-x}(x^2-4x+3)$ (You DO NOT need to show these).

parts.label: ii

solutions.latex:
Stationary points are where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$-e^{-x}(1-x)^2=0$$
Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=\left(1^2+1\right)e^{-1}=\dfrac{2}{e}$.

At $x=1$ the second derivative is $0$, so the second derivative test does not decide the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-1}\left(1^2-4(1)+3\right)=0$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts3072_1}

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2\le0$: the gradient is negative on both sides of $x=1$.

$\therefore$ a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx$, expressing the answer in the form $\ln a$ for some constant $a$.

solutions.latex:
The numerator $e^x+1$ is the derivative of the denominator $e^x+x$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$ applies with $f(x)=e^x+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln|e^x+x|\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= \ln|e^{\ln 4}+\ln 4|-\ln|e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln|4+\ln 4|-\ln|2+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4+\ln 4}{2+\ln 2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Using $\ln 4=2\ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{4+2\ln 2}{2+\ln 2}\right) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2(2+\ln 2)}{2+\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution of limits, or equivalent merit

By the symmetry of the graphs about $(\pi,0)$, the two shaded regions have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(2\sin x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right)dx \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Both graphs have the same shape each side of $x=\pi$, so the area is twice the area for $0\le x\le\pi$. For even $n$, $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}m\sin x\,dx \\ &= 2m\Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2m\left(-\cos\pi+\cos 0\right) \\ &= 2m(1+1) \\ &= 4m \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f'(x)=x^2+kx$.

The line $y=2x+1$ is a tangent to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at the point where $x=-1$.

Find $f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
The tangent has gradient $2$ at $x=-1$, so $f'(-1)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-1)^2+k\times(-1) &= 2 \\ 1-k &= 2 \\ k &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=x^2-x$. Integrate to find $f(x)$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$$
The tangent touches the curve where $x=-1$, so $f(-1)=2(-1)+1=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &= \dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}+C \\ -1 &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+C \\ C &= -\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}$$

questions.stem: Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that on the 5$^{\text{th}}$ Sunday of training, she runs 11 km.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find a simplified expression for length of her training run on the $n$th Sunday.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: On the $n$th Sunday, Helga runs 43 km. Find the value of $n$.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the total distance she runs on Sundays, in 15 weeks of training.
skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The lengths form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=3$ and common difference $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_5 &= 3+(5-1)\times 2 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 11$ (adding $2$ each time).

So on the $5^{\text{th}}$ Sunday she runs $11$ km.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=3$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= 3+(n-1)\times 2 \\ &= 2n+1 \end{aligned}$$

Put $T_n=43$ using $T_n=2n+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2n+1 &= 43 \\ 2n &= 42 \\ n &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

The sum of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, with $a=3$, $d=2$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 3+(15-1)\times 2\right) \\ &= 255 \end{aligned}$$
So she runs $255$ km in total.
criteria: Substitutes into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.55$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.6$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(A\cup B)$.
skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Two events are independent if $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$.
$$P(B\mid A)=0.6 \ne 0.55=P(B)$$
$\therefore$ $A$ and $B$ are not independent.

Use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. First find $P(A\cap B)$ from the conditional probability.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= P(B\mid A)\times P(A) \\ &= 0.6\times 0.4 \\ &= 0.24 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= 0.4+0.55-0.24 \\ &= 0.71 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For what values of $x$, in the interval $0\le x\le 2\pi$, does the line $y=-1$ intersect the graph of $y=2\cos 3x$?

solutions.latex:
Set the function equal to $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 3x &= -1 \\ \cos 3x &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$3x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Since $0\le x\le 2\pi$, we need $0\le 3x\le 6\pi$, so add $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ to these angles.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+4\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+4\pi \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The next angle, $\dfrac{20\pi}{3}$, is greater than $6\pi$, so it is too big. Divide by $3$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{9}$$
criteria: Finds the first angles for $3x$, $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=3x-\sin x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that $f(x)\ge 0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.
skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
A function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= 3(-x)-\sin(-x) \\ &= -3x+\sin x \\ &= -(3x-\sin x) \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $f(x)$ is an odd function.

$f(x)$ is odd, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin and the area from $-\pi$ to $0$ equals the area from $0$ to $\pi$.
$$A=2\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left[\left(\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}+\cos\pi\right)-(0+\cos 0)\right] \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}-2\right] \\ &= 3\pi^2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=(3\pi^2-4)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes the integral using symmetry, $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A ship ($S$) leaves Port ($P$) travelling on a bearing of $072^\circ$.

After travelling 25 kilometres, the ship is due South of a lighthouse ($L$).

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $316^\circ$.

\exfigure{162_q13_2}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle PSL=64^\circ$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Calculate the distance $LS$ from the ship to the lighthouse at this time.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

figures.cap: diagram of ships course P to S with bearings 72 and 316 degrees, lighthouse L due north of the 25 km point
solution sketch: the ship diagram marked up with the angles 44 and 72 inside the triangle and 44 at S

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{162_q13_s1}

The bearing of $L$ from $S$ is $316^\circ$, so $L$ is $360^\circ-316^\circ=44^\circ$ west of north from $S$.

The north lines at $P$ and $S$ are parallel, so co-interior angles give the angle between north at $S$ and $SP$.
$$180^\circ-72^\circ=108^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PSL &= 108^\circ-44^\circ \\ &= 64^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave only '360-316=44' and '180-72-44=64'; the reasons (co-interior angles between parallel north lines) were added by us. Solution figure 162_q13_s1 kept.

solutions.latex:
Let $M$ be the point due south of $L$, where the ship had travelled $25$ km, so $MS=4$ km. In $\triangle LMS$:
$$\angle LMS=72^\circ,\qquad \angle MLS=44^\circ$$
$\angle LMS=72^\circ$ because $LM$ is a north line and $S$ is on bearing $072^\circ$ from $M$. $\angle MLS=44^\circ$ because $LS$ is $44^\circ$ from the south line $LM$ (the back bearing of $316^\circ$ is $136^\circ$). Use the sine rule.
$$\dfrac{LS}{\sin 72^\circ}=\dfrac{4}{\sin 44^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} LS &= \dfrac{4\sin 72^\circ}{\sin 44^\circ} \\ &= 5.5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the sine rule equation, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the sine rule equation; 1 for $5.5$ km
meta.format_note: Source gave only the sine rule line, with no triangle named. Triangle LMS (M due south of L) and the angle reasons were added by us; check M against the labels on the figure. Checked: 4 sin 72 / sin 44 = 5.476, so 5.5 km.

figures.cap: piecewise linear graph of f(x) from (0,0) to (1,2), flat to (3,2), dashed drop to (3,-1), flat to (4,-1), dashed rise to (4,2), then down to (6,0)

solutions.latex:
Split the area under the graph into regions, counting area below the $x$-axis as negative.

From $x=0$ to $x=3$ the region is a trapezium with parallel sides $3$ and $2$ and height $2$. From $x=3$ to $x=4$ the region is a $1\times 1$ rectangle below the axis. From $x=4$ to $x=6$ the region is a triangle with base $2$ and height $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{2}(3+2)-1\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Regions checked against the graph: trapezium (0 to 3) area 5, rectangle below axis -1, triangle (4 to 6) area 2.

solutions.latex:
Split the integral. From part (a) and the graph, $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=5-1=4$ (trapezium minus the rectangle below the axis).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4\left(f(x)-2\right)dx &= \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx-\int_0^4 2\,dx \\ &= 4-\left[2x\right]_0^4 \\ &= 4-(2\times 4-0) \\ &= -4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits the integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down. Value 4 checked against the graph: 5 - 1.

solutions.latex:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a)$, with $f(6)=0$ and $f(5)=1$ read from the graph.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_5^6 f'(x)\,dx&=\Big[f(x)\Big]_5^6\\&=f(6)-f(5)\\&=0-1\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Values f(6)=0 and f(5)=1 are read from the figure in the question; not checked against the figure here.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Expand the integrand, then integrate each term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int\cos x\sin^2 x\,dx\\&=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C\end{aligned}$$
The second integral has the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=\sin x$, $n=2$.
$$\therefore\ \int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C$$
criteria: Expands the integrand, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for expanding the integrand; 1 for $\sin x$; 1 for $-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C$

parts.latex:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$S_n=3n^2-17n$, where $n>0$. Find an expression for the $n$th term of the series.

solutions.latex:
For any series, the $n$th term is the difference of consecutive sums, $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=S_n-S_{n-1}\\&=3n^2-17n-\left[3(n-1)^2-17(n-1)\right]\\&=3n^2-17n-3\left(n^2-2n+1\right)+17n-17\\&=3n^2-17n-3n^2+6n-3+17n-17\\&=6n-20\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_n=6n-20$$

meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: T_1=S_1=-14=6-20.

questions.stem:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $P_0=2500$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$. (Answer correct to four decimal places).

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If the population continues to decrease in this manner, what will be the expected population in May 2024? Answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ the population is $P=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}2500&=P_0e^{-k\cdot 0}\\&=P_0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_0=2500$$

In May 2014, $t=10$ and $P=1750$, with $P_0=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}1750&=2500e^{-10k}\\\dfrac{7}{10}&=e^{-10k}\\\ln\dfrac{7}{10}&=-10k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{7}{10}\\&=0.0357\ \text{(to 4 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $1750=2500e^{-10k}$; 1 for $k=0.0357$ (only the first mark is circled in the scan)
meta.format_note: Source scan circled only the first mark; rubric rewritten top-down. Checked: -ln(0.7)/10 = 0.035667.

solutions.latex:
May 2024 is $t=20$. Since $e^{-10k}=\dfrac{7}{10}$, we have $e^{-20k}=\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2500e^{-20k}\\&=2500\times 0.49\\&=1225\ \text{parrots}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the substitution with $t=20$; 1 for 1225 (follow through from the previous answer)
meta.marker_note: Follow through from the answer to part (b) is accepted.
meta.format_note: Source skipped the value of k; working completed using e^{-10k}=7/10. Checked: 2500e^{-0.714} = 1224.9, rounds to 1225.

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a shaded sector in a circle with radius $r$ and centre $O$.

The sector subtends an angle of $\theta$ at the centre of the circle.

The area of the sector is $49\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{162_q14_2}

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$ and hence show that the minimum perimeter of the sector will occur when the arc length of the sector is equal to the diameter of the circle.

figures.cap: circle with centre O and a shaded sector of radius r and angle theta

solutions.latex:
The sector area is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta=49$.
$$\begin{aligned}r^2\theta&=98\\\theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is two radii plus the arc $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2r+r\theta\\&=2r+r\cdot\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\&=2r+98r^{-1}\\\dfrac{dP}{dr}&=2-98r^{-2}\\&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}&=0\\2r^2&=98\\r^2&=49\end{aligned}$$
Since $r>0$, $r=7$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=196r^{-3}=\dfrac{196}{r^3}$$
When $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{343}=\dfrac{4}{7}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

Then the arc length is
$$r\theta=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14=2\times 7.$$
$\therefore$ the perimeter is a minimum when the arc length equals the diameter of the circle.

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$; 1 for $P=2r+98r^{-1}$; 1 for $r=7$ (as $r>0$) from $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$; 1 for arc length $=14=2\times 7$
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: 196/343 = 4/7 = 0.571.

questions.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of v against t: downward parabola from v=4 at t=0, crossing the t-axis at t=2, with the area from 0 to 3 shaded

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$ is a concave-down parabola, so its maximum is at the turning point, where $v'(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v'(t)&=-4t+2\\0&=-4t+2\\t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ s}$$
criteria: Recognises the maximum occurs at the turning point, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for recognising the maximum occurs at the turning point; 1 for $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2t^2+2t+4&=0\\-2\left(t^2-t-2\right)&=0\\-2(t-2)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ or $t=-1$; since $t\ge 0$, $t=2$.

Integrate the velocity to find the position.
$$x(t)=\int v\,dt=-\dfrac{2t^3}{3}+t^2+4t+C$$
Initially $x(0)=4$, so $C=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(2)&=-\dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}+2^2+4\times 2+4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is }\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$
criteria: Integrates to find $x(t)$, or equivalent merit
Factorises and solves $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for factorising and solving $v=0$; 1 for integrating to get $x(t)$; 1 for $x(2)=\dfrac{32}{3}$ m
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: -16/3+4+8+4 = 32/3.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=2$ (part (b)), so the distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, counting the part below the axis as positive.

\exfigure{162_q15_s1}

$$\int_0^2 v\,dt+\left|\int_2^3 v\,dt\right|$$
Using the antiderivative $F(t)=-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3+t^2+4t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance}&=F(2)-F(0)+\big|F(3)-F(2)\big|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}-0+\left|3-\dfrac{20}{3}\right|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{11}{3}\\&=\dfrac{31}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is }\dfrac{31}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the two integrals, the second in absolute value, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the two integrals (second in absolute value); 1 for the evaluation
meta.format_note: Checked: F(2)=20/3, F(3)=3, v(3)=-8 so the particle is moving left on (2,3).

parts.latex:
The function $y=f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{for } -3\le x\le 0\\ -x^2+1 & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$

Determine whether $y=f(x)$ is both continuous $\textbf{and}$ differentiable at $x=0$.

Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.

solutions.latex:
Check continuity at $x=0$: both pieces must give the same value.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f(0)&=1\\\text{right: } -0^2+1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

Check the gradients from each side. Each piece is differentiable for all real $x$ on its own.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f'(x)&=0\\\text{right: } y&=-x^2+1\\y'&=-2x,\ \text{so } y'(0)=0\end{aligned}$$
The gradients agree ($0=0$), so $f$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is both continuous and differentiable at } x=0$$
criteria: Shows continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give $1$), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for showing continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give 1); 1 for showing differentiability (both gradients are 0)

questions.stem:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the height of the water at 12 am?

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, in the domain $[0,16]$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
A family decides to go on a picnic by the river from 12 pm to 2 pm.

It is only safe to swim in the river if the height of the water is less than 4 metres.

When is the earliest time the family can swim in the river after 12 pm?

Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of h(t) over [0,16]: sine curve with midline 5, maximum 7 and minimum 3, period 8

solutions.latex:
At 12 am, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h(0)&=5+2\sin 0\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Shows the vertical transformation (midline $5$, amplitude $2$) or the horizontal transformation (period $8$), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the vertical transformation (midline 5, amplitude 2); 1 for the horizontal transformation (period 8)
meta.format_note: Sketch is the existing figure 162_q15_s2; not checked against the working here. Rubric rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
The water is safe when $h<4$. Find when $h=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=4\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{4}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{23\pi}{6},\ \ldots$$
Multiplying by $\dfrac{4}{\pi}$:
$$t=\dfrac{14}{3},\ \dfrac{22}{3},\ \dfrac{38}{3},\ \dfrac{46}{3},\ \ldots$$
At 12 pm ($t=12$), $h=5>4$, and the first solution with $t\ge 12$ is $t=\dfrac{38}{3}=12\dfrac{2}{3}$ hours. After this the height is below $4$ m.
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 12{:}40\text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds the angles, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{2}$; 1 for the angles; 1 for 12:40 pm
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: sin(19*pi/6)=-1/2 and h is below 4 on (38/3, 46/3).

parts.latex: Which of the quadratic equations has 2 distinct real and rational roots?
skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
Real rational roots need $\Delta=b^2-4ac$ to be a positive perfect square.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{A: } \Delta&=(-3)^2-4(-1)(5)=29\ \text{(not a square)}\\\text{B: } \Delta&=(-1)^2-4(4)(-5)=81=9^2\\\text{C: } \Delta&=0-4(-1)(-4)=-16\ \text{(no real roots)}\\\text{D: } \Delta&=0\ \text{(one repeated root)}\end{aligned}$$
Only B has $\Delta$ positive and a perfect square, so B has 2 distinct real rational roots.
